A read-only pre-audit raises and counts any plaintext key before altering the column, so an installation with a key is told to re-save it rather than having it copied into a column that now claims to be encrypted.

Against the real migration graph: an envelope round-trips with no loss, an unconfigured installation stores null rather than an empty key, the stored value is the envelope and not a key, and the column is no longer text.

findings.title: A locale-dependent hash is persisted and load-bearing
findings.summary: **Confirmed and fixed.** `canonicalize` sorted object keys with `localeCompare` and `fingerprint()` wrote the resulting digest to a `notNull` column that `drizzle-reporter-ingestion.ts` reads back to choose `duplicate` versus `conflict`. The defect is not that the hash is unstable across *runs* — it is that it is unstable across **machines and versions**, and the value it produced is persisted. A different ICU build, a different Node version, or a different `LANG` reorders the keys, produces a different digest for a byte-identical result, and a legitimate duplicate becomes a conflict. Keys are now ordered by UTF-16 code unit, which is exactly what `JSON.stringify` uses for object keys — so the canonical form is now a plain serialization of the object rather than a serialization in whatever order the host's collation tables produce. The comparison is written out rather than delegated, so it cannot vary with a locale option, a collation table or an ICU version. **On the tests, and one honest weakness.** The two witnesses that pin the ordering — case-sensitive keys, and punctuation — both fail against `localeCompare`, verified by reverting the line. A third case changes `LANG` and asserts the digest holds, and it passes either way: `localeCompare` without an explicit locale reads ICU's default, which is fixed when the process starts, so an in-process `LANG` change cannot move it. That test is a weaker guard than it looks and is kept only because it states the invariant in the terms an operator would; the two ordering witnesses are what actually detect the defect. One case was also cut on the way: bare integer-like keys (`10` and `2`) turned out to be the wrong witness, because JavaScript enumerates array-index-like keys in ascending *numeric* order before any comparator runs. That is a property of the input, not of collation, and asserting on it would have pinned behaviour unrelated to P-23. **What this does not do, and the plan is right about it:** it changes the hash, so every fingerprint stored under the old ordering is now stale. A row whose keys ICU and code units order differently will recompute to a different digest and be read as a new result. W7's pre-audit must recompute every stored fingerprint under the new ordering and report which rows would flip before this deploys; if any do, that is repair work, scoped separately, and not something to discover in production. What is fixed here is the class — the next hash written is stable for the life of the data.
findings.confirmedBy: W7.5. Confirmed by reading `policy.ts:72,83` exactly as described.

evidence.asserts: `canonicalize` sorts object keys with `compareCodeUnits` rather than `localeCompare`, and the comparison is written out explicitly so no runtime default — locale, sensitivity option, collation table or ICU version — can change it.

`matches JSON.stringify for case-sensitive keys` and `matches JSON.stringify where digits and punctuation are involved` both fail when the sort reverts to `localeCompare`; `is unaffected by the ambient locale` states the invariant in operator terms and is documented as the weaker guard it is.

`ignores the order the keys arrived in` and `still canonicalizes nested objects and array elements` confirm the fix did not weaken canonicalization itself — the recursion into array elements is what an ordering-only test would miss.

findings.title: The AI gateway retries statuses that are fatal by definition
findings.summary:
`kilo-gateway.ts:30` opens the try block and the fatal throw at `:45-47` is inside it, so the blanket catch at `:48-50` swallows it on attempts 0 and 1. A 401 is attempted three times.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `kilo-gateway.ts:30,45-50`. The fatal-status `throw` is **inside** the
`try` whose `catch` swallows it, so a 401 or 400 is issued three times instead of
once. `gateways.test.ts:128-136` exercises exactly this path with a 400 and only
asserts the eventual rejection — it never counts fetcher calls, so it passes over the
bug. The same catch also swallows genuine network errors, which is intended for
retries but makes the fatal throw indistinguishable from a retryable one.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A status that will never change is asked once.

The fatal-status `throw` sat **inside** the `try` whose `catch` swallowed it, so a
401 or a 400 was indistinguishable from a transport error and was issued three times.
The `catch` cannot tell them apart because both arrive as a thrown value; the
distinction is made *before* the throw, by the status, and the two are now separate
paths.

The restructure records the failure and breaks out of the retry loop, so a non-retryable
status is never retried and a genuine transport error still is. The old test asserted
only that `listModels` eventually rejected — which is true whether the request is made
once or three times, so it passed over the bug. **Counting the calls is the only
assertion that can see this defect**, and the new case does exactly that.

The counterweight matters as much: a separate case asserts a 503 *is* retried twice and
that a thrown network error *is* retried twice, because a fix that simply stopped
retrying would satisfy the row by making the gateway useless during exactly the outage
the retry exists for.

evidence.asserts: Fragments of one tool call are merged by `index` with **strings concatenated** and other values replaced, emitted once at `finish_reason` with the accumulator cleared; the provider's `index` is dropped from the assembled call as a transport detail. The OpenAI-shaped `usage` block is *mapped* onto the read model and `totalTokens` is computed when the provider omits it. A non-retryable status is recorded and breaks out of the retry loop rather than being thrown from inside the `try` that swallows transport errors.

Twelve reintroduced defects were each observed turning the suite red: the dropped tail, the unreleased reader, flat-appended fragments, replacing rather than concatenating string fragments, re-emitting on every `finish_reason`, the usage cast, the missing `totalTokens`, the dropped tool list, the removed `signal` parameter, the throwing line parser, the unbounded request, and the retried fatal status. One pre-existing assertion was **rewritten rather than kept**: it asserted that a malformed frame aborts the stream, which is the behaviour G-7 says is wrong.

findings.title: Five lease, transition and subscription defects on the execution path
findings.summary: `runner-control.ts:55` takes `_leaseId` and discards the caller's lease id; `:72-73` hashes `JSON.stringify` directly, so duplicate detection is key-order dependent; `orchestration-service.ts:47-49` lets an illegal `canTransition` fall through and returns a 200-shaped job with `cancelRequested` set; `events.ts:197` discards a `writeSSE` promise with no rejection handler; `events.ts:86,93,107` registers `onAbort(finish)` before assigning `unsubscribe`, so an abort in that window calls a no-op and the real subscription leaks. **All five confirmed on 2026-09-28. Three are defects; two are not, and the reasons are the interesting part of this row.** **The lease id was never recorded, so it could never be checked.** `acquire` bound it to `_leaseId` and the lease record held no id field at all, which means `acceptEvent` compared the runner and the fencing token and nothing else: an event naming a lease this service never issued was accepted, provided the runner was right and the token was current. The token orders *attempts*; the id says which *grant* inside the current attempt, and a record that omits it cannot answer the second question. The record now holds the id and the comparison is there. **The key-order hash made a genuine retry look like a second event.** Two events with the same content and different key insertion order hash differently, so a runner that retried after a timeout — having rebuilt its payload — was answered `conflict`. That is the expensive wrong answer: the caller cannot distinguish it from a real duplicate-sequence conflict, so the only available recovery is to re-claim the job. The comparison is now over a canonical serialisation. **The fall-through returned a 200-shaped job that had not moved.** `if (canTransition(...)) state = 'cancelled'; cancelRequested = true; return job;` — so cancelling something already finished answered 200 with a well-formed envelope whose state was unchanged, and the only way to notice was to read it closely. Fixed in wave 1.3, with the state machine, because fixing the machine and not its only production caller would have left the new predicate unused. **Two claims did not survive being tested, and both are recorded as refuted rather than as fixed.** `events.ts:197` was `void stream.writeSSE(...)` with no rejection handler, and the claim was an unhandled rejection — i.e. a way to take the process down. In the pinned Hono, `writeSSE` *resolves* after the client has gone, because cancelling the readable side of a TransformStream does not error the writable side. A test asserting an `unhandledRejection` was written, and it passed with the defect present; a second version asserting a teardown count also passed unchanged. `void` is this tree's sanctioned floating-promise escape hatch (`eslint.config.js:128-132`), so lint did not object either. **The abort-window leak at `:86,93,107` cannot happen, and the row's own file says why three lines later:** the `await` an abort can be delivered during is the refetch frame's `writeSSE`, and `if (closed || stream.aborted) return` immediately after it closes the window — there is no await between that check and the assignment, so no abort can be delivered in between. The existing test that a client disconnect unsubscribes was already green. Reordering code that has a reason to be in that order to defend against a leak that cannot occur would make the next reader hunt for a fourth teardown point that is not there; the comment at `events.ts:86` now says the window is closed, so the claim is answered where someone would otherwise repeat it. **Three fixed, two refuted, and the refutations are the part worth keeping.**
findings.confirmedBy: Findings-remediation wave 1.4. Read all four files and traced every claim. Three reproduced; the two `events.ts` claims were each turned into a test first, and neither test could distinguish the defect from the fix — which is the evidence that they are not defects.

evidence.asserts: The lease record holds the `leaseId` it was granted, and `acceptEvent` compares it. An event naming a lease that was never issued is `conflict` and nothing is stored — before the fix it was accepted whenever the runner and token matched.

A never-issued lease id is refused with nothing recorded; a retry whose payload keys are in the other order is `duplicate` rather than `conflict`; a genuinely different event at the same sequence is still `conflict`, so canonicalisation did not make the comparison weaker; and a superseded token after a re-lease is refused, which is what distinguishes the token from the id.

One `canonicalJson`, replacing three byte-identical copies. It sorts object keys, preserves array order — the one place where being order-insensitive would be a bug — and drops `undefined` properties so a spread payload has the shape of the one it copied. A fourth copy in `runner-control.ts` is what forced the extraction.

The rule itself, including that the canonical form differs from `JSON.stringify` (so the test cannot pass on a serialiser that does nothing) and that `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` do not. `Uint8Array` is hashed as bytes rather than as an object, which the three copies each got right and none of them said why.

An illegal cancellation is refused with `INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION` and a 409 rather than answered as a success, and the record is untouched — the fall-through this closes is the `orchestration-service.ts:47-49` half.
Cancelling twice is refused the second time, and `listJobs()` afterwards equals the job as it was after the first cancel — so the refusal did not mutate anything on its way out.

Unchanged behaviour, and that is the finding: the two `events.ts` claims in this row are not defects. A direct probe of the pinned Hono shows `writeSSE` resolving after the client cancels, and the `if (closed || stream.aborted) return` at line 106 closes the abort window the row names.

findings.title: Every deployment records a dev installation key
findings.summary:
`index.ts:246` passes `displayPrefix: 'dev'` unconditionally to `ensureBootstrap`, `:71` hardcodes the installation UUID `00000000-0000-4000-8000-000000000001`, and `:231` declares `let sessionBackend;` with no type.

**Two citation corrections, recorded because both point at the wrong line.** The real lines are
**`:251`** for `displayPrefix: 'dev'` and **`:236`** for `let sessionBackend;`.
`findings:check` fails a `fixed` row whose evidence path no longer exists, and a fixer
following `:246` finds the wrong statement.

**Reading taken: A (mislabel), stated explicitly as issue #9 requires. Reading B is recorded as
its own follow-up row, P-72b, and is NOT closed by this change.**

The two readings were: **A** — a hardcoded cosmetic label lands on a production row; **B** —
`ensureBootstrap` is called in production *at all*, deriving a bootstrap credential on every
boot, and the fix is to gate the call on `nodeEnv` or an explicit opt-in.

**A was chosen because it is free and B is not.** A is zero behavioural risk, because
**`display_prefix` is write-only**: `findUsable`
(`installation-key-repository.ts:139-153`) selects only `keyHash, revokedAt, expiresAt`, and
no API route, no `apps/web` code, no audit row and no UI reads it. The credential's real
identity is `hashCredential(authCookieSecret, installationKey)`, which this does not touch. B
changes what production does on first boot, and shipping that inside a good-first-issue PR
would put a production-behaviour change through a review sized for a label.

**What was verified before choosing, and it bears on the choice:** `ensureBootstrap` is at
`installation-key-repository.ts:84-123` with four call sites, and **no test anywhere asserted
the literal `'dev'`** — which is exactly why a hardcoded mislabel could sit in a composition
root indefinitely. There is also **no config surface for it**: `AppConfig` has no
`installationId` and no prefix field, and the only install-adjacent field is
`installationApiKey` ← `AUTOMATE_API_KEY`. So the label had nowhere to come from but a literal.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.** `bootstrapDisplayPrefix(config)` returns `config.nodeEnv`, and the call
site passes it. The label is now `development` / `test` / `production` rather than `dev` — the
full name costs nothing on a write-only column and reads unambiguously beside it. **`let
sessionBackend;` is now declared `DrizzleAuthSessionBackend | undefined`**, which is what it
already inferred, so `noImplicitAny` was never the reason; an unannotated `let` is one refactor
away from being the reason, and `undefined` is the meaningful half of that union.

**Calibration:** the helper was changed back to returning the literal `'dev'` and all three
assertions were observed red, including the one that matters — *does not label a production
deployment as a development key* — before being restored.

evidence.asserts: `bootstrapDisplayPrefix` derives the label from `config.nodeEnv` rather than hardcoding it, and the docstring records that Reading B was deliberately not taken.

A production deployment is not labelled with a development key; the development label is still a development one; and every value in the `nodeEnv` union produces a non-empty, space-free prefix, so a fourth environment added to the schema cannot silently inherit the wrong one.
`ensureBootstrap` is called with `bootstrapDisplayPrefix(runtimeConfig)`, and `let sessionBackend` carries an explicit `DrizzleAuthSessionBackend | undefined` annotation.

findings.title: Every boot derives a bootstrap installation key, in production included
findings.summary:
**Split out of P-72 on 2026-09-28. This is Reading B, and P-72's fix deliberately did not take it.**

P-72's title is *"Every deployment records a dev installation key"*, which supports two readings.
P-72 took the narrow one — a hardcoded cosmetic label on a production row — because
`display_prefix` is **write-only** and renaming it is behaviourally free. The wider one is this
row, and it is the more consequential of the two.

`index.ts` calls `ensureBootstrap({ installationId, keyHash, displayPrefix })`
**unconditionally whenever a database exists** — not only in development. So every production
boot derives a bootstrap credential from `hashCredential(authCookieSecret, installationKey)`
and inserts a row. P-72's fix changed only the label on that row; the derivation and the insert
are untouched.

**Why it is still open rather than fixed:** gating the call on `nodeEnv` or an explicit opt-in
changes what production does on first boot. A deployment that relies on the bootstrap key would
find it absent, and the failure mode is an installation that cannot authenticate — not a
degraded label. That needs its own design, its own migration story for installations already
bootstrapped, and its own review.

**What a fix has to answer, and none of it is answered here:**
- What a production deployment uses **instead**, on first boot, with no database row.
- Whether an installation that already has a usable key is unaffected — `ensureBootstrap`
  returns the existing hash at `installation-key-repository.ts:91-92`, so the gate can be
  additive without stranding anyone, and that is the property to build on.
- What the operator-facing behaviour is when bootstrap is unavailable: refusing to start is a
  very different decision from starting without it.
- Whether `AUTOMATE_ALLOW_DEV_SECRETS`-style explicit opt-in (the pattern
  `startup-policy.ts` already uses) is the right shape, or whether production needs a
  genuinely separate provisioning path.
findings.resolution: Production no longer derives an installation key. `mayDeriveInstallationKey` is false for `production` and true elsewhere, and a production boot with a database and no `AUTOMATE_INSTALLATION_KEY` throws with a message naming the variable and saying what deriving one would have cost. Previously `ensureBootstrap` ran on every boot that had a database and inserted a row whose credential is `hashCredential(authCookieSecret, installationKey)` — so a production deployment grew a credential nobody chose, derived from a default that is in the repository, on first boot, silently. P-72 renamed the label on that row and left the derivation, which is why the two were separate rows. The proof is that the whole production-composition suite refused to boot until a synthetic installation key was added to its valid secrets; `index-production-composition.test.ts` now asserts the refusal directly.

evidence.asserts: `mayDeriveInstallationKey` returns false only in production, and `NO_INSTALLATION_KEY` names the variable rather than failing with a null hash.
The guard runs before `ensureBootstrap`, so a production boot with no key never reaches the insert.
A production composition with no `AUTOMATE_INSTALLATION_KEY` refuses with the message — and the rest of the suite passes one, which is what made the refusal visible before it was asserted.

findings.title: A failing outbox retention sweep is indistinguishable from a quiet one
findings.summary:
`outbox-retention.ts:13-18` swallows every error with `.catch(() => undefined)`, so the operator sees the same output whether the sweep ran and found nothing or the sweep never ran at all.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A failing retention sweep is now distinguishable from a quiet one, without losing
liveness.

The swallowing was deliberate and stays that way — a purge that throws must not stop
the next attempt, and the pre-existing test for exactly that still passes unchanged in
substance. What changed is that the `.catch` is no longer the *only* place the
outcome could be observed. It was: the function was 22 lines and that `.catch` was
the sole opportunity to notice anything. A sweep that had been failing every minute
for a week was therefore indistinguishable from a sweep that had purged nothing
because there was nothing to purge — and those are opposite problems with opposite
responses, both of which look identical from the outside.

The returned handle exposes `sweeps()`, `failures()` and `lastError()`. The last
of those is cleared on success rather than latching. That is the design decision
worth naming: a sticky "last error" answers "did this ever fail?", which is a
question about history, while the operator watching a retention job is asking "is it
failing now?" — and a flag that latches makes the second question unanswerable
without also reading a timestamp. One transient blip should not turn into a
permanently alarming dashboard, because a signal that is always on is a signal that
gets ignored.

evidence.asserts: The sweep returns a handle carrying `sweeps()`, `failures()` and `lastError()`. The `.catch(() => undefined)` that made a dead sweep indistinguishable from a quiet one is gone, while **liveness is deliberately preserved** — a failing purge does not stop the next attempt — and the failure is additionally routed to an injectable `onError` so it reaches whatever logging the deployment already has. `lastError()` is cleared on success rather than latching, because an operator watching a retention job is asking "is it failing now?", and a sticky flag answers "did this ever fail?" instead.

A sweep that fails every attempt records every failure and keeps the most recent error, and the pre-existing liveness case still holds — a purge that throws does not stop the next attempt. The counterweight case fails once then succeeds, and asserts the counters are `2`/`1` and that `lastError()` is **cleared**, so the field answers "is it broken right now?" rather than latching on history. Dropping the counters entirely, keeping the swallow, or making `lastError` sticky each turn the suite red.

findings.title: An unscoped KPI request answers with a confident all-zero 200
findings.summary:
`routes/reporting.ts:12-17` returns every metric as 0 when no `runId` is given. The body is shaped exactly like a real measurement, so a caller cannot tell an absence from a zero.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

An empty population no longer claims high confidence and verified evidence.

**A correction to the row, which does not weaken it.** The summary says the route
"returns every metric as 0". It does not: the rates are `null` and the quantiles are
`null`, with `numerator: 0` and `denominator: 0`. So the row's stated consequence —
a caller cannot tell an absence from a zero — was overstated, and a fix aimed at the
zeros would have changed nothing. The real defect is two levels up and worse: the
two *claims* attached to those honest nulls were false. `results.every(...)` over
`[]` is `true`, so `confidence` came out `'high'`; and `candidates.length === 0`
returned `'verified'`. An unscoped request was therefore reporting that it had high
confidence in verified evidence, measured from nothing.

That is the dangerous shape. A null rate reads as "no data" to anyone looking at the
number, so the number was doing its job — but a reader who trusts `confidence` and
`proofCeiling` instead, which is exactly what a dashboard does, is told the empty
set is the best possible reading of itself. Absent evidence has to be labelled as
absent, and the two fields exist to label it.

evidence.asserts: `resolveProofCeiling([])` returns `unknown`, not `verified`, and `confidence` carries a `results.length > 0` guard. Both mattered because the unscoped `GET /api/v1/reporting/kpis` route calls `calculateKpis([])` and returns a five-entry body shaped exactly like a real reading: `[].every(...)` is vacuously `true`, so the empty population was reported as `confidence: 'high'` and `proofCeiling: 'verified'`. An empty population is an absence of evidence and is now labelled as one.

Every metric from `calculateKpis([])` is asserted `null` with a zero denominator, `confidence: 'low'` and `proofCeiling: 'unknown'`, and a counterweight case asserts a genuinely complete population **still** reports `confidence: 'high'` / `proofCeiling: 'verified'` with `value: 1` — because satisfying the empty case by making the field meaningless would pass the first and be useless. Reverting either guard, or lowering `confidence` unconditionally, each turn the suite red.

findings.title: The canonical utilities are triplicated
findings.summary: `stable()` is byte-identical at `quality-gate.ts:42-51` and `drizzle-execution-store.ts:130-139`, with a third copy named `canonical()` at `in-memory-execution-store.ts:53-62`. `tokenMatches` and `normalizeArtifactKind` are each duplicated, the eight-element terminal array is inlined twice in the Drizzle store despite `isTerminalPhase` existing, and `isTerminalPhase` is itself duplicated at `phase-outcome.ts:66` and `types.ts:550`. **Confirmed on 2026-09-28, and all five are fixed — but two of the row’s framings did not survive being checked, and the corrections are the point.** The row lists five duplications and reads as five instances of tidiness. Two of them are not: the eight-element terminal array inlined twice in the Drizzle store, and `isTerminalPhase` duplicated across two modules, are *the same duplication seen from two ends*. The array is the body of the function, so fixing the first and the second is one change, and a reader counting five would spend the fifth somewhere that does not exist. **A second correction, which is a correction of my own error and is recorded because it nearly went in as a defect.** While extracting `normalizeArtifactKind` I read the two copies as divergent — the in-memory one appearing to return an unrecognised kind unchanged, which `artifacts_kind_check` would refuse. That reading was wrong: it came from a grep whose context lines spanned two files, and the two copies are byte-identical. `git show HEAD:apps/api/src/execution/in-memory-execution-store.ts` settles it. A file that claims a divergence which is not there is worse than a duplicated file, because the next reader goes looking for a store that classifies artifacts differently and does not find it. **What the extraction did find, and it is small and real.** `attachment` is one of the twelve values in `artifacts_kind_check` (`packages/db/src/schema/execution.ts:322`) and had no branch in the mapping, so it fell through to `other` — schema-valid and lossy, meaning the dashboard could not filter for the attachments it had stored. The case that found it is `artifact-kind.test.ts`’s totality assertion, which walks `ARTIFACT_KINDS` and requires every value to survive; it is the assertion a de-duplication earns rather than the one it starts with. **What each duplicate actually cost, since the row implies they cost the same.** `stable`/`canonical` and `tokenMatches` are the two that are load-bearing across a security and an identity boundary: three serialisers that must agree byte-for-byte, and a constant-time comparison duplicated into two stores so that a future edit can relax it in one. `normalizeArtifactKind` cost one real behaviour, above. The terminal array cost nothing today and would have cost a migration half, because the list of terminal phases lives in the database CHECK as well as here and the two halves of a migration do not fail together. **One module now, and its name is a decision.** `digest.ts` holds `canonicalJson`, `digestOf` and `tokenMatches`; `artifact-kind.ts` holds the mapping; `phase-outcome.ts` owns the terminal vocabulary and `types.ts` re-exports `isTerminalPhase` from it. `types.ts` could not simply import the logic without a cycle, and the direction that works is the one that says the vocabulary belongs with the logic rather than with the types — `phase-outcome.ts` imports `RunPhase` with `import type`, which erases, so the re-export is safe and the reasoning is written down at the import.
findings.confirmedBy: Findings-remediation wave 1.4. Read all five sites. Four are distinct defects and one is a duplicate of another; the mapping divergence the first pass of this fix believed in is refuted by `git show HEAD:apps/api/src/execution/in-memory-execution-store.ts`.

evidence.asserts: One `canonicalJson` replacing three byte-identical copies, plus `tokenMatches` replacing two. The serialiser sorts object keys, preserves array order — the one place where being order-insensitive would be a bug, since a digest that identifies execution steps must not say `[1,2]` and `[2,1]` are the same run — and drops `undefined` properties. `tokenMatches` keeps the length check ahead of `timingSafeEqual`, which throws on a mismatch, and the comment says the length is a constant rather than a secret.

The rule itself, including that the canonical form differs from `JSON.stringify` so the test cannot pass on a serialiser that does nothing, that `[1, 2]` and `[2, 1]` do not collide, that `undefined` and absent are the same shape, and that a `Uint8Array` is hashed as bytes rather than as an object.

One mapping for both stores, with the union of both copies plus the `attachment` branch the vocabulary test found missing. The fallback is `other` and the comment says why it is not a refusal: a reporter may ship evidence the platform has not been taught to label, and losing the upload loses the thing the product exists to keep.

Every value the mapping can return is in `ARTIFACT_KINDS` taken from the schema, so a kind added to the column and forgotten here fails a test rather than the first upload that uses it — and the totality case requires every kind in the vocabulary to survive unchanged, which is the assertion that found `attachment` falling through to `other`.

No private `tokenMatches`, no private `normalizeArtifactKind`, and no inlined eight-element terminal array: `cancelRun` and `retryRun` ask `isTerminalPhase`. The inlined array is what the row called inlined, and the two sites it named were the body of a function that already existed.
The same three copies are gone, and the file no longer imports `createHash` or `timingSafeEqual` — the compiler is what proves it, rather than a reviewer noticing.

`isTerminalPhase` is re-exported from `phase-outcome.ts` rather than holding a second eight-element array, so a migration that adds a terminal phase has one list to change in this module and one CHECK to change in the database — the two halves that do not fail together.

findings.title: collectSuite has no depth cap
findings.summary:
`routes/reporter.ts:400-452` recurses into `suite['suites']` at `:446-451`, so a self-nested `suites` array on an untrusted ingestion boundary overflows the stack. The reporter payload is attacker-controlled by construction.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.** The recursion into `suites` is capped at 32 levels and a deeper report
is refused.

**Two corrections to the row, and the second one changes where the bug actually lives.**

1. **A cycle is not reachable on this path, so a cycle guard is not the fix.** The row
says "a self-nested `suites` array". This body arrives through `JSON.parse`, and JSON
cannot express a reference back to an ancestor — `JSON.stringify` refuses to even
*produce* such a body. What is reachable is arbitrary **depth**: a body of nothing but
`{"suites":[{"suites":[ … ]}]}` nested as far as the upload size allows. An earlier
draft of this fix carried a visited-set for the cycle; it was dead code with an
untestable branch, and it was removed rather than shipped with a test that cannot fail.
The same reasoning was applied to github's `optionalField` and jira's `?? ''` earlier in
this programme.

2. **The converter is only reachable from the *multipart* branch.** `parseJsonUpload`
— and therefore `convertPlaywrightJsonToUpload` and `collectSuite` — is called from
exactly one place, `reporter.ts:351`, inside `if (contentType.includes('multipart/form-data'))`.
A plain `application/json` body goes straight to `ReporterUploadSchema.safeParse` at
`:371` and never touches the recursive code at all. The attack surface is therefore a
**file upload**, which is the ordinary way a reporter submits a report, and not the JSON
API a reader of the row would assume.

**`MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` does not mitigate this**, which is the part worth keeping in mind:
it bounds how *large* a body is, not how *deeply* it nests, and a small body of nested
`suites` is well within the 5 MiB limit. The old failure was
`RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded` — not a catchable refusal, so it took
down the request rather than answering it.

32 levels is far above any real report: Playwright nests one level per directory a spec
lives in, so even a monorepo with deep test trees is single-digit. The generous ceiling
costs nothing and refuses the shape that is a denial of service rather than a report.

**The first draft of the test posted `application/json` and would have passed over the
defect entirely** — it reached a different branch and "failed" for an unrelated reason.
That is the ledger's own F-8 trap ("a fix that cannot fail because the fixture did not
match what the code walks") recurring in a new place, and it is why the test now asserts
the multipart shape explicitly.

evidence.asserts: `collectSuite` carries a `depth` that is threaded into its recursive call and refuses a report nested past `MAX_SUITE_DEPTH` (32) with a message naming the limit. The cap is separate from `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` because a size bound does not bound depth, and a small body of nested `suites` is within the size limit. No cycle guard is present: it is unreachable through `JSON.parse` and would have been a branch that cannot fail.

A 200-level report uploaded as a **multipart file** is refused with 400, and a legitimately nested 8-level report is still accepted with 202 — the counterweight, without which a cap that rejected ordinary nesting would pass the first case and be useless. The upload is multipart because the Playwright converter is only reached from that branch; a JSON body would exercise a different path and pass over the defect.

findings.title: The event allowlist is now three hand-maintained copies
findings.summary:
The laundering fix landed, but the allowlist is hand-duplicated at `shared-contracts/schemas/execution.ts:459-470`, `apps/api/src/realtime/realtime-bus.ts:46-56` and `routes/execution/schemas.ts:194-205` — three places to forget an event name.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** Three hand-written allowlists, none derived: `shared-contracts/src/schemas/execution.ts:459-470`
(`RunEventTypeSchema`), `apps/api/src/realtime/realtime-bus.ts:46-56` (a parallel
union), and `apps/api/src/routes/execution/schemas.ts:194-205`
(`CANONICAL_EVENT_TYPES`). **Derivation is available and used elsewhere** —
`durable-realtime.ts:22,30` and `apps/web/src/lib/api.ts:540` both build from
`RunEventTypeSchema.options` — which is what makes these three the exception rather
than the rule. Drift is already live: `jobs.routes.ts:71-76` gates on
`CANONICAL_EVENT_TYPES` then casts to `CanonicalRealtimeEvent['type']`, so a name
added to the contract but not to the set is silently dropped from the bus while
remaining valid. The gate that could catch it,
`realtime/src/event-type-ownership.test.ts`, is scoped to the colon-style constants
and never sees the dot-style names.

**Two citation corrections, recorded because an implementer following them finds nothing.** This row
names `durable-realtime.ts:22,30` as a derivation precedent; the real file is
`durable-realtime-bus.ts`, and the `RunEventTypeSchema.options` derivation that
actually exists and matters as precedent is **`apps/web/src/lib/api.ts:540`**, where
the SSE subscription iterates `RunEventTypeSchema.options` rather than restating
them. The row's "drift is already live" is also corrected: all three lists hold the
same ten names in the same order today, so this is **latent, not live**.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28 — the fix is a compile error, not a runtime check.**

`CANONICAL_EVENT_TYPES` is now `ReadonlySet<RunEventType>` built from
`RunEventTypeSchema.options`, and `CanonicalRealtimeEvent['type']` is `RunEventType`
with the ten-name union deleted. The cast at `jobs.routes.ts:76` is gone, and that is
the enforcement: the cast existed *only* because the set was `Set<string>`.

One wrinkle the plan did not anticipate: typing the set alone is **not** sufficient.
`ReadonlySet<RunEventType>.has(string)` does not narrow, so removing the cast produced
`TS2322: Type 'string' is not assignable to type RunEventType`. The gate needs a type
predicate — `isCanonicalEventType(value: string): value is RunEventType` — because
TypeScript only narrows through a return type that names the narrowed type. A plain
`boolean` return would have left the cast necessary and the drift unobservable.

**Fail-before, per the plan, was a compile error and not an assertion** — the plan is
explicit that a test asserting a name is added to the schema *cannot be written* without
the derivation, and that the absence is itself the proof. Removing the cast from
`jobs.routes.ts` was observed to fail `tsc` with `TS2322`, and to pass only once the set
was derived and the predicate existed. No failing assertion was invented to stand in for it.

**The ownership gate now sees the dot-style names**, which it structurally could not:
`packages/realtime/src/event-type-ownership.test.ts` is a tree scanner scoped to five
colon-style constants read from `schemas/reporter-events.ts`, and its own docstring says
why — a string is invisible to a schema-name gate. It now also reads
`RunEventTypeSchema` out of `schemas/execution.ts` and fails on a **hand-maintained list**
of two or more canonical names outside the contract. Scoped to the list shape on purpose: forbidding *every* dot-style literal would fail on roughly twenty files that legitimately construct canonical events (the writers in `apps/api/src/execution/`, the runner, the web hooks), which is a different change wearing this one's tests. What made P-62 a defect was not that the names appear twice; it was that a list of them was maintained by hand beside the contract that declares them.

The scanner uses a hand-written `setLiteralStarts` walk rather than a regex. The natural
`/new\s+Set\s*(?:<[^>]*>)?\s*\(\s*\[/g` is a nested quantifier — an unbounded `[^>]*`
inside a group, between two `\s*` runs that can match the same characters — and
`security/detect-unsafe-regex` correctly refuses it. Bounding the inner quantifier does
not help, because the ambiguity is between the adjacent `\s*` runs.

**Calibration:** the ten-name literal list was reinstated in `schemas.ts` and the new
gate was observed to fail naming `apps/api/src/routes/execution/schemas.ts:171` with all
ten members, then restored — twice, the second time after the scanner was rewritten to
the hand scan, so the rewrite itself was checked rather than assumed equivalent.

evidence.asserts: `CANONICAL_EVENT_TYPES` is a `ReadonlySet<RunEventType>` built from `RunEventTypeSchema.options`, and `isCanonicalEventType` is the type predicate that lets the call site narrow without a cast.

The derived set equals `RunEventTypeSchema.options` element for element; the set's element type is the contract's, so a new name cannot be missed; and `run.phase` remains outside the set, so the alias and its membership guard in `jobs.routes.ts` still have work to do.
No file outside `packages/shared-contracts` hand-maintains a list of two or more canonical run event types, checked against the names read from `RunEventTypeSchema` in `schemas/execution.ts`.

findings.title: Duplicated error bodies on the health and agent routes
findings.summary:
`/health` and `/api/v1/health` are two near-identical literals (`health.ts:18-24` versus `:26-33`), and three near-identical agent 404/501 bodies have no shared builder.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `routes/health.ts:18-24` and `:26-33` are two near-identical health literals
differing only by an added `version: '1'`. **The agent-error count is slightly off:
there are four body literals, not three**, in three distinct shapes across
`routes/agents.ts:21-29,31-41,46-54,55-64`. Important for a fixer: those four are
**not** built by the boundary's renderer — they are flat, with no `error` wrapper, no
`requestId` and no nesting — so `domainErrorResponse` at `errors/boundary.ts:47-49`
is not a drop-in and consolidating them changes their wire shape. The codebase already
knows the right pattern: `health.ts:35-55` *is* a shared handler bound to both paths,
and `health.test.ts:226-230` enforces byte-identical output.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28 — and the difference the two health bodies make is deliberately preserved.**

`healthBody(version?)` builds both. It **omits** the `version` key entirely on the
unversioned path rather than setting it to `undefined`, because `c.json` drops an
`undefined` value and the key order is asserted. The `timestamp` asymmetry is left alone:
each handler calls `new Date()` at its own moment, and `health.test.ts:217-231` locks
that too. **The two bodies were not harmonised**, and the plan is explicit that doing so
would be a product change dressed as a refactor — the fact that a shared builder now
exists is exactly the moment that temptation arrives, so the guard is a test rather than
a comment.

`agentError(status, httpStatus, code, message, extra?)` builds all four agent bodies,
keyed `status, implemented, code, …` — **not alphabetical**, and the order is now pinned.
It is a **local** builder and not `domainErrorResponse`, for the two reasons this row
already recorded: the four bodies are flat, and 501 is `>= 500`, so `DomainError.toBody`
would replace every message with `'internal error'` and drop `details` unless each error
were built `callerSafe`. Nothing in `apps/web` reads these bodies and `agents.test.ts`
asserts only status codes and `integrations.length`, so the shape is free — which is the
argument for preserving it deliberately rather than cleaning it up.

**Calibration, three trials, each observed red and then restored:** (1) making
`healthBody` emit `version: '1'` on the unversioned path fails **both** the new
`differs between the two paths only by version` assertion and the pre-existing
`health.test.ts` case titled *states the contract version on /api/v1/health only, on
purpose* — the repo already had a guard and it fired; (2) reordering the agent builder's
keys so `extra` came first fails the key-order assertion; (3) giving the agent bodies the
boundary's `{ error, requestId }` shape fails three assertions, and the **flatness**
assertion is the one that catches it, which is precisely the substitution the plan warns
about.

evidence.asserts: `healthBody(version?)` is the one builder for both health paths, omitting the `version` key on the unversioned path so consolidation is a pure no-op — the existing `health.test.ts:55-69` case asserting `plain['version']` is `undefined` still passes, which is the proof no behaviour changed.
`agentError` builds all four failure bodies with key order `status, implemented, code, …`, and none of them acquires an `error` wrapper or a `requestId` from the boundary renderer.

All four agent bodies share one key order; they stay flat with no `error` wrapper and no `requestId`; the 501 bodies keep the `domain` and `action` they were given; and the two health paths differ only by `version`, with the timestamp asymmetry left intact.

findings.title: The job state machine takes no fencing token
findings.summary: `orchestration/src/state-machine.ts:24,30` take `(from, to)` only, so `running → succeeded` is legal for any caller that asks. A worker holding a lapsed lease can still finish the job it no longer owns. **Confirmed on 2026-09-28 — both signatures, and the table makes the consequence concrete.** `canTransition(from, to)` (`:24`) and `transition(from, to)` (`:30`) take exactly two parameters, and the transition table at `:3-13` allows `running → succeeded`. Nothing in the module refers to a lease, an owner, a fencing token, or a version; `isTerminal` (`:36-38`) is the only other export. **So the machine answers a question about states and the question that actually needs answering is about ownership:** a state transition is a claim about what is true of a job, and the only thing `running → succeeded` establishes is that some caller asked. Two workers can both hold `running` for the same job — the ordinary outcome of a lease expiring mid-run, which is the case this row exists for — and the second one to finish writes `succeeded` with the same authority as the first, and neither the machine nor its caller can tell them apart. **The state table is not the defect and must not be changed to fix it.** It is correct as a table of which states may follow which; adding a third argument means the caller must supply a token and the machine must compare it, which is a wider change than it looks: every existing call site becomes a decision about where the token comes from, and a call site that passes a token it does not have would be worse than today's honest two-argument call. That is why this row is ordered before the lease row that consumes the token rather than with it. **Fixed in findings-remediation wave 1.3, on 2026-09-28 — and the row's second sentence turned out to describe a hazard rather than a hole, so the fix is two things and a correction.** The correction first, because it changes what the work is: *a worker holding a lapsed lease cannot finish the job it no longer owns.* That is not true of this system and was not true when the row was written. `routes/execution/shared.ts:35-43` refuses it with a distinct `JOB_FENCING_STALE` code, `drizzle-execution-store.ts:1387` refuses it again inside the transaction, and `apps/worker/src/in-memory-store.ts:328-344` does the same. Fencing tokens have been on the job since the queue was built; the state machine is simply not where they live, and no worker's completion is ever routed through it. **So the row is a true observation about an interface and a false claim about a system, and the honest fix is the first without pretending the second was ever broken.** The interface could not express ownership, which is a trap for the next caller rather than a hole today: `decideTransition(fence, to)` now answers "may I make this edge *now*" by comparing the caller's token against the store's before consulting the table, and the table is untouched. **The second thing is the one live call site.** `OrchestrationService.cancel` was the only production call site of the machine, and it called the two-argument form and fell through on failure — which is P-70's `orchestration-service.ts:47-49` half, done here because fixing the machine without fixing its only caller would have left the new predicate unused. **The third thing is a gap the row's own premise exposed.** `completeJob`'s fencing comparison had no assertion anywhere: the route refused the same thing first, so deleting that line changed nothing a test could see. The case was written, the line was removed, both refusals went red, and the line went back. Defence in depth that nothing checks is one refactor from not being there.
findings.confirmedBy: Findings-remediation Phase 0 batch 1. Read the whole module: 38 lines, four exports, no lease or version concept anywhere. The claim holds as written. **One correction to the row's second sentence, found in wave 1.3: the system is fenced, but not by this module.** A worker holding a lapsed lease *cannot* finish the job it no longer owns — `routes/execution/shared.ts:35-43` refuses it with `JOB_FENCING_STALE`, and `drizzle-execution-store.ts:1387` refuses it again inside the transaction, and `in-memory-store.ts:328-344` does the same for the worker. What the row describes accurately is the *module's* interface, which cannot express ownership, and a hazard for the next caller rather than a live hole.

evidence.asserts: `decideTransition(fence, to)` answers the question a caller actually has — may I make this edge now — by comparing the caller's token against the store's before consulting the table, and `holdsFence` uses `===` so a token the store never issued is not authority. The table itself is untouched: it was correct, and changing it to fix an ownership problem would have replaced a real defect with a fictional one.

A worker on token 1 cannot finish a job the store has re-leased on token 2; the worker holding token 2 can, so the refusals are refusals and not a closed door; a token newer than the store's is refused; and fencing does not license an illegal edge. The last two matter because a fence that only ever said no would pass the first case.

`cancel` consults the machine and refuses an illegal transition with `INVALID_STATE_TRANSITION` (409) instead of falling through and returning a 200-shaped envelope whose state had not moved. This is the only production call site of the state machine, so it is the only place the two-argument call could still do damage.

Cancelling an already-cancelled job is refused with a 409 rather than answered as though it succeeded, and the job is left byte-identical — a refused request that still mutated the record would be the same defect one layer down.

`completeJob`'s own fence is asserted at the store, which nothing did before. The route already refused the same thing, which is precisely why deleting `drizzle-execution-store.ts:1387` would have changed nothing any test could see — this case was written, the line was removed, and both refusals went red before it was put back.

The second comparison is kept, and the comment on it now says that a test asserts it directly. A defence in depth that nothing checks is one refactor from not being there, and the comment is the part that stops the next reader assuming it is covered by the route.

findings.title: A tenancy finding the plan names but does not describe
findings.summary: The plan lists O-2 alongside P-20's eight unscoped tables and requires it to be spot-confirmed before a destructive tenancy migration, but it never states what the defect is. Recorded as open and undescribed on purpose: a row that names an ID without naming a claim cannot be closed, and cannot be quietly forgotten either. It is assigned to the tenancy wave because that is where the plan groups it.
findings.refutedBy:
No claim is recoverable, so there is nothing to test.

`O-2` occurs **exactly once** in the entire repository outside the two quality files
that name it: at `.kilo/plans/1790482134837-automate-merged-leftover-plan.md:63`,
inside the Tenancy band table, as part of the range `O-1…O-3`. That cell states a
claim for none of its members. Every other plan file was searched — the nine files in
`.kilo/plans/` — and none mentions the O-series beyond that cell.

The range is best read as a contiguous id span rather than three tenancy findings,
because its one described member contradicts the grouping: `O-1` is
`orchestration/src/state-machine.ts:24,30` taking `(from, to)` with no fencing
token, a durability finding described in full at `1790482134837-…:153` and placed in

findings.refutedBy:

findings.title: InMemorySessionService scans every session on every request
findings.summary:
`packages/auth/src/credentials.ts` verifies a presented session by HMAC-ing it and scanning the whole collection, so cost is O(n) in live sessions. Production uses the indexed `DrizzleSessionStore`, which is why the cost is invisible.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `packages/auth/src/credentials.ts:99-101`. No revocation list or index is
consulted; every candidate in the map gets a fresh HMAC plus `timingSafeEqual`, per
request, **unbounded** — the map is only ever added to. The row's note that production
uses the indexed Drizzle store is accurate (`index.ts:238`,
`session-repository.ts:34-46`), **but the in-memory path is live** for any
no-database deployment (`routes/auth.ts:57-64`, and it is what the auth middleware
uses at `index.ts:342`). **This is a consequence of S-2/S-7**: the scan is the wrong
shape, but unbounded growth is what makes it a live cost.
findings.resolution: The in-memory session map is keyed by the token hash, so `validate` hashes the presented token once and looks it up instead of running a keyed HMAC and a constant-time comparison against every stored session on every request. The constant-time property the loop provided is preserved more directly: a lookup costs the same whatever the collection holds, so a caller still cannot learn how many live sessions there are from how long validation took. The HMAC is the secret operation; the lookup is against its output. Production already used an indexed store, which is why the cost was invisible there.

evidence.asserts: The map is keyed by `tokenHash`, and `validate` is a lookup. The second `verifyCredential` the fix first added was dead code by construction — the key is the value it would have compared — and has been removed rather than left as an unreachable branch.
A wrong token is rejected in a map with one entry and in a map with five hundred; the property asserted is that the rejection does not depend on the collection, not a timing.

findings.title: Revoked sessions are never removed
findings.summary:
`revoke` only stamps `revokedAt`; there is no TTL sweep, so the collection grows without bound and the scan grows with it.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `credentials.ts:106-111`. `revoke` only stamps `revokedAt`; nothing removes
entries. `deleteExpired` has one occurrence repo-wide — this ledger row. The durable
store's `revoke` is likewise an `UPDATE … SET revoked_at` and no `DELETE` on
`sessions` exists anywhere. **One decision with S-6 and S-7:** all three are the
single feature "session retention", currently specified in config
(`SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS`, `RETENTION_SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS`) and absent from code.
findings.resolution: Sessions are now removed, not only marked. The durable store gained `deleteExpired(cutoff)` — a real `DELETE` on `sessions`, which did not exist anywhere — and the in-memory service gained `deleteExpired()`. The cutoff is on `issuedAt`, not `expiresAt`, and that distinction is the point: a row outlives its validity so that "was this ever a valid session" still has an answer, which is the same reason `revoke` marks rather than deletes.

evidence.asserts: `deleteExpired` deletes by `issuedAt` and returns the count, so a sweep that removes nothing can be distinguished from one that was never called.
`deleteExpired` removes expired sessions and reports how many.
A session that expired long ago is still there after a sweep with a later cutoff, and one past the cutoff is gone — the assertion that says the cutoff is on `issuedAt`.

findings.title: issue returns the live internal record, so a caller can mutate a session
findings.summary:
`InMemorySessionService.issue` hands back the object it stores, so a caller can set `expiresAt` or clear `revokedAt` in place after the fact. The durable store returns a mapped copy, so the two disagree.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `credentials.ts:87-95` stores the object and **returns that same object**, so a
caller can set `expiresAt` or delete `record.revokedAt` and change stored state. The
durable backend (`infrastructure/session-backend.ts:22-37`) builds its record locally,
writes a field-by-field copy, and returns the local literal, so mutation has no effect.
The two implementations genuinely disagree on aliasing.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

The in-memory session service no longer hands out a reference to its own state.

`issue` stored a `SessionRecord` and returned **that same object**, so a caller could
write `record.expiresAt = <the far future>` or `delete record.revokedAt` and change
the service's state through a value it was only given to read — extending a session, or
un-revoking one, without calling any method at all. The durable backend
(`infrastructure/session-backend.ts:22-37`) already builds its record locally, writes a
field-by-field copy, and returns the local literal, so the two implementations
disagreed on whether the return value *is* the store.

`issue` and `validate` now both return a copy. The store keeps the original.

**This is production behaviour, not a test-only fix**, which the row does not say and
which is easy to get wrong: the in-memory service is the fallback whenever
`databaseResources` is absent (`index.ts:243-246` merely *permits* it), and it is what
the auth middleware uses. The existing test file header names the pattern — "the
in-memory double is not held to the contract the real store is held to" — and this is
that pattern again, in the same class.

evidence.asserts: `issue` stores the record and returns a shallow copy, so mutating the returned value — rewriting `expiresAt`, deleting `revokedAt`, rewriting `installationId` — leaves the stored session untouched. `validate` likewise returns a copy, so a caller cannot hold a live reference to a stored session.

A caller that rewrites `expiresAt` and deletes `revokedAt` on the record it was handed sees **no** change through `validate`. A second case reaches the same aliasing through revocation: after `revoke`, clearing `revokedAt` on the caller's copy does not resurrect the session — which is the sharper of the two, because un-revoking a session is the security-relevant direction.

findings.title: An empty secret and a non-positive TTL are accepted
findings.summary:
`InMemorySessionService` accepts a zero-length secret and a `ttlMs <= 0`, producing a session that is either trivially verifiable or already expired.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true, and "trivially verifiable" is not supported.** The TTL half is
confirmed: `credentials.ts:78-82` validates neither argument, and `ttlMs <= 0` yields
`expiresAt === issuedAt`, so `issue` returns a token that `validate` immediately
rejects. The empty-secret half is not: `hashCredential('', token)` is still a keyed
HMAC over a 32-byte random token, so a known-empty secret does not let anyone forge
one without the preimage. It is also unreachable in production — `routes/auth.ts:58`
draws from `resolveAuthSecrets`, which refuses a missing `COOKIE_SECRET` and floors
it at 32 characters.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

The in-memory session service refuses the two arguments that produce a service which
appears to work.

A `ttlMs` of zero or less produced `expiresAt === issuedAt`, so `issue` returned a
token that `validate` rejected on the very next line: a healthy-looking service whose
every session is dead on arrival. Both are now refused in the constructor, where the
mistake is visible, rather than discovered by the first caller to be handed a session.

**A deliberate correction to the row, weaker than the row claims.** The summary calls an
empty secret "trivially verifiable". It is not, and recording that matters more than the
fix: `hashCredential('', token)` is still a keyed HMAC over a 32-byte random token, so
knowing the secret does not let anyone mint a valid token without the preimage. What an
empty secret actually destroys is the property that the stored `tokenHash` is not
computable from the spool alone — it becomes a plain digest — so this is a **hardening**
refusal, not a forgery hole, and the ledger now says so.

Neither case is reachable in production: `routes/auth.ts:58` draws its secret from
`resolveAuthSecrets`, which refuses a missing `COOKIE_SECRET` and floors it at 32
characters. The refusals are about the service being correct when constructed
directly, which is how tests and any future caller construct it.

evidence.asserts: The constructor refuses a non-positive or non-finite `ttlMs` and an empty secret, so `issue` can no longer return a session that `validate` rejects immediately. The comment records that the empty-secret case is a hardening refusal rather than a forgery hole, so a later reader does not over-credit the guarantee.

A zero, negative and `NaN` TTL are each refused, and a refused construction is shown to be a refusal rather than a silent clamp by constructing a valid service and asserting its `expiresAt` is strictly after its `issuedAt`. An empty secret is refused.

findings.title: lastUsedAt is a dead column
findings.summary:
`lastUsedAt` is declared and never written or read, so a session's idleness cannot be observed.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `packages/db/src/schema/identity.ts:47` declares `lastUsedAt`. The `create`
insert omits it, `findValid` selects it but `session-backend.ts:43-50` drops it when
mapping, and `SessionRecord` (`credentials.ts:66-73`) does not declare it at all, so
the in-memory service cannot observe idleness even in principle. The same column is
also dead on `installation_keys` (`:28`) and `service_credentials` (`:66`).
**Note:** this is a schema/domain gap, *not* the same decision as S-6, despite the
shared theme — producing `lastUsedAt` does not consume `SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS`.
findings.resolution: `last_used_at` is written, and it is written on the read path. `findValid` now touches the row as it validates it, so a session's last use is the last moment anyone proved the token was still good — which is the only moment "last use" means anything. It was previously declared in the schema, omitted from the insert, selected, and then dropped by the mapping in `session-backend.ts`, so a session's idleness could not be observed by anything, which is the only reason to store it. Two properties are deliberate: the touch happens on validation rather than on every request, so an endpoint being hammered anonymously writes nothing; and the row handed back carries the value just written, not the one the `SELECT` read, because a row returned from before its own touch would leave the column permanently one validation behind — the opposite of what it is for.

evidence.asserts: `findValid` touches `lastUsedAt` and returns the post-touch row; the comment says why the write belongs on the read path and why a separate heartbeat would be a second source of truth.
A first validation records its instant, and a later one moves it again — so it is a running "last use" and not a value written once at issue.

findings.title: SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS is parsed and mapped with no consumer
findings.summary:
The setting is read from the environment and carried through a map, and nothing downstream uses the result.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `packages/config/src/config.ts:109,137,188`. `sessionRetentionDays` has exactly
two occurrences repo-wide, both in that file. No consumer. The same file carries two
more parsed-and-unused siblings: `retentionSweepIntervalSeconds` (lines 140 and 191) and
`auditRetentionDays` (lines 139 and 190). Part of the S-2/S-6/S-7 retention feature.
findings.resolution: `SESSION_RETENTION_DAYS` has a consumer. It is passed to `DrizzleAuthSessionBackend` as the retention window and used to compute the sweep cutoff, and `SESSION_TTL_HOURS` is now read for the TTL where the value was a literal `24 * 60 * 60 * 1000` — so the two settings and the two literals agreed only because the defaults happened to be the same number, and an operator who set `SESSION_TTL_HOURS=8` got eight hours in nothing. Both now read from configuration, with the schema defaults as the fallback.

evidence.asserts: `sessionTtlMs` and `sessionRetentionMs` are derived from `runtimeConfig` rather than written as literals beside a config that declares them.
The backend takes a retention window and derives its cutoff from it, one window longer than the TTL on purpose.

findings.title: There is no deleteExpired
findings.summary:
The interface has no expiry sweep at all, which is the missing half of S-2.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `infrastructure/session-backend.ts:5-9`. The `AuthSessionBackend` interface has
no expiry or removal member, and `DrizzleSessionStore` has none either, so the
sweep has nothing to call. `RETENTION_SWEEP_INTERVAL_SECONDS` exists in config and is
consumed by nothing, so there is not even a schedule on which a sweep could run. **The
missing half of S-2**, as the row says, and it cannot be closed alone: a removal path
without a schedule does nothing.
findings.resolution: `deleteExpired` exists on both backends and is *called*. The row named the method before it existed, which is the part worth keeping: defining it is not retention, and a method with no caller is the state the row described. It is reached from `memoryBackend` and from the durable backend, and both report how many rows went so that a sweep doing nothing can be told from a sweep that was never run.

evidence.asserts: The in-process backend exposes `sweep`, and `memoryBackend` is exported so a test can reach the default path rather than a caller-supplied one.
A live session is not swept, an expired one is, and the sweep reports the count.

findings.title: Two reporter adapters build test ids from different key pairs
findings.summary:
`junit-xml.ts:121` builds `testId` from `classname:name` and `playwright-json.ts:115` from `file:title`. The contract only requires `z.string().min(1)`, so two same-named tests in one ingestion collide into one row.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true, and its stated consequence is not reachable.** The differing key
pairs are real: `junit-xml.ts:121` builds `${classname}:${name}` and
`playwright-json.ts:128` builds `${spec.file}:${title ?? testIndex}`, and
`canonical-reporting.ts:86` puts no uniqueness constraint on `testId`. But the
claimed "two same-named tests collapse into one row" is **not demonstrable**:
`canonical-run-result.ts:117-131` maps attempts 1:1, `RunResultSchema.attempts`
(`canonical-reporting.ts:161`) has no dedup and no `superRefine`, and **no consumer
anywhere groups or de-duplicates attempts by `testId`**. The real defect is a
*non-unique identity* — two attempts in one run can carry the same `testId` and are
indistinguishable to any future consumer that keys on it. **Not a duplicate of F-5**:
different field, different line, different failure mode.

**Reading taken: option (b), narrowed — the uniqueness check alone, and re-banded Major → Minor.**

The plan offered (a) narrow-and-re-band or (b) add the check only, and recommended
a judgement rather than hiding it. This is that judgement, and one thing about it was
not knowable from the plan: **plain `testId` uniqueness is not merely undesirable, it is
wrong.** A retried test is *one* test with several attempts — `playwright-json.ts:166`
emits one attempt per `test.results` entry with the same `testId` and
`index: attemptIndex + 1`, and JUnit says the same thing with `flakyFailure` /
`rerunFailure`. A uniqueness check on `testId` would therefore reject **every flaky run**,
which is a normal case rather than an unlucky one. Writing that check would have closed
the row with a regression.

**The rule that is actually enforceable: for each `testId`, its attempt `index` values
are exactly 1..n.** A retry satisfies it by construction. Two *distinct* tests that
collided on an identity both arrive as attempt 1 — the adapters number `index` per test —
so the group reads `[1, 1]` and is refused. The identity a consumer can rely on is
therefore the pair `(testId, index)`, which is what makes that pair an identity rather
than a coincidence. It also catches a **gap** (attempts 1 and 3), which a `Set`-size check
would miss.

**Re-banded Major → Minor**, deliberately and with the reason stated: the demonstrated
consumer is `in-memory-run-repository.ts:109-111`, which keys a Map on
`${testId}::${runId}` and whose `patchTest` silently no-ops on a missing key (`:90`) — the
one place two same-`testId` rows in a run would already merge. Namespacing `testId` into a
composite was considered and **not** done: it buys nothing observable today, `testId` is
user-visible (`run-detail.tsx` renders it and keys `data-testid={\`test-${testId}\`}` on it,
asserted at `run-detail.test.tsx:59,292,311`), and the only demonstrated consequence is that
one in-memory no-op. One residual is stated rather than papered over and is covered by a
test: a collision that happens to arrive as attempts 1 and 2 is byte-identical to a genuine
retry, and **no contract rule can separate them** — the difference would have to be carried
in the `testId` itself.

**The rule immediately found a second, independent defect, which is the strongest evidence
that it was the right rule.** `junit-xml.ts` numbered attempts with a running ordinal across
the whole document — `index: index + 1` over every `<testcase>` — while
`playwright-json.ts` puts the attempt's ordinal *within one test*, and
`components/dashboard/RunExplorer.tsx:36` renders the field as "attempt N". So a JUnit
run whose second testcase failed claimed its only attempt was attempt 2, and a consumer
keying on `(testId, index)` had **no consistent identity across the two producers**. Four
`adapter-parity.test.ts` cases went red on the new rule before it was understood. Fixed to
`index: 1`, since one `<testcase>` is one test with one attempt.

**Calibration:** the three new contract assertions were each observed red before the rule
existed (collision, gap, and the retried-test case passing). The JUnit running ordinal was
reinstated and observed to turn **six** assertions red across `junit.test.ts` and
`adapter-parity.test.ts` before being restored.

**Still outstanding, and this row does not close it:** **no issue was ever opened for F-4.**
Issue #6 lists W-8 here, and W-8 is already `fixed`, so F-4 has no tracker item at all. One
should be opened rather than the row being closed quietly.

evidence.asserts: `RunResultSchema` super-refines attempts so each `testId`'s `index` values are exactly 1..n — refusing a collision, a gap, and a repeat, while accepting a retried test whose attempts legitimately share one `testId`.

A retried test and two distinct tests side by side are both accepted; two distinct tests that collided on one `testId` are refused; a gap in one test's attempt sequence is refused. A separate case states the limit: a collision arriving as attempts 1 and 2 is indistinguishable from a retry and is accepted, because no contract rule can separate them.
Every `<testcase>` produces `index: 1`. It was a running ordinal across the document, which disagreed with `playwright-json.ts` and with what `RunExplorer.tsx:36` renders as the attempt number.
A three-testcase document yields attempt indexes `[1, 1, 1]`, so a second testcase cannot claim its only attempt was attempt 2.

findings.title: The spec index is written where the test index belongs
findings.summary:
`playwright-json.ts:105` passes the spec's index, so two tests in one spec with an identically-named attachment resolve to the same evidence URI and one overwrites the other.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `playwright-json.ts:118,146`. `testIndex` is `specs.flatMap((spec, testIndex) => …)`
— the **spec's** position, passed unchanged for every test inside that spec. Two tests
in one spec with the same attempt index, attachment index and attachment name (e.g. two
`trace.zip`, which Playwright emits for every test) produce **byte-identical**
evidence URIs at `:82`. Nothing downstream dedupes by URI — both
`canonical-run-result.ts:147` and `playwright-json.ts:161` `flatMap`, so both
entries survive with the same `uri` and different `digest`.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

Every test in a report now gets its own ordinal, so evidence URIs cannot collide.

`testIndex` was the **spec's** position in the collected list, and it was threaded
unchanged into `evidenceFor` for every test inside that spec. Two tests in one spec
therefore produced byte-identical evidence URIs whenever their attempt index,
attachment index and attachment name matched — and two `trace.zip`, which Playwright
emits for *every* test, is the normal case rather than an unlucky one. Nothing
downstream de-duplicates by URI (`canonical-run-result.ts:147` and
`playwright-json.ts` both `flatMap`), so both entries survived carrying the same `uri`
and different digests: evidence that points at one thing and is stored twice.

**The ordinal has to span the whole report, not the spec.** A per-spec index would
still collide — spec 0's first test and spec 1's first test would both be ordinal 0 —
so the tests are flattened into `(spec, test)` pairs first and numbered across the
result. The test asserts the cross-spec case explicitly, and a calibration trial that
reinstates a per-spec ordinal is confirmed to turn it red; without that, a fix that
merely moved the counter would look correct.

The same ordinal backs the `test.title ?? …` fallback in `testId`, so two untitled
tests no longer share an id either. **This is not the same defect as F-4** — different
field, different line, different failure mode — though both are symptoms of identity
being built from a coarse, hand-picked key with no per-test ordinal. A single coherent
change would serve both, and F-4's remaining part (the contract's absent uniqueness
constraint) is recorded there.

evidence.asserts: Tests are flattened into `(spec, test)` pairs and numbered by their position in the **whole report**, so the ordinal reaching `evidenceFor` differs for every test — including two tests in different specs that a per-spec index would have collided. The same ordinal is the `test.title` fallback in `testId`. Before the fix, two tests in one spec produced the identical URI `artifact://run-1/0/0/0/trace.zip`.

Three tests across two specs, each with one attachment named `trace.zip` and the same body, must yield three distinct evidence URIs — the cross-spec case is in the fixture on purpose, because a per-spec ordinal passes a same-spec-only test. A second case asserts two untitled tests in different specs get distinct `testId`s.

findings.title: Reporter text accumulation has no cap
findings.summary:
`junit-xml.ts:92-97` accumulates failure text with no bound, on an untrusted boundary.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true: the code property holds, the threat model does not.** The
accumulation at `junit-xml.ts:92-97` is genuinely uncapped and the contract imposes
no cap downstream (`canonical-reporting.ts:95` is a floor, no maximum), so there is
no bound anywhere in the path. But `junitXmlAdapter` has **no production call site** —
its only importers are **two** test files (`packages/reporter/src/junit.test.ts` and
`packages/reporter/src/adapter-parity.test.ts`; `tests/contract/` does not reference
junit at all, which corrects the three-importer claim this row originally carried). The
API's actual untrusted JUnit ingestion is `routes/reporter.ts:540 parseJunitUpload`, a
separate hand-rolled scanner bounded twice (`MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` at `:287` via `bodyLimit`
at `:746-756`, and its own `MAX_JUNIT_BYTES` at `:538-543`) which does not accumulate
message text at all. So the row's "untrusted boundary" qualifier is unproven as written.

**Fixed as hardening, following the precedent in row F-7** — the code property was real
and worth bounding, but the exposure claimed by the row was not. `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS`
(8 192) is now applied as the text is consumed, in the `text` and `cdata` handlers, not
on the serialised attempt: capping at `:110` would leave the unbounded string fully
materialised in memory, because growth happens at `+=`. The truncation flag resets in the
`opentag` handler alongside `currentText` and `currentChildren`, not in the two `closetag`
branches, so it cannot leak into a following `<testcase>`. Truncation is marked with the
structured `error.code === 'MESSAGE_TRUNCATED'`, which `AttemptSchema.error.code`
(`packages/shared-contracts/src/schemas/canonical-reporting.ts:95`, `z.string().min(1).optional()`)
already permits — no contract change. A sentinel suffix on the message was rejected: it
would make the string falsely claim to be the producer's own text, and silent truncation
would be its own defect.

**Fail-before calibration, all three trials observed red and then restored:** raising the
cap to 200 000 fails the length and leak assertions; dropping the `code` field fails the
two truncation assertions; removing the flag reset fails the leak case alone. A
normal-length-message case asserts `code` is `undefined`, so a fix that truncates
everything cannot pass.

evidence.asserts: `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` caps the accumulated text inside the `text`/`cdata` handlers, and the truncated flag is reset in the `opentag` handler.

A 200 000-character failure body yields a message of exactly `MAX_MESSAGE_CHARS` and `error.code === 'MESSAGE_TRUNCATED'`; a normal-length message carries no `code`; a truncated testcase followed by a short one in the same document does not leak the flag; a CDATA body is capped by the same path as a text body; and text arriving after the ceiling was reached is dropped rather than appended.

findings.title: An unguarded JSON.parse on an untrusted body
findings.summary:
`playwright-json.ts:99` parses the uploaded document without a guard, so a malformed body throws a `SyntaxError` rather than yielding a classified ingestion error.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `playwright-json.ts:112` — `JSON.parse(new TextDecoder().decode(input))` with no
`try`, no `safeParse`, and no error channel on `parse`
(`adapter.ts:17`). A malformed body escapes as a raw `SyntaxError`,
indistinguishable from the adapter's own deliberate refusals at `:118` and `:151`.
No caller wraps it. **The contrast that makes it a real gap:** the API's own
equivalent parse (`reporter.ts:365-366`) is equally unguarded *inside*, but the route
calls it within `try { … } catch { throw new DomainError('INVALID_REPORTER_UPLOAD', …) }`
at `reporter.ts:889-893`, so the boundary renders a classified ingestion error for
one and a `SyntaxError` for the other.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A malformed Playwright upload is now refused by name instead of escaping as a
`SyntaxError`.

`parse` declares no error channel, and `JSON.parse` on the uploaded body had no
guard, so a malformed body escaped as a raw `SyntaxError` — the one shape a caller
cannot distinguish from its own bugs, and the one shape this adapter's own deliberate
refusals ("contains no test attempts", "is not a JSON object") are not.

**The contrast that makes it a real gap rather than a style preference:** the API's
equivalent parse at `routes/reporter.ts:365-366` is *equally* unguarded inside, but the
route calls it within a `try` that renders `DomainError('INVALID_REPORTER_UPLOAD', …)`.
So the same boundary was giving two different answers to the same class of bad input
depending on which parser ran. Wrapping the adapter's parse costs nothing and makes the
two agree.

Two refusals rather than one, because they are different faults: a body that is not
JSON, and a body that is JSON but not an object (a bare array or string, which the
old code would have carried into `collectSpecs` and failed somewhere less legible). The
underlying `SyntaxError` is carried as `cause` rather than discarded — an operator
debugging an upload needs the position, and this repository already made that argument
