findings.title: An attachment name is interpolated unencoded
findings.summary: **Confirmed, and the fix is in — but this row stays open, because the proof is not.** `playwright-json.ts:71` interpolated the attachment name into the evidence URI unencoded: `artifact://${runId}/${testIndex}/${attemptIndex}/${attachmentIndex}/${name}`. The name is the only segment an outside party chooses — it arrives inside a Playwright report uploaded by a build, so a pull request controls it — and a name containing `?` starts a query, `#` starts a fragment, and `/` adds a path segment. The consequence is not a malformed string but a **different artifact reference**: the evidence URI is what a reader follows, so a crafted name makes it resolve to the wrong artifact or to nothing, and nothing reports it. The name is now `encodeURIComponent`-encoded. The other four segments are deliberately left unencoded because they are ours — a run id we generate and three indices — and the comment says so, since claiming they were encoded would be a claim that is not currently true. **Why it is open.** The plan's standard is a test that was shown to fail before the fix and pass after, and I could not calibrate the fixture in the time available: the synthetic Playwright report did not match what `collectSpecs` expects, so the adapter returned no attachments and every case read `undefined` — a test that fails for the wrong reason is exactly the kind this repository keeps finding and refuses. The test was removed rather than left red, and the source change is left in because it is typechecked and the encoding is unambiguous. **What closing this needs:** a fixture whose report shape `collectSpecs` actually walks — an existing adapter test to copy the shape from — and then four cases: an ordinary name unchanged, a name with `?`, a name with `#`, and a name with `/`, each asserting the recorded URI round-trips to the same name. The positive case matters as much as the rest, because an encoding that mangled normal names would make every evidence URI unreadable, which is worse than the defect.
findings.confirmedBy: W4.9. Confirmed by reading the adapter exactly as described.

evidence.asserts: The recorded URI carries no query and no fragment, has exactly the five segments the adapter writes, and the name round-trips. The first version asserted only the round trip, which passes for an *unencoded* `report?x=1` because `decodeURIComponent` of it is itself — so the assertion that actually catches the defect is the one about query and fragment.
The name is `encodeURIComponent`-encoded; the other four segments are deliberately not, and the comment says so rather than claiming they are.

findings.resolution: The encoding was already in `playwright-json.ts`; what was missing was the proof, and the row said why it was missing — the first attempt at the test blamed a synthetic report that did not match what `collectSpecs` walks. It was not the fixture. It was the **context**: `ProducerContext` needs `sourceUri`, `sourceDigest`, `producerVersion`, `adapterVersion` and `projectId`, and the guessed context was missing them, so every case failed on a Zod error about `provenance` and read as an empty result. The fixture was blamed twice before the context was read. `playwright-evidence-uri.test.ts` now copies the real context from `adapter-parity.test.ts` and asserts four things: an ordinary name is unchanged and round-trips, a name containing `?`, `#` or `/` cannot restructure the URI, and all three together. Verified failing against the unencoded adapter and passing with it.

findings.title: close() never unsubscribes
findings.summary: `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` drops the unsubscribe handle on close, so every subscriber outlives the bus that owns it. Production wires `DurableRealtimeBus`, whose per-subscriber isolation is already fixed.
findings.confirmedBy:
W3.1. Confirmed by reading `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` as described.

`close()` was `() => undefined`, so it closed nothing. The listener stayed registered on the bus for the life of the process: a closed subscription kept receiving events and kept its closure — and whatever it captured — alive. The subscription now tracks the listeners it added and removes exactly those, leaving other subscriptions untouched, and `close()` is idempotent. `listenerCount` is exposed so a leak is observable rather than inferred.

evidence.asserts: The behaviour named in the finding is gone, and the replacement is asserted in `bus-contract.test.ts` against the specific false statement the old code made.
A fresh 15-case suite written around the failure rather than the happy path; the four cases that could be attributed to one reverted line were each shown to fail against the old code.

findings.title: The cursor guard accepts Number('') and Number('0x10')
findings.summary: `bus.ts` coerces the cursor with `Number`, so an empty string becomes 0 and `'0x10'` becomes 16 — both pass the guard, and both are nonsense as a cursor.
findings.confirmedBy:
W3.1. Confirmed by reading `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` as described.

`Number(afterCursor)` accepted `''` as 0 and `'0x10'` as 16, both of which passed the old `isInteger && >= 0` guard. The empty string is the one that matters: it is what a client sends when it has no cursor, and coercing it to 0 makes "I have nothing" indistinguishable from a deliberate "send me from the beginning". `parseCursor` accepts `0`, a leading-digit decimal, and a safe integer — nothing else, including whitespace, signs, exponents and hex.

findings.title: Subscribing with no cursor reports "caught up" while missing everything
findings.summary: A subscriber with no cursor is told it is up to date, which is a false statement about a stream it has not read a single event of.
findings.confirmedBy:
W3.1. Confirmed by reading `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` as described.

**The worst of the five, because it was silent.** `subscribe()` substituted `this.cursor` for a missing cursor, so a brand-new subscriber was told it was caught up on a stream it had read not one event of. Nothing errored, nothing looked wrong, and every event published before the subscription was permanently omitted — the failure mode is a client that quietly shows a fresh dashboard for a run that has been going for an hour. A missing cursor now means "from the beginning": the subscription asks from zero and lets `gap` report honestly whether the retained window still covers the origin. Reverting the single line makes three of the new tests fail.

findings.title: The buffer drops by count, not by bytes
findings.summary: The O(n) `shift()` eviction is bounded by an event count, so N large events exceed the memory bound the count was chosen to enforce.
findings.confirmedBy:
W3.1. Confirmed by reading `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` as described.

The bound was an event count, so `historyLimit: 100` permitted 100 events of any size, and one frame carrying a stack trace is orders of magnitude larger than one carrying a status string. A count is not a memory bound. Both are now enforced and the older event evicts while either is exceeded, with `retainedCount` and `retainedBytes` exposed so a caller can tell which one bound. The measurement is approximate on purpose: serializing every event to size a budget that is itself approximate would cost more than the budget saves, and what matters is that the number scales with the payload so one large event cannot slip past.

findings.title: A per-process cursor is minted beside the durable outbox sequence
findings.summary: `bus.ts` numbers cursors `1..n` per process while the durable store numbers them from the outbox sequence, so the two numbering schemes are unrelated and neither is authoritative.
findings.confirmedBy:
W3.1. Confirmed by reading `packages/realtime/src/bus.ts` as described.

Cursors were numbered `1..n` per process while `DurableRealtimeBus` numbers them from the outbox sequence, so the two schemes are unrelated and neither is authoritative. `initialCursor` lets a process continue the durable numbering rather than inventing its own, which removes the silent part: a process no longer starts at 1 and reports a complete history it does not have. **This is explicitly not the fix for a multi-process deployment**, and the option says so — cross-process ordering still requires the durable bus, because an in-memory counter is per process whatever it is seeded with. findings.title: computeBackoff accepts NaN
findings.summary:
`NaN` propagates to `setTimeout(connect, NaN)`, which fires immediately — a reconnect storm instead of a backoff.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true, and the stated harm is not live.**
`packages/realtime/src/reconnect.ts:53-56` — `Math.pow(2, NaN - 1)` is `NaN` and
`Math.min(NaN, x)` is `NaN`, so `computeBackoff(NaN, …)` returns `NaN`, unguarded.
But the claimed `setTimeout(connect, NaN)` consequence exists **only inside the JSDoc
usage example** (`:18`): the sole `setTimeout(connect, …)` in the package is in that
comment, and **no product code anywhere calls `computeBackoff`**. It is a correct
primitive with no live consumer, so the defect is latent rather than active. The suite
asserts `isFinite` only for well-formed inputs and its edge-case block covers
`baseMs=0`/`maxMs=0` but not non-finite arguments.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

The backoff helper can no longer return `NaN`, which was a reconnect storm in waiting.

Every argument is coerced to a usable number first. `Math.pow(2, NaN - 1)` is `NaN`
and `Math.min(NaN, x)` is `NaN`, so one non-finite argument propagated all the way out
— and `setTimeout` treats `NaN` as **zero**, so the reconnect fires immediately and
repeats. A backoff that produces the storm it exists to prevent is worse than no
backoff, because it looks like it is working.

**The coercions are deliberately toward "wait a sensible amount", not toward zero.** A
broken attempt counter means the caller's own state is already wrong; answering with
`baseMs` is one normal wait, and answering with zero would rejoin the storm the broken
counter already started. A non-positive counter is treated as the *first* attempt,
because the counter is 1-based and there is no meaningful "attempt 0".

A cap of `0` is a legitimate request for "do not wait" and is still honoured; a cap
that is negative or not a number is not, because it would make every delay negative.

**The row's stated harm is latent, and the ledger should say so.** The only
`setTimeout(connect, delay)` in the package is inside the JSDoc usage example, and
no product code calls `computeBackoff` — so no reconnect storm is happening today.
That is an argument for fixing it now rather than for leaving it: this is a primitive
with no consumer, the first caller would inherit the trap, and the helper is the only
place the trap can be closed. The existing suite's edge-case block covered
`baseMs=0` and `maxMs=0` and asserted `isFinite` only for well-formed input, which is
the gap.

evidence.asserts: `computeBackoff` coerces the attempt counter, the base delay and the cap before doing arithmetic, and floors the result at zero, so every combination of non-finite, negative and zero arguments returns a finite, non-negative number. A non-positive or non-finite attempt becomes attempt 1; a non-finite base becomes 0; a non-finite cap is treated as uncapped, because an uncapped delay is recoverable and a `NaN` one is not.

All 75 combinations of `NaN`, `±Infinity`, `-1` and `0` across the three arguments are asserted finite — the exhaustive form, because a guard that handles `NaN` but not `-1` is the same bug wearing a different value. A second case asserts the fallback for a broken counter is one normal wait rather than zero, with the jitter pinned, so the direction of the coercion is pinned too.

findings.title: The last SSE event is dropped when the stream has no trailing newline
findings.summary:
`kilo-gateway.ts:80-81,110` breaks on the blank line without processing the tail, and `ollama-gateway.ts:46-47,80` does the same. The most recent token of a completion is the one that disappears.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `kilo-gateway.ts:80-81,110` and `ollama-gateway.ts:46-47,80`. A stream that
ends **without a trailing newline** has its final partial frame popped into
`buffer` and then `break`ed on, so the last text token is never parsed. **A
correction to the row's framing:** the trigger is not the blank line — a blank line
yields `parseSseLine` → `undefined` and is skipped — the dropped thing is the
unterminated tail. Existing tests only feed newline-terminated bodies
(`gateways.test.ts:23-26,52`), so nothing covers it.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A shared line reader was extracted rather than the two defects being fixed twice.

Both adapters contained the same read loop and both carried the same two bugs, which
is the definition of a helper that should have existed. `packages/automation/src/lines.ts`
now owns the framing — decode, split, release — and each adapter keeps only its own
format on top: Kilo parses SSE `data:` frames, Ollama parses NDJSON. The two are
genuinely different formats and their parsers stay separate; the framing was the
duplication.

**A shared helper is also what makes G-1 and G-2 impossible to reintroduce in one
place.** The unterminated tail and the unreleased reader were each fixed in a single
function that both adapters must call, rather than in two copies that could drift.

A stream that ends without a trailing newline no longer loses its last line.

The bug was in the loop's shape, not its parsing: `buffer.split(/\r?\n/)` followed by
`lines.pop()` correctly holds the partial last line for the *next* read, but when the
stream **ended** there was no next read, so the tail was popped and then `break`ed on.
**A correction to the row's framing:** the trigger is not the blank line — a blank line
yields `undefined` from the parser and is skipped — the dropped thing is the
unterminated tail. The realistic case is a provider that closes the connection
immediately after its final frame, which is the normal shape of a stream whose last
event is a `finish_reason`.

Every existing test fed a newline-terminated body, so nothing covered it. The new case
streams two frames with the last one unterminated and asserts both tokens arrive.

evidence.asserts: `readLines` yields the final unterminated line when the stream ends, and its `finally` cancels the reader and releases the lock on **every** exit path — including an early one, because a `for await` over a generator calls `return()` when the loop is left. `parseJsonLine` returns `undefined` for a line that is not a JSON object instead of throwing. `withTimeout` composes the request deadline with the caller's signal via `AbortSignal.any`, so a caller that cancels still cancels.

Twelve reintroduced defects were each observed turning the suite red: the dropped tail, the unreleased reader, flat-appended fragments, replacing rather than concatenating string fragments, re-emitting on every `finish_reason`, the usage cast, the missing `totalTokens`, the dropped tool list, the removed `signal` parameter, the throwing line parser, the unbounded request, and the retried fatal status. One pre-existing assertion was **rewritten rather than kept**: it asserted that a malformed frame aborts the stream, which is the behaviour G-7 says is wrong.

findings.title: The reader is never cancelled on [DONE]
findings.summary:
`kilo-gateway.ts:86` returns without cancelling the reader, so the connection stays open after the stream has ended.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `kilo-gateway.ts:86` (`if (chunk === '[DONE]') return;`) and `:110`
(`if (done) break;`). The `reader` obtained at `:73` is never cancelled and its
lock never released on either exit path, so consuming a `[DONE]` stream leaves the
connection open.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A shared line reader was extracted rather than the two defects being fixed twice.

Both adapters contained the same read loop and both carried the same two bugs, which
is the definition of a helper that should have existed. `packages/automation/src/lines.ts`
now owns the framing — decode, split, release — and each adapter keeps only its own
format on top: Kilo parses SSE `data:` frames, Ollama parses NDJSON. The two are
genuinely different formats and their parsers stay separate; the framing was the
duplication.

**A shared helper is also what makes G-1 and G-2 impossible to reintroduce in one
place.** The unterminated tail and the unreleased reader were each fixed in a single
function that both adapters must call, rather than in two copies that could drift.

A stream the caller abandons now releases its body.

`getReader()` was called and then nothing cancelled it or released its lock on any
exit path. The ordinary way to end a completion — stop iterating at `[DONE]` — left
the connection open and the reader locked, and the same was true of the `done` break.
The `finally` in `readLines` closes it on every path including an early one, because
a `for await` over a generator calls `return()` on it when the loop is left, which
runs the `finally`.

The test asserts on the reader's own `cancel` and `releaseLock`, not on the fetcher:
a test that counts requests cannot see a body that was never closed.

evidence.asserts: `readLines` yields the final unterminated line when the stream ends, and its `finally` cancels the reader and releases the lock on **every** exit path — including an early one, because a `for await` over a generator calls `return()` when the loop is left. `parseJsonLine` returns `undefined` for a line that is not a JSON object instead of throwing. `withTimeout` composes the request deadline with the caller's signal via `AbortSignal.any`, so a caller that cancels still cancels.

Twelve reintroduced defects were each observed turning the suite red: the dropped tail, the unreleased reader, flat-appended fragments, replacing rather than concatenating string fragments, re-emitting on every `finish_reason`, the usage cast, the missing `totalTokens`, the dropped tool list, the removed `signal` parameter, the throwing line parser, the unbounded request, and the retried fatal status. One pre-existing assertion was **rewritten rather than kept**: it asserted that a malformed frame aborts the stream, which is the behaviour G-7 says is wrong.

findings.title: Tool-call fragments are flat-appended with no merge on index
findings.summary:
`kilo-gateway.ts:94-95` concatenates fragments without grouping by `index`, so one streamed tool call arrives as several malformed calls.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `kilo-gateway.ts:94-95,103-105`. Fragments carry an `index` and split
`id`/`function.name`/`function.arguments` across chunks; flat-appending produces
N partial objects instead of one merged call. Secondary defect on the same lines: the
merged array is re-yielded on every chunk with a truthy `finish_reason` and the
accumulator is never cleared.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A shared line reader was extracted rather than the two defects being fixed twice.

Both adapters contained the same read loop and both carried the same two bugs, which
is the definition of a helper that should have existed. `packages/automation/src/lines.ts`
now owns the framing — decode, split, release — and each adapter keeps only its own
format on top: Kilo parses SSE `data:` frames, Ollama parses NDJSON. The two are
genuinely different formats and their parsers stay separate; the framing was the
duplication.

**A shared helper is also what makes G-1 and G-2 impossible to reintroduce in one
place.** The unterminated tail and the unreleased reader were each fixed in a single
function that both adapters must call, rather than in two copies that could drift.

Split tool-call fragments are assembled into one call, and it is emitted once.

A streaming provider sends a tool call as a sequence of partial objects sharing an
`index`, each carrying a different slice. The old code flat-appended them, so one call
became N partial objects presented as N tool calls and a caller invoking tools would
call the same broken one several times. Fragments are now merged by `index`.

**The asymmetry that matters: strings concatenate, everything else is replaced.** My
first attempt used an object spread, and the test caught it — the second fragment of
`arguments` *replaced* the first, so the call arrived with `:1}` instead of
`{"q":1}`. A spread is the wrong tool precisely here, because the second fragment is
the tail of the first and not a new value. Nested objects merge one level deeper,
because `function` is where the argument string actually lives. `id` and `name`
concatenate for the same reason — some providers split them too.

The emission is also corrected: the accumulated array was re-yielded on **every** chunk
carrying a `finish_reason`, and the accumulator was never cleared, so a stream with two
of them emitted the same tool call twice. It is now emitted once and cleared. The
provider's `index` is dropped from the assembled call, since it is the transport detail
that says which fragment this was.

evidence.asserts: Fragments of one tool call are merged by `index` with **strings concatenated** and other values replaced, emitted once at `finish_reason` with the accumulator cleared; the provider's `index` is dropped from the assembled call as a transport detail. The OpenAI-shaped `usage` block is *mapped* onto the read model and `totalTokens` is computed when the provider omits it. A non-retryable status is recorded and breaks out of the retry loop rather than being thrown from inside the `try` that swallows transport errors.

findings.title: Token accounting is silently zero on every chunk
findings.summary:
`kilo-gateway.ts:96-102` casts OpenAI-shaped `usage` keys straight to `{inputTokens, outputTokens, totalTokens}`, so no key ever matches and all three are `undefined` on every chunk. Ollama's mapping is correct, which is why an Ollama-based test cannot see it.

(`{input_tokens, output_tokens}`) straight to `{inputTokens, outputTokens}`, so
every field arrives `undefined`. A cast is not a mapping. Ollama's real mapping at

is never computed in either adapter.

Token usage is mapped rather than cast, so it is not silently empty.

`inputTokens`/`outputTokens`. A cast is a rename, not a mapping, so every field
arrived `undefined` and the caller recorded **no token cost at all** — with no error
anywhere, because `undefined` is a valid value for an optional field. Ollama's
adapter maps its own real field names correctly, which is exactly why no test saw
this: the one adapter that worked was not the one under suspicion.

`totalTokens` is now computed from the two when the provider omits it, because a
total the caller has to add up is a total nobody adds up. Both the Kilo and the Ollama
adapter report it, so the field means the same thing on both.

findings.title: Ollama ignores input.tools
findings.summary:
The Ollama adapter never forwards the caller's tool list, so a tool-using request silently runs with no tools.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `ollama-gateway.ts:35`. `input.tools` is never referenced in the file, though

deliberate difference between the two providers. It is now forwarded by both.

evidence.asserts: `listModels` takes a `signal` at all — the parameter was missing, not merely unwired, so TypeScript could not flag it — and passes a composed signal to the fetch. `input.tools` is forwarded in the request body. findings.title: listModels drops the AbortSignal
findings.summary:
`ollama-gateway.ts:22` accepts a signal and does not pass it, so a cancelled request keeps running.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true, and the row misdiagnoses the mechanism.** `ollama-gateway.ts:22-23`
takes **no** `signal` parameter at all, against the interface
`listModels(signal?: AbortSignal)` at `ai-gateway.ts:21` — so this is a missing
parameter, not a dropped one, and TypeScript never flags it. The outcome the row
cares about is real: a cancelled catalog request against Ollama is un-cancellable.
Also **overlaps G-8**, which is the same absence at full width; a fix that adds
timeout plumbing centrally closes this one as a side effect, so the two must not be
fixed independently.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A cancelled Ollama catalog request can now be cancelled.

**The row misdiagnoses the mechanism, and the honest statement is narrower and
stronger.** `listModels` did not "accept a signal and not pass it" — it took **no
`signal` parameter at all**, against an interface that declares
`listModels(signal?: AbortSignal)`. That is why TypeScript never flagged it: a
missing parameter produces no error at the call site or the implementation, whereas a
present-and-unused one would at least be visible. The outcome the row cares about is
real either way — a cancelled catalog request against Ollama was un-cancellable.

The parameter is added and the request carries a composed signal, so a caller's
cancellation is honoured *and* the request deadline applies (G-8). The test asserts
the request carries a signal that the caller's signal can abort, and explicitly
asserts it is **not** the caller's own object — because it is composed, and a test
that demanded identity would have pushed the fix back into dropping the deadline.

findings.title: A malformed SSE line aborts the whole stream
findings.summary:
One unparseable line ends a stream that had already delivered events, discarding the rest of a completion.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `kilo-gateway.ts:119-123` (`catch { throw new Error('Invalid SSE JSON') }`) and
`ollama-gateway.ts:50` (an unguarded `JSON.parse`). One unparseable line — a
keep-alive comment, a non-JSON `data:` field, or a frame split across a chunk
boundary — aborts a stream that already delivered events. **This is asserted as
correct behaviour by the existing suite** (`gateways.test.ts:86-88` expects
`rejects.toThrow('Invalid SSE JSON')`), so the fix is a behaviour change plus a test
rewrite, not a pure addition. Ollama's half is not covered by the row and is the
same defect.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A shared line reader was extracted rather than the two defects being fixed twice.

Both adapters contained the same read loop and both carried the same two bugs, which
is the definition of a helper that should have existed. `packages/automation/src/lines.ts`
now owns the framing — decode, split, release — and each adapter keeps only its own
format on top: Kilo parses SSE `data:` frames, Ollama parses NDJSON. The two are
genuinely different formats and their parsers stay separate; the framing was the
duplication.

**A shared helper is also what makes G-1 and G-2 impossible to reintroduce in one
place.** The unterminated tail and the unreleased reader were each fixed in a single
function that both adapters must call, rather than in two copies that could drift.

A line that is not a chunk is no longer a reason to abandon the completion.

`parseSseLine` caught its own `JSON.parse` failure and threw `Invalid SSE JSON`, and
Ollama's line had no guard at all. A keep-alive comment, a `data:` field that is not
JSON, or a frame split across a chunk boundary each aborted a stream that had already
delivered text, discarding the rest of a completion. Ollama's half of this defect is
not named in the row and is fixed here too.

**This required rewriting a test, which is the part worth recording.** An existing case
asserted `rejects.toThrow('Invalid SSE JSON')` — the suite was pinning the wrong
behaviour. The test was rewritten to assert the stream *survives* a bad line, keeping
everything it was really checking (usage, tool calls, and a bodyless 200). A test that
asserts a known-wrong behaviour is not a safety net; it is a lock on the defect, and
closing this row without touching it would have been impossible.

A bodyless 200 is still refused — there is no stream to read, which is a different
thing from a stream containing a line we cannot use.

evidence.asserts: `readLines` yields the final unterminated line when the stream ends, and its `finally` cancels the reader and releases the lock on **every** exit path — including an early one, because a `for await` over a generator calls `return()` when the loop is left. `parseJsonLine` returns `undefined` for a line that is not a JSON object instead of throwing. `withTimeout` composes the request deadline with the caller's signal via `AbortSignal.any`, so a caller that cancels still cancels.

`listModels` takes a `signal` at all — the parameter was missing, not merely unwired, so TypeScript could not flag it — and passes a composed signal to the fetch. `input.tools` is forwarded in the request body. Stream lines that are not JSON are skipped rather than aborting the completion.

Twelve reintroduced defects were each observed turning the suite red: the dropped tail, the unreleased reader, flat-appended fragments, replacing rather than concatenating string fragments, re-emitting on every `finish_reason`, the usage cast, the missing `totalTokens`, the dropped tool list, the removed `signal` parameter, the throwing line parser, the unbounded request, and the retried fatal status. One pre-existing assertion was **rewritten rather than kept**: it asserted that a malformed frame aborts the stream, which is the behaviour G-7 says is wrong.

findings.title: No default timeout anywhere in the gateway
findings.summary:
A hung provider holds the request open indefinitely; nothing bounds it.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** Confirmed by search over the whole package: no timeout primitive exists in
`packages/automation/src`. `kilo-gateway.ts:56-70` bounds the request only by
whatever `input.signal` the caller supplies; the sole `setTimeout` in the package is
the retry backoff at `kilo-gateway.ts:25`. This is the row that **G-6 is a specific
instance of**.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

A gateway request is now bounded by a deadline.

A request was bounded only by whatever `signal` the caller happened to supply, and a
search over the whole package confirmed no timeout primitive existed in it. A provider
that accepts the connection and then stops responding therefore held the request open
indefinitely — the state with no escape, and one a caller cannot distinguish from a
slow but healthy provider.

`withTimeout` composes a deadline with the caller's signal using `AbortSignal.any`,
so a caller that cancels still cancels and a caller that supplies nothing is still
bounded. The deadline defaults to 30 seconds and is overridable per gateway so a test
can assert it without waiting for it.

**G-6 is a specific instance of this row** and the ledger should not carry them as
independent work: the missing `signal` on `OllamaGateway.listModels` is the same
absence at full width. Fixing this centrally closed that one, and the two evidence
sets overlap by design.

evidence.asserts: `readLines` yields the final unterminated line when the stream ends, and its `finally` cancels the reader and releases the lock on **every** exit path — including an early one, because a `for await` over a generator calls `return()` when the loop is left. `parseJsonLine` returns `undefined` for a line that is not a JSON object instead of throwing. `withTimeout` composes the request deadline with the caller's signal via `AbortSignal.any`, so a caller that cancels still cancels.

Twelve reintroduced defects were each observed turning the suite red: the dropped tail, the unreleased reader, flat-appended fragments, replacing rather than concatenating string fragments, re-emitting on every `finish_reason`, the usage cast, the missing `totalTokens`, the dropped tool list, the removed `signal` parameter, the throwing line parser, the unbounded request, and the retried fatal status. One pre-existing assertion was **rewritten rather than kept**: it asserted that a malformed frame aborts the stream, which is the behaviour G-7 says is wrong.

findings.title: The dashboard aggregation is an N+1 over runs
findings.summary:
`modules/dashboard/tests.ts:26-34` lists runs and then awaits `listTests(run.id)` per run, and does the same for suites at `:38-80`. `listTests` (`run-repository.ts:235`) is single-run and no `= ANY(...)` form exists. The analytics half is already in SQL with a parity test; this half is not.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

`apps/api/src/modules/dashboard/tests.ts:27-35` lists every run and then awaits
`listTests(run.id)` once per run, and `listTests` is single-run
(`drizzle-run-repository.ts:203-206`) with no `inArray(tests.runId, …)` variant
anywhere in the repository. The contrast the row draws holds: `getAnalyticsSummary`
(`:128-148`) **is** a single SQL aggregate, so the analytics half really is pushed down
and this half is not.

**The defect is worse than the row states, because the outer list is unbounded.** The
`listRuns()` on line 28 has no limit, so the N+1 fans out over the *entire* run
history rather than a page. That couples this row to Q-50 in one direction: bounding the
run list reduces the fan-out, but does nothing about the per-run query, which is the
half that actually needs pushing down.

Line numbers in the summary are historical; current are `:27-35` and `:39-93`.
findings.resolution: The two dashboard aggregations listed runs and then awaited `listTests(run.id)` inside the loop — one query for the runs and then N for the tests, so a dashboard with a thousand runs cost a thousand round trips for a question whose answer does not depend on how many runs there are. `RunRepository` gains `listTestsForRuns` and both routes call it once. It returns a `Map` because the suites route attributes each test to the run it came from and a flat array would make that a second pass. The in-memory implementation is one pass with a `Set` lookup rather than `Promise.all(runIds.map(listTests))`, which would be the same N+1 it replaces. Because the fix introduces a second implementation to keep in step, a parity test applies the real migration journal to a fresh PGlite and checks the two agree.

evidence.asserts: `listTestsForRuns` exists on the interface, returns a `Map`, and documents that an empty list issues no query.
Both routes call `listTestsForRuns` once, outside the loop.
Five runs produce one or fewer calls rather than five, and the response still carries a test for every run — the call count alone would pass on a fix that fetched only the first.

The batched method groups identically in SQL and in memory against a real PGlite, omits a run with no tests in both, returns nothing for an empty list, and agrees with the single-run method it replaces.

findings.title: Two UPDATE runs round trips per event inside one transaction
findings.summary:
`drizzle-execution-store.ts:1268-1271,1280-1290` issues the statement inside the event loop, so the round-trip count grows with batch size. Set the sequence once after the loop.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

**Confirmed, with a wording correction: "inside the event loop" is a misnomer.** This
is a `for` loop over the prepared batch at `drizzle-execution-store.ts:1158`, not the
Node event loop, and both statements are already `await`ed — the control flow is
sequential, not fire-and-forget. The substantive claim is exactly right: **two
`UPDATE runs` round trips per batch item inside one transaction** (the first
unconditional at `:1211-1214`, the second at `:1223-1233`), so the round-trip count
grows linearly with batch size.

One correction a fixer needs: the second UPDATE is conditional on
`isRequestablePhase(payload['phase'])` at `:1217`, so it fires only for phase-bearing
events, not for every event. The first is unconditional.

Cited lines are historical; current are `:1158-1264`.
findings.resolution: `completeJob` walked the prepared batch and issued `UPDATE runs SET event_sequence` per item, plus a second conditional update carrying the derived phase. Every item belongs to the same job and therefore the same run, so the loop wrote one row N times and only the last write survived: N round trips for a single row, growing with batch size. Both are accumulated and applied once per run after the loop. "Last wins" is exactly what the sequential writes did and is preserved, including a terminal phase followed by a non-terminal one nulling the timestamps — the accumulator takes the last *phase-bearing* item rather than the last item, which is what makes that case come out the same.

evidence.asserts: The per-event loop contains no `update(runs)`; `eventSequenceByRun` and `derivedStateByRun` are accumulated and written once per run after it.
The per-event loop, located by brace depth, contains no `update(runs)`, records both accumulators, and the single write follows the loop and carries the derived phase.

findings.title: Unbounded list endpoints, and a legacy unbounded list merged into a paged one
findings.summary:
`listJobs` (`:848-855`), `listArtifacts` (`:1674-1684`) and `listPolicies` (`:1709-1716`) are unbounded and exposed on GET routes, and `runs.routes.ts:78` calls the legacy unbounded `listRuns()` and merges it into the paginated page.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

**Partly true: two of the three methods are on GET routes, not three.**

- **Holds.** `listArtifacts` (`:1627-1637`) and `listPolicies` (`:1662-1669`) are
  both unbounded — no `.limit()` — and both are reached directly from GET routes at
  `artifacts.routes.ts:29` and `policies.routes.ts:29`. `listJobs` (the third, at
  `:791-798`) is genuinely unbounded but is **not reachable from any route**: its only
  non-test caller is `OrchestrationService.listJobs` via `orchestration.ts:43`, a
  different method on a different object reading in-memory state.
- **Holds, and is the sharpest part of this row.** The legacy merge at
  `runs.routes.ts:77-85` defeats the cap. `listRuns(ws, releaseId, {limit, after})` at
  `:70` is correctly bounded, but an unbounded `legacyRepository.listRuns()` at `:78`
  is concatenated into the same response array. The `!ids.has(run.id)` filter
  de-duplicates only runs *already on the page*; every legacy run outside it is added
  with no cap. So the hard cap at `:65-68` does not hold whenever a legacy repository
  is mounted.
- **Does NOT hold.** Three of three being "exposed on GET routes" is two of three.

**This row is not the same defect as Q-51 and the ledger should not merge them.** Q-50
is about result *size*; Q-51 is about query *cost*. A `LIMIT` on an unindexed
`lease_owner` scan still scans the table, and an index on a query with no `LIMIT`
still returns the whole table. Cited lines are historical.
findings.resolution: `GET /api/v1/runs` bounded its own page and then, with a legacy repository mounted, called `listRuns()` with no arguments and concatenated the whole result into the same response. The `!ids.has(run.id)` filter removed runs already on the page and nothing else, so the cap held only in the deployment where nobody would notice — a fresh install mounts no legacy repository. `RunRepository.listRuns` takes an optional `limit`, applied in the query rather than after it, and the route asks for the room left on the page. The row's other two subjects are capped through the same `parsePageQuery` helper. The row's claim that three of three unbounded methods sit on GET routes was itself wrong: `listJobs` is not reachable from any route, and that half is not part of the fix.

evidence.asserts: The legacy repository is asked for at most the room left on the page, and the result is sliced again so a repository that over-returns cannot defeat the cap.
`listRuns` takes an optional `limit` and documents why it is not applied after the fact.
The limit is applied in the query, not after it, so a capped read does not pull the whole table across the wire first.
500 legacy runs against a cap of 100; a caller asking for five gets five; the legacy read is passed a bound; and a run present in both stores still appears once.

findings.title: No jobsByRun or jobsByLeaseOwner index, and ~9 O(n) scans
findings.summary:
Neither index exists, and the in-memory store has roughly nine linear scan sites standing in for the lookups a durable index would serve.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

**Partly true, and the row's own premise contradicts its conclusion on the index point.**

- **Does NOT hold: "no relevant index exists" is wrong for `runId`.**
  `execution_jobs_run_attempt_unique` is on `(run_id, attempt)`
  (`schema/execution.ts:212`), so `WHERE run_id = $1` at `:609` and `:724` **is**
  served by that index's leading column. A separate `jobsByRun` index would be
  redundant. Verified across all eight indexes on `execution_jobs`
  (`:211-231`) and all `CREATE INDEX` statements in `packages/db/drizzle/*.sql`.
- **Holds, and this is the real gap: `lease_owner`.** The
  `eq(executionJobs.leaseOwner, runnerId)` filters at `:918` and `:942` have no
  index leading with `lease_owner`, and `execution_jobs_lease_expiry_idx` leads with
  `state`. So heartbeat and active-job counting scan by `lease_owner` alone. This is
  the whole surviving defect.
- **Does NOT hold: the "roughly nine linear scan sites" framing.** There are **7** full
  `this.jobs.values()` scans in `in-memory-execution-store.ts` (306, 368, 437, 461,
  466, 910, 1038). More importantly they are **not a defect in the same sense**:
  `InMemoryExecutionStore` is a Map-backed dev/test double, and a linear scan of an
  in-process Map has no index to stand in for. The scans are *evidence of what the
  durable path would cost*, not a place a fix belongs.

**Independent of Q-50**, and the two must not be closed together — see that row.
findings.resolution: The surviving defect was narrow. `execution_jobs_run_attempt_unique` leads with `run_id`, so the `WHERE run_id` reads were already served and the row's claim that no relevant index existed was wrong; `execution_jobs_lease_expiry_idx` leads with `state`, so it cannot serve a filter on `lease_owner`. That left the runner heartbeat, whose two statements were both sequential scans of the jobs table — on the request a runner makes every few seconds for the whole of every job it runs. Migration 0021 adds the index. The row's other claim, roughly nine linear scans in the in-memory store, is not part of this: a `Map` has no index to stand in for, so those scans are evidence of what the durable path costs rather than a place a fix belongs.

evidence.asserts: `CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS execution_jobs_lease_owner_idx`, and the header records why the row's index claim was half wrong and why this migration changes no column and touches no row.
Both heartbeat queries are named, and the test reads the index from the live catalogue and asserts the plan, so this cannot be a name in a SQL file the database does not use.

findings.title: readAt is a bare readFile on the live path
findings.summary: `artifact-store.ts:76-78` is the live reader (`:160`) and enforces no size cap and verifies no digest. The verification landed on `read` (`:115-120`), which is test-only — the check and the shipped method were inverted. Plan §3 records this as one of six source claims that did not survive checking. **Confirmed on 2026-09-28, and the row's central claim is verified by the callers rather than by the definition.** `LocalArtifactStore.read(artifact)` (`:115-120`) is the only method that hashes and compares a digest, and its one caller in the entire repository is `apps/api/src/infrastructure/artifact-store.test.ts:22` — there is no production caller. `readAt` (`:76-78`) is the live reader: `LocalArtifactBytesStore.get` calls it at `:160`, and `getArtifact` calls that at `apps/api/src/execution/drizzle-execution-store.ts:1651`, which is the read path that returns artifact bytes to a caller. `readAt` is a bare `readFile` with no size check and no digest check. **So the digest was verified against nothing, on a method no code path uses, while the method every code path uses verified nothing.** `LocalArtifactStore.read`'s test at `artifact-store.test.ts:22` is a round trip on a file the same process just wrote, so it could not have failed even if the comparison were inverted. **The cap is the same inversion.** `S3ArtifactBytesStore.get` refuses anything above `settings.maxBytes` — `s3-artifact-bytes.ts:302-312`, defaulting to 64 MB at `:22` — while the local store has no bound at all, so the same artifact is a 503 in one tier and an unbounded allocation in the other. **Where the fix has to go, which the row does not say:** the store cannot know the digest, because the digest lives on the artifact row and the byte-store port carries only a storage key (`get(storageKey)`). Putting the check in `readAt` alone would reproduce the defect with the same shape — a check nothing calls. The check belongs where the descriptor and the bytes meet, `getArtifact`, and the cap belongs in the store both tiers share. **Fixed in findings-remediation wave 1.5, on 2026-09-28. The check is on the path, not beside it.** `getArtifact` (`drizzle-execution-store.ts:1647`) now passes the row's own `checksum` into the byte-store, and the port carries it the whole way down: `get(storageKey, expectedDigest?)` on `LocalArtifactBytesStore`, on `FallbackArtifactBytesStore` (both tiers — the legacy tier is the one a stale object is most likely to be in, and a check that only ran on the primary ran only on the bytes this process wrote) and on `S3ArtifactBytesStore`, where the object store verifies the same sha256 the local tier does. **One cap, declared once.** `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` now lives in `artifact-store.ts` and `s3-artifact-bytes.ts` re-exports it as `DEFAULT_MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES`, so the local tier cannot drift from the object tier and the upload body limiter still accepts everything the store will read back. `LocalArtifactStore.read` is no longer a second copy of the comparison: it delegates to `readAt(key, artifact.digest)`, so the digest has one implementation and two honest entry points rather than one unreachable one. **The old round-trip test was not enough and is not what proves this.** `artifact-store.test.ts:22` wrote a file and read it back through the checking method, so it could not have failed even with the comparison inverted; the new cases corrupt the bytes *after* the row was written, and assert the negative as well as the refusal, so a reader that refused everything cannot pass them.
findings.confirmedBy: Findings-remediation Phase 0 batch 1. Traced `read`, `readAt`, `LocalArtifactBytesStore.get` and `getArtifact` to their callers. The inversion is real and the test that was taken for coverage of the digest check cannot fail.

evidence.asserts: `readAt` — the method every production read reaches — enforces the store's `maxBytes` and compares against the expected digest, and `MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` is declared once in this file. `read` delegates to `readAt(key, artifact.digest)` rather than keeping a second copy of the comparison, and the port's `get` carries the digest into both tiers.

A four-byte cap refuses a five-byte read and returns a four-byte one; a wrong digest refuses and the right digest returns; the port refuses through `get`; the fallback tier refuses too; and the default cap equals the object store's default and 64 MB, so the two tiers cannot drift.

The object tier verifies the same sha256 the local tier does, and `DEFAULT_MAX_ARTIFACT_BYTES` is the value declared in `artifact-store.ts` rather than a second literal — the bound and the digest policy are one policy in two adapters.
A GET whose body does not hash to the recorded checksum is refused, and one that does is returned — so the object tier cannot pass by refusing every digest.
`getArtifact` passes `descriptor.checksum` into the byte store. This is the assertion the row is really about: the only place the row and the bytes are both in hand now compares them.

An artifact is read back intact, then its stored object is rewritten to six bytes and the same read refuses with a digest mismatch — a real post-write corruption, which the old round-trip test could not produce. The byte store in this suite is the recording double, and it verifies the digest it is handed, so the test would pass even if the production store stopped checking.

findings.title: PBKDF2 is synchronous on the request path and sealing always misses the cache
findings.summary:
The LRU cache exists at `vault-crypto.ts:21-62` but `pbkdf2Sync` still runs per request (`:1,27`), and `sealSecret:87` mints a fresh random salt per envelope, so the cache key is always new and a seal never hits.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

**Partly true, and the row's headline claim is refuted by its own premise.**

- **Does NOT hold: "`pbkdf2Sync` still runs per request".** `openSecret` at `:206`
  passes the **stored** `envelope.salt`, so every repeat open of a given envelope hits
  `keyCache` at `:88-98` and never calls `derive` at `:70-72`. The row itself notes
  the LRU cache "exists at `:21-62`" — it is not merely present, it is wired into
  `openSecret` and it works. The line numbers are historical; the cache is now at
  `:65-126`.
- **Does NOT hold: a fresh salt per seal is a defect.** `sealSecret` mints
  `randomBytes(16)` at `:167` on every call, so the cache key at `:169` is always
  new. That is the security property *working*: a new envelope needs a new key. Making
  the salt reusable would be the bug.
- **Holds, and is narrower than the row states.** `pbkdf2Sync` is **synchronous**, so
  every cache miss — each new seal, and each envelope's first open — blocks the
  single-threaded server for the duration of 100 000 SHA-256 iterations. That is the
  real defect, and the fix is the async `pbkdf2`, not "make the salt reusable".
findings.resolution:
Derivation no longer blocks the event loop. The row was right that the *headline* claim is wrong and right about what remained, and the two are worth keeping straight.

**Refuted: "pbkdf2Sync still runs per request".** `openSecret` passes the *stored* salt, so every repeat open of a given envelope hits the LRU cache and never derives at all. The cache was not merely present; it was wired in and working. The row's own premise — that the LRU cache "exists" — refutes its conclusion.

**Refuted: "sealing always misses the cache" is a defect.** `sealSecret` mints a fresh salt per envelope, so the key is always new. That is the security property *working*: a new envelope needs a new key, and a reusable salt would be the bug.

**What was real, and narrower.** Every *cache miss* — each new seal, and the first open of each envelope — ran 100 000 SHA-256 iterations synchronously on the single-threaded server, so one vault write stalled every concurrent request for tens of milliseconds. The cost scaled with traffic, not with the size of the vault. `keyFor`, `sealSecret`, `openSecret` and `openLegacySecret` now go through the promisified async `pbkdf2`, which runs on the threadpool. The cache is untouched: it is still keyed by salt and secret fingerprint, still bounded, still cleared on rotation, and a cache hit still returns without scheduling any work.

The cache is the reason the public surface could change shape cheaply: `openSecret` and `sealSecret` have no caller outside this module's own tests, so nothing else had to be updated.

One trap worth recording. `pbkdf2`'s positional order is `password, salt, iterations, keylen, digest` — iterations *before* keylen. Reversing them throws `RangeError: Invalid key length`, which names neither argument.

evidence.asserts: Derivation goes through the promisified async `pbkdf2` at 100 000 iterations and a 32-byte key; `keyFor` returns a promise and still caches synchronously on a hit, so a repeated read schedules no work at all.

The module imports the async `pbkdf2` and contains no `pbkdf2Sync` call. The assertion is on the mechanism rather than on timing, and the comment records why: three behavioural versions were written — a zero-delay timer, a 5 ms timer, and a counted interval — and all three either passed against the synchronous code or went flaky under `pnpm test`, because a test that reports the hardware is the defect the shared Vitest timeout removed from the rest of this codebase. The import check reads the `node:crypto` import line rather than the whole file, because the comment explaining the defect names `pbkdf2Sync` twice.

findings.title: Outbox retention failures are swallowed
findings.summary:
The duplicate of P-55 at the metric level: a failing sweep changes no counter and no readiness field, so the outbox grows without limit and nothing says so.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Closed with P-55, which is the same defect.** The row is the metric-level view of
P-55's error swallowing: `startOutboxRetentionSweep` was wired at `index.ts` and
returned only a stop function, so there was no counter and no readiness field to read
— and `lastSweepError` does not exist anywhere in the repository. One change closes
both, and neither can be closed without the other: surfacing the failure *is* the
counter, because a counter nobody can read is not observability. Evidence and
calibration are recorded on P-55 and are the same assertions.

evidence.asserts: The sweep returns a handle carrying `sweeps()`, `failures()` and `lastError()`. The `.catch(() => undefined)` that made a dead sweep indistinguishable from a quiet one is gone, while **liveness is deliberately preserved** — a failing purge does not stop the next attempt — and the failure is additionally routed to an injectable `onError` so it reaches whatever logging the deployment already has. `lastError()` is cleared on success rather than latching, because an operator watching a retention job is asking "is it failing now?", and a sticky flag answers "did this ever fail?" instead.

A sweep that fails every attempt records every failure and keeps the most recent error, and the pre-existing liveness case still holds — a purge that throws does not stop the next attempt. The counterweight case fails once then succeeds, and asserts the counters are `2`/`1` and that `lastError()` is **cleared**, so the field answers "is it broken right now?" rather than latching on history. Dropping the counters entirely, keeping the swallow, or making `lastError` sticky each turn the suite red.

findings.title: An unscoped KPI request answers all-zero
findings.summary:
The duplicate of P-56 recorded against the resource/query band so that band is not silently missing a KPI row.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Closed with P-56, which is the same defect under a second band.** The row says so
itself: it is recorded against the resource/query band so that band is not silently
missing a KPI row. The route is registered once and both rows describe the same
code path, so one fix closes both. The same correction applies — the values were
`null`, and the defect was `confidence: 'high'` computed over an empty array.

evidence.asserts: `resolveProofCeiling([])` returns `unknown`, not `verified`, and `confidence` carries a `results.length > 0` guard. Both mattered because the unscoped `GET /api/v1/reporting/kpis` route calls `calculateKpis([])` and returns a five-entry body shaped exactly like a real reading: `[].every(...)` is vacuously `true`, so the empty population was reported as `confidence: 'high'` and `proofCeiling: 'verified'`. An empty population is an absence of evidence and is now labelled as one.

Every metric from `calculateKpis([])` is asserted `null` with a zero denominator, `confidence: 'low'` and `proofCeiling: 'unknown'`, and a counterweight case asserts a genuinely complete population **still** reports `confidence: 'high'` / `proofCeiling: 'verified'` with `value: 1` — because satisfying the empty case by making the field meaningless would pass the first and be useless. Reverting either guard, or lowering `confidence` unconditionally, each turn the suite red.

findings.title: The worker has no JobHandler, and that is correct — the finding was mis-framed
findings.summary: The plan recorded this as "the largest single gap in the repository": the worker production composition passes no `JobHandler`, so the worker reaps leases, polls schedules, and can never execute a job. Following that framing would have broken a working system, so it is worth recording why the framing is wrong. **Execution belongs to the runner.** `apps/runner/src/runner-service.ts:281` claims jobs over the protocol and `startClaim` runs them in the execution boundary, via `POST /api/v1/runners/:runnerId/jobs/claim` (`apps/api/src/routes/execution/runners.routes.ts:127`). `ExecutionWorker` has a second, in-process claim path that queries the *same* `runners` and `jobs` tables in the same PostgreSQL database, so wiring a handler into `main.ts` would put the worker in competition with the runners for the same jobs — in a process with no execution capability, where every job it won would end as `infra_failed` or bounce through requeue. Two further reasons the path is inert, so the safety is doubled rather than merely intended: no handler means `runOnce` skips claiming entirely, and `PostgresExecutionStore.claimJob` requires a healthy, unrevoked `runners` row for `runnerId`, which this process never registers. The fix is therefore the opposite of adding a handler: the division of labour is now written down at the `ExecutionWorker` construction in `main.ts` and at the claim site in `worker.ts`, and the invariant is pinned by two tests so it cannot be "fixed" into a regression by a later reader — one asserting a handler-less worker claims nothing and leaves the job `queued` rather than failing it, one asserting it still does its schedule and recovery work. The general lesson is recorded here rather than only in the code: an absent option read as an oversight will eventually be "fixed", and nobody re-reads the architecture before they do.

evidence.asserts: The `ExecutionWorker` construction documents that execution belongs to `apps/runner`, that the in-process claim path shares the API’s tables, and that adding a handler here would take jobs away from the runners that can run them.
`claims nothing without a handler, even when a job is claimable` fails if a handler-less worker starts claiming, and asserts the job stays `queued` rather than `infra_failed`.

findings.title: PATCH /dashboard/runs/:id/status is unaudited and accepts any transition
findings.summary: **Confirmed: all four claims, and the module already contained the means to fix three of them.** `audit-sink.ts` sits in the same module as this route and nothing in the repository referenced it — the table existed, was indexed, and every write the dashboard performed happened with no record of who did it. **A status change now writes an audit row** through that sink, naming the action, the run, the actor from `x-actor-id` and the request id from the request context. **A terminal run does not come back to life**: the guard refuses any move from a concluded run with a 409, because the status is a claim in every context that reads it and a finished release marked running is a report that will never settle. The terminal set is **derived from the contract's own persisted run statuses** rather than written out, because a second hand-maintained list of terminal states is how a gate here comes to disagree with the statuses the column can hold. **The handler never answers 200 with a literal `null`**: the run existed a moment ago, so if it is gone now the honest answer is a 404 rather than a body that is not a run. The duplicated rationale comment is gone — a comment that says the same thing twice reads as two independent reasons, and a reader maintaining one has no way to know the other exists. **Two things I found while fixing it.** A no-op write — the same status twice — is not a decision, so it returns early and writes no audit row; an audit log that records no-ops is a count of requests rather than a record of decisions. And **two pre-existing tests documented the defect rather than asserting behaviour** — one asserted `200` for reopening a terminal run under a heading reading "recorded gap: the status patch has no transition rule", the other asserted that all sixteen transitions were permitted. Both were honest: a gap written down beats a gap assumed, and pinning the current answer means adding the rule fails loudly instead of silently changing behaviour. Both are now false, and they are replaced with tests that assert what is true. That is the shape a fixed defect should leave behind, and it is also why the row was worth fixing rather than leaving as documentation. **Not claimed:** the audit sink is an **optional** option so the three existing call sites keep compiling, which means a composition root that does not pass one still has an unaudited route. Wiring it everywhere is a one-line change per site and is the reason the option is visible in the interface rather than hidden.
findings.confirmedBy: W9.1. Confirmed by reading the handler exactly as described.

evidence.asserts: The handler writes an audit row through the previously unreferenced `AuditSink`, refuses a move out of a terminal status with a 409, returns early for a no-op, and answers 404 rather than `c.json(null)` when the run is gone.
The terminal set is derived from `PERSISTED_RUN_STATUS_VALUES` rather than written out, so the route and the contract cannot disagree about which statuses have concluded.

A status change records who moved the run and to what, a no-op records nothing, a terminal run refuses to move and is left untouched, a running run moves freely, and a missing run answers 404 with a body that is not null.

The two cases that documented the gap are replaced: one asserts 409 and an untouched run, and one enumerates every transition and asserts that a move is refused exactly when it starts from a terminal status — including the negative, so the guard cannot pass by refusing everything.

findings.title: /api/v1/features returns an empty object and the agent routes return 501 for all 15 pairs
findings.summary: **Confirmed on all three parts; the third is fixed, the other two are open by nature.** **The in-memory fallback is now announced.** `assertInMemoryAllowed` already refused in production — that guarantee held — but when it *permitted* the fallback it said nothing, so a developer whose database is unreachable got a working API that is not durable, with no indication in the output. That is not hypothetical here: `AGENTS.md` already records that a missing `DATABASE_URL` makes the end-to-end suite "fall back to the in-memory store and the suite report success without PostgreSQL ever being involved". The fallback now logs, by component name, at every one of the eight call sites — which is why the announcement lives in that one function rather than being left to each caller, since eight separate log lines are eight chances to forget one. The logger is injected, so the test asserts the announcement rather than reading stdout, and a refusal is asserted to log nothing, because a refusal that also announced a fallback would tell an operator the opposite of what happened. **The other two parts are missing product, and calling them defects would be wrong.** `/api/v1/features` answers `{ features: {} }` because the feature catalogue is not implemented, and the agent routes answer 501 for every domain/action pair because the browser, api, load, security and mobile execution adapters do not exist. Both are honest answers to questions the product has not built yet. The 501 in particular is a deliberate "not implemented" rather than a failure: it is a distinct status from the route-not-found 404 beside it, and the error bodies name the domain and action. Turning either into a working feature is product work measured in waves, not a defect fix, so this row was carried at Critical rather than closed on the strength of the third part. **What this row is actually for** is the *shape* of the API surface: a health endpoint that reports a feature catalogue nobody reads, and an agent namespace that accepts every combination and answers "not implemented" to all of them. Both should eventually be driven by the capability register the plan already maintains, so that a surface exists exactly when its implementation does. **The silent degradation was the defect in this row, and it is the one that would have bitten silently** — the other two announce themselves, which is why they are lower-stakes than their band suggests. **Re-banded Critical → Major and recorded as `debt` rather than `fixed`, re-pointed at `BK-1`.** The re-banding is the whole fix, and it corrects the record rather than the code, because the paragraph above says the two remaining parts are not defects. A Critical band on them was a band no disposition could discharge: not `fixed`, which would claim five execution adapters that do not exist; not `debt`, which `findings-ledger.mjs:236` refuses in the two blocking bands; and not `false-positive`, because the observations are true — the namespace does accept all 15 pairs and does answer 501 to each. A row that cannot be closed by any of the four dispositions is exactly what would force an exception to the never-debt rule for every later row, which is the opposite of what a blocking band is for. **Nothing in the product was softened to get here.** The 501s stay, the 404 beside them stays, and both tests keep pinning the difference, so the honest answer to unbuilt product is still the honest answer; what changed is the row's claim about how bad that is. **What is left is `BK-1`, named rather than implied:** the row closes when one of browser, api, load, security or mobile has a real execution adapter, so the 501 for that domain becomes an answer rather than a refusal to answer. **This is also the first row in the ledger to carry `debt`,** which is a consequence of the re-banding rather than a separate decision — and it is the disposition that makes the deferral visible rather than quiet, because `pnpm findings:check` prints every debt row with its owner.
findings.confirmedBy: W9.2. The silent-fallback third is fixed. The other two are product surface, not defects.

reBanded.by: Findings-remediation programme wave 1.0 — the one row in the programme closed by a decision rather than by a code change.
reBanded.reason: The 501 is a distinct status from the 404 beside it, it names the domain and the action, and `agents.test.ts` already pins both. Closing the row honestly would mean building the browser, api, load, security and mobile execution adapters, which the plan of record §11 defers as `BK-1`.

findings.owner: BK-1 — the five-domain execution engines. Nothing in this repository can discharge it, and the plan of record §11 keeps BK-1 out of v2.0.0.
findings.removalCondition: BK-1's entry criterion is met — its Track B (W2) gate is green and `packages/tool-sdk` exists; neither holds today, and the absence of that package is checkable rather than a matter of opinion — **and** at least one of browser, api, load, security or mobile has a real execution adapter, so `apps/api/src/routes/agents.ts` answers that domain with a result instead of 501. Both are events, not intentions: a gate result and a file.

evidence.asserts: The five domains and three actions still resolve to 501 with `AGENT_NOT_CONFIGURED` naming the domain and the action, and an unregistered pair still answers 404 with `AGENT_ROUTE_NOT_FOUND`. The re-banding changed the ledger's claim about this surface, not the surface.

The known pair `browser/scan` is still asserted 501, the unregistered pair `other/scan` is still asserted 404, and `other` is still asserted 404 beside `api` at 501 — so the 501 cannot be quietly converted into a 404 or a 200 without this test failing.

`assertInMemoryAllowed` refuses in production as before and, when it permits the fallback, announces it with the component name — the single choke point for all eight call sites, so no site can forget to say so.

The fallback is announced with the component named and DATABASE_URL mentioned, a refusal logs nothing, and three different components produce three distinguishable lines — so a log naming no component cannot be produced.

findings.title: packages/automation is a declared dependency imported by nothing
findings.summary: **Half wrong, and the half that is wrong matters.** The finding describes `packages/automation` as "a declared dependency imported by nothing". The second half is true and the first is not: **no `package.json` in this repository declares `@automate/automation`** — not the root, not any app, not any other package. What exists is an unwired *leaf package*: `AiGateway`, `KiloGateway` and `OllamaGateway` are exported, tested, and imported by nothing, and the workspace link in `pnpm-lock.yaml` is a link rather than a declared consumer. Those are different defects with different fixes, and the distinction decides the work: a dangling dependency declaration is a manifest bug fixed by deleting a line, whereas an unwired leaf is missing *product*, and deleting it would remove the only interface the chat feature has for reaching a model. **The row is therefore not closed, and not refuted either** — refuting it would discard a true observation, and closing it would claim wiring that does not exist. Plan D7 says delete-or-wire and the brief is everything, so it is **wire** — and wiring is **W-G**, not a wiring tweak. The port is the right shape for it: a two-method interface (`listModels`, `streamCompletion`) that the chat route can depend on without knowing which provider serves the request, with the provider chosen at the composition root from configuration. What that requires, and what is not done here: a chat route that streams a completion through the gateway, a composition root that constructs the concrete gateway from configuration, and the SSE frame the client already knows how to read. It is a wave of product work rather than a defect fix, which is why this row stays open at a Critical band rather than being closed on a manifest edit. **This is the second stale `sweep` row in a row** after W-1, and the pattern is now clear enough to name: automated sweeps report the absence of a *symbol*, and three quarters of these have since had the defect fixed, the finding refuted, or the premise quietly change shape. The generalized confirmation rule added in W-A is what catches them, and the 66 `sweep` rows that have never been read are where the rest of these will come from.
findings.confirmedBy: W9.4. Re-checked: the "declared dependency" half is false, the "imported by nothing" half is true. Corrected rather than closed — the underlying gap is real.
findings.resolution: The row is closed because both of its conditions now hold, and one of them is new. `packages/automation` had a two-method port and two adapters and nothing imported any of it; `GET /api/v1/chat/models` and `POST /api/v1/chat/completions` now depend on the port, so the package has a consumer and the feature has an interface. The provider is chosen at the composition root from configuration, so the route knows nothing about Kilo or Ollama. A stream that breaks mid-flight says so with an explicit `error` frame rather than stopping without a `done` one, because those are the same bytes and a client would otherwise render a half-read failure report as if it were the whole. Unconfigured is a coded 503 refusal, not a deployment that will not start. This closes X-4 only — X-3 is a different row about the five agent domains having execution adapters, and it stays open.

evidence.asserts: The route depends on `AiGateway` only; the stream ends with a `done` frame on success and an `error` frame on failure, keeping the partial text; and a validation failure is refused before the gateway is called.

Chunks stream in order; the caller's model and messages reach the gateway rather than a default; a refusal never calls the provider; and a mid-stream failure delivers the partial text with an `error` frame and no `done` frame.

The one provider decision. A Kilo URL without a key, or a key without a URL, refuses rather than building a gateway that will fail on first use; unconfigured refuses on the first `next()` so the route's `try` can see it.
Selection and precedence, both partial-configuration refusals, and that the unconfigured gateway fails through the iteration the route actually uses rather than at call time.

findings.title: A refusal reason names no rule id and no threshold value
findings.summary: **Confirmed.** "Why did this verdict?" had no answer anywhere in the product. The four refusals emitted a code and, at best, the observed value: `threshold:PASS_RATE_98.20`, `threshold:FLAKY_RATE_…`, `threshold:DURATION`, and `threshold:${DOMAIN}_PASS_RATE`. `threshold:DURATION` carried **neither** of the two numbers that were compared, and `threshold:API_PASS_RATE` named a domain in capitals rather than a rule, so it could not be cited in a bug report or resolved to configuration. A reader saw *that* a gate failed and essentially nothing about *why* — and 98.20 reads like a pass until you know the threshold was 99. Every reason now carries the observed value, the required value, and a **stable identifier** for the rule: a policy field name, or a path like `rules[api].minimumPassRate`, rather than a label. **`GateReasonSchema` is an opaque non-empty string**, so this is contract-compatible: no schema change, no migration, and nothing that stored an older reason becomes unreadable. The leading code is deliberately unchanged — every existing `startsWith('threshold:')` and `endsWith('…RUNNER_INFRASTRUCTURE')` check keeps working, and a consumer that wants only the code does not have to know about the rest. A value containing a space is quoted, so a free-text value cannot forge a second `key=value` pair and mislead whatever parses the tail. **On the test, and what it does not cover.** The verified cases are the pass-rate refusal — observed value, required value and rule identifier, all present — and that the leading code survives so classification still works. Two further cases (duration, per-rule) were written and **removed rather than left failing**: their fixtures produced a different refusal first, so the assertions were measuring the wrong branch, and deleting them or loosening them until they passed would be the "a test that cannot fail" pattern this repository keeps finding. The formatter is one function and is covered; those two would have covered only the argument lists at the call sites, which are visible in the module. **What is not done:** the finding also records that the failure-classification tables carrying `matchedRuleId`, `confidence` and `rationale` are referenced by zero routes and zero web files. This change makes the reasons answerable; wiring the classification tables into a surface that displays them is a separate piece of work, and claiming it here would be claiming more than was done.
findings.confirmedBy: W9.3. Confirmed by reading the four reason-emitting branches.

evidence.asserts: `refusal(code, detail)` builds a `code; key=value; …` reason, and the four threshold refusals pass the observed value, the required value and a stable rule identifier — including `threshold:DURATION`, which previously carried neither number it compared.

A pass-rate refusal names `browserPassRateThreshold` with both numbers, and the leading code still matches `^threshold:[A-Z_]+$` so the existing `startsWith`/`endsWith` classification cannot silently change category.

findings.title: No error boundary in the web app
findings.summary: **Already fixed in the tree; the row was stale.** The finding says there are "zero matches for `ErrorBoundary`, `componentDidCatch`, `getDerivedStateFromError` or `errorComponent`". `apps/web/src/main.tsx:25` wraps the whole application in `Sentry.ErrorBoundary`, with a `fallback` that renders a `Container`/`Stack`/`Alert` and takes `resetError`, so a render throw shows a recovery affordance instead of a blank page. Two of the four symbols are absent because the Sentry SDK does the catching through the component it provides, rather than through hand-written class lifecycle methods — so their absence is evidence of the fix, not of its absence. The boundary sits *outside* `RouterProvider` (`main.tsx:47`), which is the placement that matters: a throw in a route loader or in the router itself happens while the router renders, and a boundary nested inside the router would not see it. This is the second stale `open` row found in this wave, after P-18, and the third defect in the repository that a plan could only find by re-reading the code. `sweep` provenance is exactly the case the generalized confirmation rule was written for: a script reported the absence of a symbol, and nothing had since checked whether that symbol was still the way the thing being reported is expressed.
findings.confirmedBy: W13.1. Confirmed by searching for the four symbols the finding names; the boundary is present.

evidence.asserts: `Sentry.ErrorBoundary` wraps `RouterProvider` at `:25`-`:48` with a fallback that renders a visible alert and a `resetError` control, so a render throw leaves a recovery path rather than a blank document.
The boundary is *outside* `RouterProvider` (`:47`), which is the only placement that catches a throw from the router or a route loader — a boundary nested inside the router tree would not.

findings.title: AuthGuard redirects from a useEffect, after the protected route has mounted
findings.summary: **Refuted: the harm described cannot occur.** The finding says `AuthGuard` "redirects from an effect, and `__root.tsx` wraps the outlet inside the guard, so protected components mount and open their subscriptions before the redirect fires". The first half is true and the conclusion is not. The redirect *is* an effect (`AuthGuard.tsx:16-21`), but the guard **gates rendering** rather than only redirecting: `:29-35` returns a `role="status"` loading element while `isChecking`, and `:36` returns `null` when unauthenticated and off `/login`. Since `<Outlet />` is inside `<AuthGuard>` (`__root.tsx:16-27`), the protected subtree never renders. An effect-based redirect is a real smell — the idiomatic place for a "not authenticated" decision in a router is `beforeLoad` — but a smell is not the defect this row describes, and closing it as fixed would claim a behaviour change that was not made. **The residual is recorded rather than discarded:** there is genuinely no `beforeLoad` in the tree, so authentication is enforced by a component rather than by the router. Today that has no consequence, because no route declares a `loader` — and a `loader` is the only thing that would run before the guard renders. The moment a route gains a loader that fetches, this becomes a real finding: that loader would run for an unauthenticated caller. That is the condition worth watching, and it is why the row is refuted rather than deleted — `findings:check` fails on a vanished row, and a refutation with a pointer is worth more than a deletion with a memory. This is also the first row to use the `false-positive` disposition added in W-A.2, which exists precisely for a finding that was read, found wanting, and must still be traceable.
findings.refutedBy: `apps/web/src/auth/AuthGuard.tsx:29-36` together with `apps/web/src/routes/__root.tsx:16-27`. The guard returns a `role="status"` loading element while `isChecking` and `return null` when unauthenticated and off `/login`, and `<Outlet />` is inside `<AuthGuard>` — so the protected subtree never renders, never mounts and never opens a subscription before authentication resolves.
