Checked on 2026-09-27 that no other path renders `<Outlet />` outside the guard.

findings.title: Auth state is module-level mutable global state
findings.summary:
`useAuth.ts:6-8,19` holds the session in module scope and exports a `resetAuthState()` that orphans live components, so two concurrent sessions cannot hold independent state.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `apps/web/src/auth/useAuth.ts:6-8,49-54`. `resetAuthState` calls
`listeners.clear()`, but the subscribing effect runs once with `[]` deps
(`:66-73`), so a mounted component's `setCurrentStatus` is never called again — it
is orphaned while the module says `'checking'`. **The row's "two concurrent sessions"
framing is the weak half:** one page has one cookie jar, so the real cost is test
isolation and a forced workaround. `lib/api.ts:176-180` does a full
`window.location.assign` on session expiry precisely *because* "the auth status is
module state in `useAuth`". `resetAuthState` has **no production caller** — every one
of the eleven call sites is a test.
findings.resolution: A rejected add to quarantine was caught with `console.error` and nothing else, so a reader who submitted a test that was already quarantined saw their form sit there unchanged with no sign anything had happened — and submitting again fails identically. The failure is now rendered in the form and the fields are deliberately kept, because clearing them on a failure is the second way to lose the work. A test asserts the message is on screen *and* that nothing reached the console, so a regression to a bare console call fails rather than passing quietly. The route was also at 6.89% line coverage despite being reachable from the sidebar; it now has nine tests covering the states a reader actually sees.

evidence.asserts: The refusal is rendered in the form with an `alert` role, and the fields are not cleared on failure.

A rejected add shows the message and keeps the typed text; a successful add closes the form and sends no blank reason; a failed load is reported rather than rendered as an empty list; and a case asserts `console.error` was NOT called, which is the assertion that would catch the original defect returning.

findings.title: useCommandActions.register can loop infinitely
findings.summary:
`:93` depends on the raw `actions` array and `:13` compares by object reference, so a caller passing fresh literals each render produces `changed` → `notify()` → `useSyncExternalStore` re-render → a new array. The only production caller escapes via `useMemo`, so the next caller detonates.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `apps/web/src/hooks/useCommandActions.ts:13` compares registration by object
identity (`existing !== action`) and `:93` depends on the raw `actions` array.
`register` → `updateCache()` creates a new array identity → `notify()`, so a
caller passing inline literals in a component that also subscribes loops. The sole
production caller escapes today via `useMemo` with stable deps. Secondary defect worth
folding in: the effect cleans up with `deregister(ids)` *before* re-registering, so
the store transiently empties and notifies twice per effect run.
findings.resolution: `useCommandActions` depended on the array's identity, and every caller writes its list inline — `useCommandActions([{ id, label, onSelect }])` is a new array of new objects on every render. The effect re-ran on every render; its cleanup called `deregister`, which notified; its body called `register`, which notified because every object was a new reference. The notification re-rendered the caller, which produced a new array, which re-ran the effect, until React stopped it by throwing. The effect now depends on a derived signature of ids, labels and callback names. Comparing the actions inside `register` would not have been enough, and the reason is worth keeping: the cleanup deregisters *before* the body registers, so the deregistration is itself the notification.

evidence.asserts: The effect depends on `signature`, not on `actions`, so an equivalent list does not re-run it.

A component that both registers inline actions *and* reads the store renders at most five times; the cycle needs both halves, which is why the single-hook version passed against the broken code. A second case asserts a changed label still re-registers, because simply ignoring a new array would also ignore a changed command.

findings.title: Each page holds two EventSource connections and two pollers
findings.summary:
`routes/dashboard.tsx:338` calls `useRuns` before the `:341` early return, so every dashboard child opens its own pair. Per plan D8 the layout is restructured rather than a dependency added.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `apps/web/src/routes/dashboard.tsx:357` calls `useRuns(api)` before the
`if (!isExactDashboard) return <Outlet />;` at `:360`, and the child lists runs
again at `dashboard/index.tsx:48`. On `/dashboard/runs` the layout's hook therefore
opens a **second `EventSource('/api/v1/events')`** (`useRuns.ts:85` →
`api.ts:498`) and a second 5-second poller (`useRuns.ts:107`) that nothing
renders. On `/dashboard/runs/:runId` it is two EventSources but one poller, since
`useRunDetail` has none.

**Confirmed, fix written and then withdrawn, 2026-09-28. Recorded because the reason is the
useful part.**

The fix is to give the hook a component boundary: split the layout into one that
returns `<Outlet />` and a `CommandCenter` that calls `useRuns`, because a hook cannot
be called conditionally and the only way not to run it is not to be mounted. That change
was written, and it works.

It was withdrawn for a reason worth recording rather than hiding: the split cost **one
line of coverage** in `apps/web`, and that package's floor was raised to 98.23
deliberately earlier in this programme. The ratchet immediately reported
`apps/web: lines 98.1 < 98.23` — which is the ratchet working exactly as designed, one
change after it was set. Landing the fix without the covering test would have traded a
real resource leak (a second `EventSource` and a second 5-second poller on every visit
to `/dashboard/runs`) for a red gate, and a red gate that gets silenced is worse than a
documented open row.

**So this row stays open with the fix known.** The change is four lines and needs one
test that visits `/dashboard/runs` and asserts the child alone subscribes — that test
was not written, so the change is not in the tree.
findings.resolution: Both halves were the same defect twice. `subscribeToRunEvents` constructed an `EventSource` per call, so a page with both `useRuns` and `useRunDetail` mounted held two connections to `/api/v1/events` — the ordinary case, because the dashboard layout renders an `<Outlet />` while `CommandCenter` calls `useRuns` — each with its own dedup map and reconnect bookkeeping. The source is now shared and reference counted, because a bare singleton has the opposite failure where the first unmount closes a connection the others are reading, and strict-mode double-invocation needs a guarded release. And `useRuns` refreshed the whole list every five seconds *and* listened to the stream, so a healthy page paid a full list fetch for something the stream had already pushed; the poller now runs only while the stream is down, which is the only case where polling is the only way to learn anything.

evidence.asserts: One shared source with a reference count, one dedup map, and `resetRunEventStream` exported for tests with a comment saying so.

Two subscribers open one connection; releasing one does not close it for the other; a double release does not close a connection another subscriber is reading; a new connection is opened after the last one leaves; and the empty `EventSource` case is inert.
The poller reads `isLiveRef` and returns immediately while the stream is connected.
Fifteen seconds of connected time produce no list fetch; after the stream reports down, the same fifteen seconds produce three.

findings.title: A missing run renders null and a 404 is detected by string-matching an error message
findings.summary:
`run-detail.tsx:193` renders `null`, `:179` matches on `error.message` while the API returns a distinct `code` (`boundary.ts:159`), and `lib/api.ts:104` uses `schema.parse`, so a `ZodError` reaches the user verbatim.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Partly true, and one of the row's three claims is already stale — the row must not
be closed as a unit or it will claim a fix that was never made.** The
`run-detail.tsx:193` `return null` is literally there, and `:179` does detect a 404
by string-matching `error.message`. But the match works *only* because the server's
English prose contains "not found": the API returns a distinct
`{ error: { code: 'RUN_NOT_FOUND', … } }`, and `lib/api.ts:255-273` reads only
`body.error.message`, keeping `status` and **discarding `code`** — while
`error.status === 404` is already available and unused. **The `schema.parse`/
`ZodError` claim is fixed in the tree:** `api.ts:307-313` now uses `safeParse` and
throws `ResponseContractError`. The `return null` is defensive — a live component
rarely reaches it — but it is the only unguarded state.

**Half fixed, 2026-09-28 — and the other half was wrong.** A row that is only half right should
say which half, rather than being closed and claiming a fix that was never made.

**Fixed: the 404 is matched on the status, not on the message.** The component read
`error.message` looking for the words "not found". That worked only because the server's
English prose happened to contain them — the API sends a distinct
`{ code: 'RUN_NOT_FOUND', message, requestId }` with a 404 status, and
`lib/api.ts` discards the code while keeping the status. Translate the string, or reword
it, and a missing run silently became a generic error.

The status is read through `error instanceof ApiError && error.status === 404` rather
than a cast, because the hook types the value as `Error` while storing an `ApiError`.
An error that is not an `ApiError` carries no status and falls through to the generic
state, which is the honest answer for an error of unknown provenance.

**The row's own test was the bug.** The 404 case was built as
`new Error('Run not found (404)')` — a plain Error whose *message* carried the words
the component matched on. That fixture made the string match look correct, and it would
have kept passing against a correctly fixed component. It is now `ApiError`, and the
case set is stronger: a 404 with French prose still resolves as "not found", and a 500
whose message says "run not found" is reported as a real failure. That second case is
the fail-before — before this change the message won.

**Not fixed, and the row is wrong about it: the `return null` is unreachable, not
merely rare.** `useRunDetail` dereferences `run.releaseId` immediately after the fetch
(`hooks/useDashboard.ts:131`), so a null run raises a TypeError inside the hook and
arrives at the component as an *error*. A guard that renders a blank page for a state
the code cannot produce is dead code, and the alternative — a rendered message — is one
uncovered branch, which `apps/web` cannot absorb: this package sits at a floor that was
deliberately raised to 98.23, and the branch drops it to 98.10. Making the state
reachable means optional-chaining the hook first, which is a real change with its own
risk and did not belong in the same pass. The guard keeps its original shape, and the
reason it cannot yet be improved is written where a reader will find it.

evidence.asserts: `RequestContractError` exists and is distinct from `ResponseContractError`; `createRun` uses `safeParse` and throws before any fetch.
An unbuildable body rejects with `RequestContractError`, not `ResponseContractError`, and no fetch was made.

findings.resolution: The row was partly stale and must not be closed as if all three claims were live. The 404 string-matching was already fixed — `run-detail.tsx` checks `error.status`, with a comment recording that. The `null` render for a missing run is a deliberate decision with a stated reason, not a defect. **The third claim was real**: `createRun` called `CreateRunRequestSchema.parse`, which throws a bare `ZodError`; a `ZodError` *is* an `Error`, so every hook's `caught instanceof Error ? caught : …` passed it through and the UI rendered `error.message`, which for Zod is a JSON dump of every field that disagreed. A reader saw a wall of schema internals for a failure that is a bug in this application. `RequestContractError` now names it, `createRun` uses `safeParse`, and nothing is sent — a request that cannot be built is a client bug, and firing a malformed one would turn it into a server error instead. The two errors stay separate because the distinction is the point: a response the *server* sent is the server's to answer for.

findings.title: Three formatDate definitions, none of them locale- or time-zone-aware
findings.summary:
Defined at `dashboard.tsx:36`, `dashboard/index.tsx:43` and `run-detail.tsx:42`, all bare `toLocaleString()`, with zero uses of `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in either tree. Unacceptable in an evidence UI, where a timestamp is the claim.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** **Confirmed, and the three definitions are genuinely three.** Repo-wide there are
exactly three `formatDate` and the only `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in the repository is
in `apps/worker/src/scheduler.ts:13` — none in `apps/web/src`, so the
locale/time-zone blindness holds. **But they are not identical**, which a straight
dedupe would get wrong: signatures differ (`string`, `string | null`,
`string | null | undefined`) and the empty fallbacks are `'Not started'` vs
`'UNKNOWN'` vs absent. A shared helper must take the fallback as a parameter, or two
of the three screens change what they render.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28 — deduplication only, and the locale half is deliberately left open.**

`apps/web/src/lib/format.ts` holds one `formatDate(value, emptyState)`. The fallback is a
**required** parameter, not an option with a default, because `'Not started'` (the run
never began) and `'UNKNOWN'` (the field is unknown) are different user-visible claims;
a default would have picked one silently and turned a refactor into a product change.
`dashboard/index.tsx` passes `'Not started'` at its one call site, `run-detail.tsx` binds
`'UNKNOWN'` in a local wrapper for its five, and `dashboard.tsx:319` — where `createdAt`
is a required `string` with no empty state — keeps a thin non-fallback wrapper rather
than being handed an invented user-visible string.

**Locale behaviour is unchanged on purpose.** Introducing `Intl.DateTimeFormat` here would
alter rendered output, and bundling it into the dedupe would make the assertions stop being
evidence for a refactor. The only `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in the repository is
`apps/worker/src/scheduler.ts:13`, which sets an explicit time zone — that is where the
follow-up starts. The row's title half therefore remains open work, narrowed to locale and
time zone, and is recorded as such rather than being closed by a change that did not make it.

**No snapshot was added.** `apps/web` has no snapshot convention — no `toMatchSnapshot`, no
`__snapshots__`, no inline snapshots, and no existing test asserting any rendered date — and
introducing a snapshot framework for one helper was not the trade. `format.test.ts` asserts
that a fixed input returns the string `toLocaleString()` produced, and that each empty value
returns the caller's fallback rather than any built-in one.

**Calibration:** hardcoding `'Not started'` inside the helper was reintroduced and turned
exactly the forwarding assertion red (`Tests 1 failed | 246 passed`), which is the specific
guard against a 'fixed' dedupe quietly turning run-detail's `'UNKNOWN'` into `'Not started'`.
`run-detail.test.tsx` and `index.test.tsx` kept passing throughout, because they assert the
`UNKNOWN` values through other fields.

evidence.asserts: The single shared `formatDate` takes the empty-state string as a required parameter and returns it for `null`, `undefined`, and `''`.

For a fixed input the output is the same string `toLocaleString()` produced, and `formatDate(null, 'Not started')` and `formatDate(null, 'UNKNOWN')` return their own caller's fallback — the assertion that keeps the two screens' different claims.

findings.title: Rendered timestamps are locale- and time-zone-undefined
findings.summary:
**Split out of W-7 on 2026-09-28, deliberately.** W-7's title claimed two things: three duplicate
`formatDate` definitions, and none of them locale- or time-zone-aware. The dedupe landed
and is `fixed`; the locale half did not, and closing W-7 wholesale would have recorded a
fix that was never made.

`apps/web/src/lib/format.ts` still calls `new Date(value).toLocaleString()` with no locale
and no time zone, so the same run shows different text on two machines. In an evidence UI a
timestamp is the claim, and a claim that renders differently per viewer is not reproducible.
The only `Intl.DateTimeFormat` in the repository is `apps/worker/src/scheduler.ts:13`, which
sets an explicit time zone — that is the precedent to follow.

**The fix:** construct the formatter once with an explicit locale and an explicit time zone,
and route `formatDate` through it. **Why it was not in W-7's PR:** it changes rendered bytes,
which makes a pure refactor indistinguishable from a behaviour change and stops the existing
assertions being evidence. It needs its own review and its own before/after evidence of the
text it changes.
findings.resolution: `formatDate` rendered `toLocaleString()`, which produces the viewer's zone and says nothing about it: the same run read as `13:30` in Tel Aviv and `12:30` in Berlin, and a reader comparing it against a CI log in UTC had no way to tell which was right. Both readings look correct to the person who produced each, which is what made it invisible — and for a product whose whole claim is evidence, a timestamp that cannot be correlated with a log cannot be checked. The zone is now appended via `timeZoneName: short`. The *wording* stays locale-dependent on purpose, because `25/09/2026` against `9/25/2026` is the reader's own convention and only the zone changes what a timestamp means. Unparseable values now fall back too: `new Date('not a date').toLocaleString()` is the literal string `Invalid Date`.

evidence.asserts: The rendered time names its zone, and an unparseable value returns the caller's fallback rather than `Invalid Date`.

The rendering ends in a zone name; the same instant rendered under two zones contains the same minute in both; an unparseable value is the fallback; and the two callers' distinct fallbacks are still distinct.

findings.title: /dashboard/quarantine is registered but absent from the route manifest
findings.summary:
`router.ts:9,16` registers it, `route-manifest.ts:1-7` does not list it, so `Sidebar.tsx:4,39` never links it: a finished screen with a 24-case suite, reachable only by URL. `route-manifest.test.ts` validates the manifest against itself and therefore cannot see this.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `router.ts:9,16` registers `/dashboard/quarantine`;
`route-manifest.ts:1-7` does not list it; and `Sidebar.tsx:4,39-40` reads
`visibleRoutes` from the manifest, which is the **sole** nav source. The
test-blindness half is also right: `route-manifest.test.ts:16-20` asserts
`visibleRoutes` against a hard-coded three-path array and checks each entry against
`isApplicationPath`, which is **defined in the same module** (`:15`) — nothing
imports the router tree, so the manifest can disagree with `router.ts` indefinitely.
Consequence beyond navigation: `isApplicationPath('/dashboard/quarantine')` is
`false`, so the route is invisible to whatever gates on application paths.

**Fixed, 2026-09-28.**

The route is listed, and the test now checks the manifest against the **router**
instead of against itself.

Two parts, and the second is the real fix.

`routeTree` is exported so it can be read, and the manifest test walks it and asserts
every registered application path appears in the manifest. The old test compared the
manifest to `isApplicationPath`, which is **defined in the module under test** — so it
proved the manifest agrees with itself. `/dashboard/quarantine` sat in the router while
being absent from the manifest, and nothing failed: the route was reachable by URL,
invisible to the sidebar, and invisible to `isApplicationPath` too, so whatever gates
on application paths also could not see it.

The check asserts against a **second hand-written list** would have been the same defect
in a different file, so the paths are read from the route tree itself. Two calibration
trials: dropping the route from the manifest turns it red, and un-exporting `routeTree`
turns it red too, so the invariant cannot be quietly disarmed.

**The "a test that cannot fail" lesson, third occurrence in this programme.** The fix was
one line. The reason nobody noticed was the test.

evidence.asserts: `/dashboard/quarantine` is declared in the manifest with `visible: true`, so the sidebar — whose only navigation source is `visibleRoutes` — can reach a route the router already registered.
`routeTree` is exported. It was a module-local const, so the manifest could not be checked against it by anything, which is what allowed the disagreement to persist.

Every path the router registers and that `isApplicationPath` recognises must appear in the manifest, reading the paths from `routeTree` rather than from a second list. Removing the quarantine entry fails this; un-exporting `routeTree` fails it too. The previous assertions — manifest against a hard-coded array, and against `isApplicationPath` defined in the same module — could not detect either.

findings.title: An OS theme change never propagates
findings.summary:
`ThemeProvider.tsx:37` samples `matchMedia(...).matches` once with no `change` listener, `index.html` has no pre-hydration script, and `localStorage` access is not wrapped in try/catch.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `ThemeProvider.tsx:37` samples `matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches`
**once**, inside an effect whose deps are `[theme]`, and there is no
`addEventListener('change', …)` anywhere in `apps/web`. `index.html` has only
`<script type="module" src="/src/main.tsx">` — no pre-hydration theme script. Both
halves hold: the sample happens in an effect so there is a flash of the default, and
no listener means a mid-session OS change never reaches the DOM. Extra exposure at the
same site: `as Theme` at `:25` is an unchecked cast, so a hand-edited or stale value
like `"blue"` is written straight to `data-theme`, and storage access is unguarded at
both ends.
findings.resolution: The provider asked `matchMedia` once and returned, so a reader on the default theme — the only setting that promises to follow the system — got the OS's answer at page load and nothing after. Switching to dark at 6pm left them on a white page until they reloaded, and nothing looked wrong. It subscribes now, and unsubscribes on unmount: a provider that remounts on a route change would otherwise leave a listener holding a closure for the life of the page. The handler is one named function referenced by both `addEventListener` and the cleanup, because a second arrow in the cleanup is not the same function and `removeEventListener` would silently do nothing. An explicit choice drops the subscription, because an OS change must not undo a theme the reader picked.

evidence.asserts: System mode subscribes to the media query and unsubscribes through the same named handler; an explicit theme removes the subscription.
An OS change propagates in both directions and the listener count drops to zero on unmount; choosing a theme explicitly drops the listener and a later OS change does not override it.

findings.title: A per-process cursor is minted beside the durable outbox sequence
findings.summary: **Confirmed exactly: six derivations, six different fallbacks, no shared context.** The sites were the error boundary (`index.ts`), a second reader in `errors/boundary.ts`, the shared execution helper, the deadline middleware, and the two dashboard audit writers — and the fallbacks were not merely redundant but *disagreeing*: some generated a UUID, one stored `null`, one stored the literal `'unknown'`. So the same execution could report three different ids depending on which layer noticed it, which is worse than having no id: a log line, an event row and an artifact metadata entry that *should* correlate do not, and the absence of a match looks like a missing log rather than a defect. `observability/request-context.ts` establishes the id once through `AsyncLocalStorage`, and every reader takes it from there. The middleware is registered **first**, before security headers and everything else, because a context established after the first thing that can fail is a context the first thing that can fail does not have. Two decisions inside it are worth naming. **The id is echoed on the response**, because a generated id a client never sees cannot be quoted in a bug report and is therefore useless for correlation from outside. **And a client-supplied id is validated, not trusted** — the value flows into log lines and persisted audit rows, and six independent sites each deciding independently whether to trust it is six places to get the sanitising wrong. A value that is not a short identifier is *replaced*, not truncated, because a truncated attacker string is still an attacker string and a log line is the wrong place to be lenient about what another system will parse back out of it. **Outside a request the id is absent rather than invented** — `currentRequestId()` returns `undefined` and `requireRequestId()` returns the fixed string `NO_REQUEST`, because a fabricated id in an audit row looks findable and is not. `runWithRequestId` lets a background job establish the same context the HTTP path does, so the id has one way in rather than one way in and six ways of being absent. **A signature that lied was removed.** The dashboard audit helper was `defaultContextFor(request)`, and once the id came from the context the request was no longer read. Prefixing the parameter with `_` would have satisfied the linter while leaving a function that accepts a request and ignores it, and a name saying "For" an input that is not an input; it is now `defaultContext()` with no parameter. **Three dashboard test files were testing an application that did not exist.** They build their own Hono instances, so when the helpers stopped reading the header they recorded `null` and three suites failed. Mounting `requestContext` in them is the correct fix rather than reverting to header reads, and it is the same drift the finding describes reached from the other side: a second copy of the application that nobody keeps in step with the real one. Tests for the module are about **agreement**, not existence — that every reader in one request sees the same value, that three concurrent requests do not share one, and that the value survives an `await`, which is the point of `AsyncLocalStorage` over a module-level variable: a variable is correct until two requests overlap, and then a handler reads whichever request most recently set it.
findings.confirmedBy: W11.1. Confirmed by reading all six derivation sites and searching for AsyncLocalStorage across apps/api/src, which returned nothing.

evidence.asserts: `normaliseRequestId` is the only place a client-supplied id is trusted, and it replaces rather than truncates anything that is not a short identifier; `requestContext` establishes the context and echoes the id on the response.
`app.use(requestContext)` is registered before security headers and every other middleware, and the error boundary reads `requireRequestId()` instead of re-deriving from the header.

Every reader in one request sees the same value, three concurrent requests each see their own, the value survives an `await`, a hostile header is replaced rather than trimmed, and outside a request the fallback is `NO_REQUEST` rather than a correlatable-looking UUID.
`defaultContext()` takes no request parameter — the signature no longer claims a dependency the function does not have, and the audit row records the context's id or nothing.

findings.title: x-request-id is advertised to CORS but never set on a response
findings.summary: The header is only ever read, while `security-headers.ts:57` lists it in `DEFAULT_EXPOSED_HEADERS`. The CORS layer advertises a header the server never sets.
findings.refutedBy:
The row's premise — that the header is "only ever read" — does not survive reading
the writer. `requestContext` at `apps/api/src/observability/request-context.ts:101-104`
sets it:

    const requestId = normaliseRequestId(c.req.header('x-request-id'));
    c.header('x-request-id', requestId);

and it is the **first** middleware in the real app (`index.ts:315`, registered
*before* `createSecurityHeaders` at `:316`), so every response through the composed
app carries the header. `apps/api/src/observability/request-context.test.ts:51-56`
asserts the echo end to end, so this is not an untested behaviour either. The
`DEFAULT_EXPOSED_HEADERS` list at `security-headers.ts:57` advertises a header
that genuinely is set, which is what that list is for. The sweep most likely matched
the `x-request-id` *reads* at `boundary.ts:65` and `security-headers.ts:46,57` and
never saw the write. Checked 2026-09-28.

findings.title: The error boundary's log seam is never supplied a logger
findings.summary:
`ErrorBoundaryOptions.log` exists and `boundary.ts:57` defaults to `console.error`, but `index.ts:115-120` passes only `requestId` and `reportError`, so production never gets a logger. Ten further bare `console.error` sites remain in product code.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `errors/boundary.ts:20-22` declares the `log` seam and `:86` defaults it to
`console.error`, but the only production construction (`index.ts:115-125`) supplies
no `log`. The seam is used only by tests. **The row's count is approximately right,
not exact:** there are 8 bare `console.error` sites in product code outside the
default (`index.ts:305,332`, `durable-realtime-bus.ts:84,124`,
`middleware/auth.ts:101`, `drizzle-execution-store.ts:1588`,
`drizzle-realtime-feed.ts:118,144`) plus one `console.warn` in
`startup-policy.ts:88`. There is **no logger module** in
`apps/api/src/observability/` — only `request-context.ts` and `sentry.ts` — so a
fix has to introduce one or route through Sentry.
findings.resolution: The error boundary is given a logger. `ErrorBoundaryOptions.log` was declared and documented as injectable, and `index.ts` supplied `requestId` and `reportError` and nothing else — so every failure in the API reached a `console.error(message, context)`: a message string and a loose object side by side, unparseable and unqueryable. Nothing could have caught it, because every test supplies its own collector, so the test path was always populated and the production path never was. `observability/logger.ts` emits one JSON object per line, injected downward from the composition root as a single `LogSink`.

evidence.asserts: A caller cannot relabel a record — `level`, `msg`, `time` and `service` are the record identity and a colliding value is kept under `fields`; a sink that throws is swallowed; `JSON.stringify(new Error(...))` being `{}` is handled.
An unhandled failure produces a structured record with the request id, path and cause, and a failing logger cannot change the error response.
The composition root constructs one logger and passes `logger.error` as the boundary seam.

findings.title: The /metrics endpoint exposes process state only, and says so
findings.summary:
Zero occurrences of a metrics route and no metrics dependency in any package, so run outcomes, gate verdicts, event freshness, queue latency, runner health, cancellation counts, artifact bytes and AI token cost are all unobservable.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** Total absence, and the search is recorded because a claim of absence needs
evidencing. `metrics|prom-client|openmetrics|opentelemetry|prometheus` across every
`package.json`: **zero matches**. `/metrics` route, `PromClient`,
`createCounter`, `Histogram(`, `Gauge(`: no matches. Every `metrics` hit in the
tree is one of four unrelated things — a DB `metrics` jsonb column
(`schema/dashboard.ts:108`), the `metrics` key of the *reporting* response
(`routes/reporting.ts:17`), a runner heartbeat field, and a web `METRICS` constant
mirrored in the e2e budget spec. `route-manifest.test.ts:186` enumerates the
registered routes and no metrics route is mounted. Corroborating detail the sweep
missed: `startup-policy-extra.test.ts:32` carries `metricsToken: undefined` in a
fixture cast `as never` — a vestige of a planned endpoint. **Fixing O-5b first
matters:** a `/metrics` surface with no readiness state and no sweep counters to
export would have nothing to say.
findings.resolution:
A `/metrics` endpoint exists at `GET /metrics`, and the decision worth recording is not that it was added but **what it is allowed to contain**.

**No metrics library, on purpose.** The Prometheus text exposition format is `# HELP` / `# TYPE` / samples, and the whole of it needed here was a dozen lines. `prom-client` would have added a transitive dependency tree and a **global default registry** — mutable process-wide state, which is the one thing this codebase has spent two waves removing, and which a test suite importing two registries has to be careful with. A self-hosted single-node install whose metrics are process state and one in-memory counter does not need a registry framework; it needs the text. ADR-006 is the posture: single node, self-hosted, and no infrastructure nobody asked for.

**The content decision, which is the substance of this fix:**

- **No run, test, suite, artifact or tenant data.** Those are the customer's quality data, and a metric label is a dimension an operator groups by, not a place to put a test name. A new metric carrying a run id would be unbounded cardinality — a memory leak with a scrape on top — and the customer's data in a place nobody audited.
- **No database query.** A scrape is an unauthenticated GET, so every query it makes is a query anybody can make repeatedly, and the answer would be a count of the customer's rows. `collect()` takes no arguments and is synchronous, which is the type-level statement of that and is asserted, so the next collector cannot quietly become async.
- **Status class, not status code, and no per-URL labels.** Six fixed series (`1xx`–`5xx`) whether or not a class has been hit, so a series never appears and disappears; a status outside the five is dropped rather than coerced, because the handler chose it and an unexpected value is a bug that a fabricated class would hide. `GET /api/v1/runs/:id` is one series, not one per run.
- **The counter is monotonic and in process memory.** It resets on restart, which is what `rate()` is for; a persistent counter would need a table and an extra write on the request path to answer a question `rate()` already answers.

The route is unauthenticated because there is nothing in it to authenticate for, and the first metric needing a scope of its own goes on its own path with its own gate — a decision to make with evidence rather than a policy pre-empted here.

**What is still not observable, stated rather than implied.** The row listed run outcomes, gate verdicts, event freshness, queue latency, runner health, cancellation counts, artifact bytes and AI token cost. None of those is a process fact, and every one of them is a **query** — so exposing them here would mean an unauthenticated endpoint that reads the customer's data on request, which is the opposite of what "instrumented" should mean. Queue depth and outbox lag are the two this install actually wants and they are deliberately **not** in this first version: they need a cheap counted query, and a counted query on a scrape path is a load knob. The register row `ops.metrics-endpoint` carries the same decision, and the next increment is a decision to make with a measurement behind it rather than a gap nobody named.

evidence.asserts: The registry, the exposition renderer, and the content decision in its header. `collect()` is synchronous and takes no arguments, which is the type-level statement that a scrape performs no query, and `renderExposition` escapes backslash, double quote and newline in a label value so a value that came from a request cannot end a sample and have its remainder read as the next line.

The format assertions are on the rendered text rather than through a parser, because a parser shared with the writer would pass if both were wrong the same way. `escapes a label value, so a value cannot forge a sample` pins the three required escapes; `omits HELP and TYPE for a metric with no samples` pins that an empty family is absent rather than a parse warning; `drops a status it has no class for, rather than inventing one` pins that an impossible status is dropped rather than coerced; `exposes process state and the request counter, and nothing derived from a run` pins the content decision at the level of the metric names and label keys.

`health.get('/metrics', ...)` serves the body with an explicit `content-type` header object. The third argument to `c.body` is a headers *object*, and passing the content-type string itself leaves Hono's own `text/plain;charset=UTF-8` in place — the route answering without the version a scraper negotiates on, and invisible in a browser.

`serves the exposition content type, which a scraper refuses without` pins the exact header string; `answers with a well-formed body and no database, because it queries nothing` runs the route with `databaseUrl` deliberately absent and parses every sample line; `does not expose run, test or tenant data` asserts the content decision at the surface a scraper actually reads, for `run_id`, `workspace`, `tenant`, `test`, `suite` and `artifact`.

`recordRequest(c.res.status)` is called after `next()` resolves, in the middleware that already runs once per request on every path. An error the boundary turned into a 500 is therefore counted as the 500 it became, and a second middleware would have been a second registration order to reason about for the sake of a number.
`['GET', '/metrics']` is in `CANONICAL_API_ROUTES`, so the route cannot be added without being claimed as canonical — and cannot be claimed without being tested.

The route is in `UNAUTHENTICATED_ROUTES` with a reason longer than the contract's floor, and the test's reverse direction asserts a listed route is actually served. A stale entry hides a real one, so both directions are load-bearing.

Register row `ops.metrics-endpoint` carries the content decision as the authority: process state and one in-memory counter, no run, test, suite, artifact or tenant data, no per-URL labels, and no database query. A page generated from the register cannot claim more than the row says.

findings.title: Readiness cannot report a failed store
findings.summary:
`lastSweepError` has zero occurrences repo-wide, and the realtime `lastError` is a local variable at `durable-realtime-bus.ts:108` that is never surfaced. Plan §3 records the source claim that "readiness reports degraded stores" as one of six that did not survive checking.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.** `durable-realtime-bus.ts:108` declares `let lastError: unknown` as a
function-local, whose only other appearance is the `console.error` at `:124`.
`lastSweepError` has **one** occurrence repo-wide: the ledger row itself. And
`routes/health.ts:35-55` knows exactly two conditions — `DATABASE_URL` unset, and
the `SELECT 1` failing — so there is no seam a degraded store could reach even if
`lastError` were exported. `health.test.ts:194-197` asserts the failure body is
exactly those two fields, so a fixer must change that test too.
findings.resolution:
Readiness now answers for a store that has *lapsed*, not only for one that is unreachable. It knew exactly two conditions — `DATABASE_URL` unset and the `SELECT 1` failing — so an instance whose database was perfectly reachable while the realtime bus had been failing to publish for an hour reported `ready`. A load balancer cannot tell those apart, and routing to an instance that is up and not working is the failure a readiness probe exists to prevent.

`HealthRouteOptions.degraded` takes the store's own view of its dependencies and is wired from the composition root, because a readiness probe that opens its own connection to ask "is the connection working" cannot see a dependency that *is* connected and is nonetheless failing. The store knows; the probe has to be told. Optional, so omitting it means "nothing to report" — honest for a deployment with no such store, and it keeps every existing caller working unchanged.

`DurableRealtimeBus.lastPublishError()` replaces a function-local `lastError` whose only other appearance was a `console.error`; `lastSweepError` had one occurrence repo-wide, and it was this row. **It is cleared on the next successful publish**, so it means "failing *now*" rather than "has ever failed" — a sticky flag would report a recovered bus as broken for the life of the process, and a readiness probe that cries wolf gets ignored.

Two details worth recording. A degraded dependency is reported *after* the database probe, so a request that is both degraded and unreachable reports the unreachable one — the harder fact. And the existing test that pinned the database-failure body to exactly two fields had to change; that is the test doing its job, since a readiness answer that silently grew a `degraded` field would be drift rather than a decision.

evidence.asserts: A store reporting a degraded dependency answers 503 with that dependency named and the store's own reason; a store reporting nothing degraded answers 200 with no `degraded` key at all, so the new field cannot become noise.
`lastPublishError()` is null before any failure, carries the failure after one, and is cleared by the next successful publish — the "failing now, not ever" property a sticky flag gets wrong.

The composition root passes the durable bus's view of itself, so the seam has a producer and not only an interface. A `let` captured in a closure loses its narrowing, so the handler is built once as a const — the inline form type-checks against the `undefined` branch and reports nothing, which is the opposite of what it does.

The degraded store is 503 and names the dependency; the healthy store is 200 with no `degraded` key. The pre-existing assertion that the database-failure body is exactly two fields still holds, so the new shape is a decision rather than a growth.

findings.title: Six scripts exist and are wired nowhere
findings.summary: `migrate:plan`, `migrate:validate`, `smoke:local`, `smoke:rehearsal`, `compose:config` and `quality:baseline` were in no workflow, not in `verify`, and not in `verify:release`, so the migration gate had never run in CI. Tiered per plan D6 and referenced by named jobs; `gate-tooling.json` records the tool each needs so a forgotten install is a failing test.

evidence.asserts: Every newly wired script has a row naming the binary it needs, so the test that audits workflows has a table to audit against.
`the committed workflows are wired correctly` runs `auditRepository()` and asserts zero findings, which is what makes an unwired script a failure rather than an omission.
The reporting job names `migrate:plan`, `migrate:validate` and `compose:config`; the nightly names `smoke:local`, `smoke:rehearsal` and `quality:baseline`.

findings.title: playwright.config.ts used __dirname in an ES module
findings.summary: The root package.json declares `"type": "module"`, so Playwright loaded the config as an ES module and `__dirname` at `:41` and `:110` threw `ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined in ES module scope` before a single test was collected. A committed `playwright.config.local.ts` had grown around the crash and is deleted. `import.meta.dirname` is now used, as `eslint.config.js` already did.

evidence.asserts: `const configDir = import.meta.dirname` replaces both `__dirname` uses, and the config loads: `playwright test --list` collects 18 tests across 6 files in 2 projects.

findings.title: An unidentified full-suite flake
findings.summary: The plan recorded a full suite reporting `1 failed / 1495 passed` once in nine runs with no identifiable test. It is `tests/contract/capability-register.test.mjs`, case `reports a real commit as the baseline, and refuses one that is not`: the file takes 1.14 s alone and 15.13 s under `pnpm test`, where thirty-odd packages run in parallel, and that case crossed the 5 000 ms default per-test timeout at 6 668 ms with `Test timed out in 5000ms`. Every assertion had passed; the harness ran out of budget. The case also spawned the script twice for one assertion, which doubled the cost of the slowest test in the file for no added evidence. One spawn, and an explicit budget with the reason recorded.

evidence.asserts: `SPAWNING_TIMEOUT_MS` is passed to every case in the file, and the forged-baseline case calls `check(file)` once into `forged` instead of twice.

findings.title: node --test interference between the scripts/lib suites
findings.summary: Recorded as not reproducible, monitoring, which plan §W0's gate accepts in place of a named test. Measured on the current tree: 39/39 pass with `--test-concurrency=1` and 39/39 pass without it, in 686 ms and 311 ms. The same measurement on the CI baseline branch is 46/46 either way, in 1 177 ms serial and 5 028 ms concurrent — so concurrency costs a 4x wall-clock penalty on this machine without changing a single verdict. The contention is not reproducible because the contending writer is not in this tree: on the CI baseline branch `scripts/lib/oci-build-integration.test.mjs` copies the whole `scripts/` tree into a temp directory per case and spawns Node subprocesses against a stub runtime, which is what saturated the runner. Every suite in this tree is read-only over the repository, so there is nothing to contend for. `--test-concurrency=1` stays, and the reason is recorded here rather than left as a bare flag.
findings.owner: BK-1 — the runner surface. Nobody re-owns this unless the contending writer (`scripts/lib/oci-build-integration.test.mjs`, which copies the whole `scripts/` tree per case and spawns Node subprocesses) returns to this repository. Every suite currently here is read-only over the tree, so there is nothing to contend for.
findings.removalCondition: Revisit when either of these becomes true, and not before: a suite in this repository writes to a shared path outside its own temp directory, or a `node --test` failure is observed whose verdict differs between `--test-concurrency=1` and the default. Until then the flag stays, and the cost is a 4x wall-clock penalty on this machine with no change to a single verdict, which is cheaper than a flake nobody can reproduce.
findings.resolution:
Moved from `open` to `debt`, which is the disposition the row had already reached by measurement: not reproducible, monitoring, with the flag staying. An `open` row asks for a fix, and there is no defect here to fix.

The measurements stand: 39/39 pass with `--test-concurrency=1` and 39/39 without, in 686 ms and 311 ms; on the CI baseline branch 46/46 either way, in 1 177 ms serial and 5 028 ms concurrent. Concurrency costs 4x wall-clock on this machine and changes no verdict.

The reason it is not reproducible is worth keeping, because "could not reproduce" is usually where a row goes to die: the contending writer is not in this tree. `scripts/lib/oci-build-integration.test.mjs` copies the whole `scripts/` tree into a temp directory per case and spawns Node subprocesses against a stub runtime, which is what saturated the runner. Every suite here is read-only over the repository. So the cause is identified even though the symptom is not, and the owner and removal condition name what would bring it back.

findings.title: Turbo had no global dependency on its own gate inputs
findings.summary: `globalDependencies` named the lockfile, the tsconfigs and the lint config, and nothing else. Editing `coverage-baseline.json`, `.semgrep.yml`, `.gitleaks.toml`, `playwright.config.ts`, `commitlint.config.js`, `vitest.config.ts`, `vitest.shared.ts` or `scripts/gate-tooling.json` left the `test` task's cache key untouched, so `pnpm test` could replay a result produced against the previous contents of a file the gate reads.

evidence.asserts: `globalDependencies` lists `vitest.config.ts`, `vitest.shared.ts`, `playwright.config.ts`, `commitlint.config.js`, `coverage-baseline.json`, `docs/quality/complexity-baseline.json`, `scripts/gate-tooling.json`, `.semgrep.yml`, `.gitleaks.toml` and `.jscpd.json`; `tsconfig*.json` already covers `tsconfig.scripts.json`.

findings.title: Three cross-references pointed at things that do not exist
findings.summary: `eslint.config.js:98` cited a nonexistent `docs/quality/debt-baseline.json` where the real ratchet is `docs/quality/complexity-baseline.json`; `review-rules/rules.json:128` named `pnpm secret:scan` where the script is `pnpm security:secrets`; and `docs/quality/coverage-exclusions.md:29` claimed nothing asserts a successful production composition, which `index-production-composition.test.ts:275-337` now does in eight cases including one that composes and exports a fetchable app.

evidence.asserts: The `cognitive-complexity` comment names `docs/quality/complexity-baseline.json`, the file the ratchet actually writes.
The `secret.detected` rule's `fix` names `pnpm security:secrets`, a script that exists in the root package.json.
`describe('a valid production configuration')` asserts a composition that succeeds, which is what the coverage exclusion now says it does.

findings.title: The secret history scan was not in the umbrella gate, and commitlint was not in CI
findings.summary: `security:secrets` scans the working tree, which cannot see a credential that was committed and later removed — the ordinary shape of an `git rm` or an edit that strips a secret. `security:secrets:history` existed and was in no gate, so `pnpm verify` passed over the history. It is now in `security:verify`, and commitlint runs as a named CI job.

evidence.asserts: `--history` is a supported mode that scans every commit rather than the working tree.
A named `commit-message` job runs `pnpm exec commitlint --from --to` over the push range.

findings.title: The coverage ratchet was reachable only from a dispatch-only workflow
findings.summary: The ratchet was the only gate that could prove a coverage floor had not been lowered, and it ran in `release-gate.yml:50`, which is dispatch-only. A PR could lower a floor and merge. It is now a required job in `unified-ci.yml` with a per-package table in the job summary. The job reads the coverage artifacts the test job produced and re-verifies each summary against the `provenance.json` stamp beside it, so a stale or restored-from-cache summary is rejected rather than believed.

evidence.asserts: A `coverage-ratchet` job needs `unit-and-coverage`, downloads the coverage artifacts and runs `pnpm coverage:ratchet`.
The per-package table is written to `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY`, and `staleCoverageFinding` still rejects a summary whose stamp does not match the current inputs.

findings.title: No rule caught a fail-open default or a double assertion at a contract
findings.summary: `new Date(0) as unknown as Date` and `requireProductionSecrets: false` are the two shapes the plan names, and nothing in the tree rejects either: the first silences the compiler at a schema boundary, the second disables a security check. `no-fail-open-default` is now a review rule, and `as unknown as` is a lint error under `packages/db/src/schema/**` and `packages/shared-contracts/**`.

evidence.asserts: `@typescript-eslint/no-unnecessary-type-assertion` and a `no-restricted-syntax` selector banning `TSAsExpression` inside a chain of two `as` operators apply to the two contract trees.
`no-fail-open-default` is declared with a severity, a category and a fix, and `review-rules-check.mjs` validates the declaration.

findings.title: The plan's verified-fixed list carries no evidence for thirteen of its seventeen rows
findings.summary: Plan §3 lists P-1, P-2, P-4, P-15, P-27, 45, 46, 48, 54, 58, F-1, F-2, F-3, R-2, the `makeApi()` typed defaults, the `Table.tsx` keyboard sort and the unknown-`NODE_ENV` rejection as verified fixed, and instructs that they not be redone. Two carry a path a reader can check today — R-2 at `durable-realtime-bus.test.ts` and the keyboard sort at `Table.test.tsx` — and the other fifteen name no evidence at all. A claim with no path cannot be machine-checked, which is the whole point of the ledger, so the claim itself is the open row. Closing it means adding one `fixed` row per finding with the test that proves it.
findings.resolution:
The list is withdrawn as evidence, and the general form is a gate. The merged-leftover plan listed seventeen findings as "verified fixed — do not redo" and named evidence for two. **Every one of the other fifteen identifiers no longer resolves** — the ledger was renumbered, so `P-1`, `P-2`, `45`, `R-2` and the rest are not rows in `docs/quality/findings-ledger.json` at all. A list that instructs a future reader not to redo work, on the strength of identifiers that point at nothing, is worse than no list: it forecloses the question without answering it. The list is struck through in place, with the withdrawal and the reason beside it, and the current state of those areas is left to the ledger — where a `fixed` row carries its evidence and `findings:check` reopens the claim if that evidence is deleted. Each of the fifteen fixes is deliberately *not* re-asserted: nobody re-verified them now, and claiming otherwise would be inventing provenance, which is the defect the row is about.

`docs:check` now fails on any document asserting something is "verified fixed", "resolved" or "done" with no backticked path that exists. Verified by injecting such a claim into `CONTRIBUTING.md` and watching it fail.

One false positive on the way, and it is the interesting one: decision F7 in the v2 plan is a finding *about* this list — it names the phrase in order to say the list has no evidence — and the gate read the description as a fresh claim. A document has to be able to write down the defect without tripping the check for it, so a quoted phrase is skipped, the same rule the unused-claim gate uses.

evidence.asserts: A "verified fixed" claim with no checkable path is a finding, across README, AGENTS, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG and every non-historical plan. Quoted phrases are skipped so a document can describe the defect without tripping it. **This is the whole of the evidence.** The withdrawn plan the gate was written against is a local session artefact under `.kilo/plans/`, excluded by `.git/info/exclude`, so it has never been committed and cannot be cited here — and the ledger rule that a closed finding must name an existing path correctly refuses to accept it as one. The gate is the durable proof; the plan was the example.

findings.title: The capability register contradicts itself and two of its real rows cite dead evidence
findings.summary: `tool.playwright` is `mock` at `:37` while `quality.browser` is `real` at `:39` for the same execution. Of 39 rows, 15 are real, 14 mock, 6 deferred, 2 missing and 2 obsolete; there is no `quality.mobile` row; and two `real` rows cite dead code (`RunExplorer`) or a CI file. The Evidence column cites paths, not executable commands, so the register's own rule is unmet.
findings.resolution:
Two of the row's three complaints were right and one was the row's own error, so the resolution is different for each.

**`tool.playwright` (mock) against `quality.browser` (real)** — the first attempt was a gate forcing the two rows to agree, and it was wrong: the register's own vocabulary says "a qualification is not a substitute for a status; **split a capability when its pieces have different truth values**", which is exactly what these two rows are. A gate that forced equality would have forbidden the register from following its own rule, and would have reported a legitimate distinction as a defect. Both titles and qualifications now name which half each measures — isolation of execution, against evidence reaching the dashboard — and each says so in the other's terms.

**Two agent domains had no row at all.** `AgentDomainSchema` declares `browser`, `api`, `load`, `security` and `mobile`; the register described three. A reader could not tell whether `load` and `mobile` were missing, deferred, or simply forgotten, which is the failure the register exists to prevent. Both are now `deferred` rows with the honest reason, and `docs:capability-register` fails when any domain in the schema has no `quality.<domain>` row. Verified by deleting the row and watching it fail.

That gate initially broke all four contract tests, because the suite runs the script against single-row fixture registers to prove each failure mode — and requiring five `quality.*` rows of one made every case fail for an unrelated reason. It now runs when the register claims to describe quality domains and is inert when it does not, which is the only way it can be correct about a document scoped to something else.

**The dead-evidence half was already closed** by the register's existing path check, which verifies every cited path exists; the row was written before that check or against a register that had drifted since.

evidence.asserts: Every domain in `AgentDomainSchema` has a `quality.<domain>` row, read from the schema rather than listed here, so adding a domain without a row fails. The check is inert for a register that describes no quality domains, which is what keeps the contract suite's fixtures working.
41 rows: `quality.load` and `quality.mobile` are accounted for, and `tool.playwright` and `quality.browser` each state which half of Playwright capability they measure and name the other row.

findings.title: Forty-two hand-rolled error call sites and twenty-five bodies with no code
findings.summary: There are 42 `error(c, status, code, message)` call sites and 0 have been migrated to `DomainError` — `execution/jobs.routes.ts` 22, `runs.routes.ts` 9, `runners.routes.ts` 6, `artifacts.routes.ts` 2, `policies.routes.ts` 1, `shared.ts` 1, `execution.ts` 1. Separately 25 bodies use a bare `{ error: string }` with no `code` field, which `AGENTS.md` itself forbids. The error surface was larger than when the wave was scoped. **Fixed in findings-remediation wave 1.2b, 2026-09-28 — and the row is larger than it was scoped.** Both halves are done: the forty-two `error(c, …)` sites and the bodyless `c.json({ error: '…' })` sites, together eighty-three refusals across thirty files, and every one of them is a `throw new DomainError(code, message)`. **The real content turned out to be the taxonomy, not the call sites.** `ErrorCode` had thirty-four codes; the API answers eighty. Every one of the forty-six that were missing is now a name, and `STATUS_BY_CODE` is a `Record<ErrorCodeValue, number>` — so adding a code without a status does not compile, which is the check the old `error()` helper could not perform on a bare `string`. **Two sites decided their status somewhere other than at the call site**, which is the arrangement the table removes: one passed `decoded.status` and one read a code from a helper that had already chosen a 409 beside it. Forty others wrote the status as a literal beside the code, and nothing compared the two — a test that asserted the body shape would have passed either way. **The count went to zero once before and the row stayed open for a year.** So the fix ends in a gate, not in a number: `apps/api/src/errors/error-surface.test.ts` reads every product file and fails on an `error(c, `, on an `error: '…'` or ``error: `…` `` body, and on a second `app.onError`. Its fourth case runs the scanner against a source that *does* contain the defect, because a source-reading gate that silently matched nothing would pass forever — which is exactly how the first version of it passed a file it had not read a line of. **Three things the migration found that the row does not name.** `routes/runner.ts` registered its own `app.onError` — a second error boundary, which `AGENTS.md` forbids, and the reason a runner client had to match the string "Unauthorized" with no code to branch on; its private `UnauthorizedError` class existed only for that handler to recognise. `events.ts` answered a missing realtime workspace with a 500, filing a configuration mistake under application defects. And the boundary replaced the message on *every* 5xx, which is right and was wrong for two answers: `NOT_CONFIGURED` ("Authentication is not configured") and `ARTIFACT_BYTES_UNAVAILABLE` are 5xx responses whose message and details are about a resource the caller named, and blanking them sends an operator to a support ticket instead of a checklist. `DomainErrorOptions.callerSafe` is that one exception, documented as such, and `missingArtifact` drops the one field that does not qualify — `storageKey`, a server-side path. **The response shape is unchanged and that is the point.** A caller sees `{ error: { code, message, requestId, details } }` from every refusal in the API, whether it used to come from the removed helper or from a hand-built `c.json`. What changed is that the code now exists, and that `details` is the only place anything beyond the code and message appears. **Twenty-six test files were changed, and the change is the same in every one: they mount the real error boundary.** A test that mounted a route group into a bare `Hono` and asserted a hand-built body was testing a second renderer — and after the migration it would have been asserting Hono's default 500. `test-support/error-boundary-app.ts` mounts a group the way `index.ts` mounts it, `requestContext` first; the order matters, because the first version of that helper installed only the boundary and every audit row a handler wrote then recorded `requestId: null`. Three assertions also became stronger rather than merely restyled: a reporter, a dashboard and the login limiter now assert a `code` where they used to assert a sentence, which is the only part of this change a client can use.
findings.confirmedBy: Findings-remediation wave 1.2b. Every site enumerated by a scanner, every message mapped to a code by hand, and the three defects the migration surfaced rather than caused recorded in the summary.

evidence.asserts: Eighty codes and one `Record<ErrorCodeValue, number>` behind them, checked in both directions by the generator that writes it. `callerSafe` is the one documented exception to the 5xx redaction, and it exists because two answers whose message names a resource the caller supplied were being replaced with "internal error".

Renders every `DomainError` through `DomainError.toBody`, and exports `domainErrorResponse` for the one place a failure must be *returned* rather than thrown — Hono's `bodyLimit` hook. Same function, two entry points, so a hook cannot become the second renderer.

The gate. Fails on an `error(c, `, on an `error: '…'` or ``error: `…` `` body in any product file, and on a second `app.onError`. Its fourth case runs the scanner against a source that does contain the defect, because a source-reading gate that matches nothing passes forever — which is the failure mode this row had once already.

Mounts a route group the way `index.ts` does, `requestContext` before the boundary. The order is the assertion: the first version installed only the boundary, and the only test that could see it — a quarantine write — recorded `requestId: null` while the header it sent sat unused.

No `error()` helper, and `missingArtifact` refuses instead of returning a response. Its 503 is `callerSafe` and carries the artifact id, run id, size and checksum — the caller's own resource — with `storageKey` deliberately dropped, which is the field that does not qualify.

No private `app.onError` and no `UnauthorizedError`. The runner client can now branch on `UNAUTHENTICATED` instead of matching the string "Unauthorized", and an internal defect inside a handler is no longer something this file can answer as an authentication failure.

Names the body it asserts (`ErrorBody`) instead of casting to `Record<string, unknown>`, and asserts a code beside every message. A reporter is the one client that reads these programmatically, so this is the case that proves the migration was lossless rather than merely green.

findings.title: The execution store is 2 166 lines and holds two of the top complexity offenders
findings.summary: `apps/api/src/execution/drizzle-execution-store.ts` grew 148 lines past the point the previous plan scheduled the split, and six tasks target it. `docs/quality/complexity-baseline.json` records per-function offenders (`ceiling: 15`, `count: 31`) and has no file-length notion, so the correct gate is the offender count plus the two named functions: `:1357` at complexity 65 and `:1098` at complexity 39, the latter being exactly the finding-49 transaction.

findings.title: The canonical production compose cannot boot the API
findings.summary: **Confirmed, then fixed in both stacks.** `apps/api/src/startup-policy.ts:90-97` really does throw when `config.objectStore` is unset in production, and the comment there is right about why: artifact bytes are evidence, and on one process's filesystem they disappear with it. The enforcement was never the problem. The problem was that the deployment contradicted it — `docker-compose.unified.yml` set `NODE_ENV: production` on the API with none of the five `OBJECT_STORE_*` variables, so the documented production stack could not have booted; and `compose.dev.yml` ran a MinIO service that no service depended on and no endpoint named, so the dev stack ran a store nothing used. This is the same class of defect as a gate with no instrument: the check was real, the thing it checked was never wired up, and nothing noticed. The dev stack is why it survived so long. Its API is `NODE_ENV: development`, the production policy genuinely does not apply, and `ARTIFACT_ROOT` would have sufficed — so the dev deployment was genuinely working while carrying a dead service. **Both** stacks now declare the five variables, and the dev stack's MinIO is wired to the API with a `service_healthy` wait so it is load-bearing rather than decorative. `OBJECT_STORE_ALLOW_INSECURE` is set deliberately and narrowly, with the reason inline: the endpoint is `http://minio:9000` on the compose network, the policy refuses plain HTTP in production unless that flag is set, and claiming https to a local store would be a false claim. A deployment with a real S3 endpoint over TLS omits the line and the policy enforces the stricter path. The store is MinIO with a named volume, not a container filesystem, because losing artifact bytes with the container is the exact failure the policy exists to prevent, and its root credentials come from the operator's environment rather than being written into a committed file. `pnpm compose:config` cannot catch this class — it resolves interpolation and reports syntax, and a compose file that simply omits five variables is a perfectly valid compose file — so `scripts/lib/compose-contract.mjs` now reads the committed files and asserts the wiring, scoped to the services that actually run the API image. Scoping mattered: the first version applied the rule to every service declaring `NODE_ENV: production` and immediately flagged `worker` and `runner`, which is the rule being wrong rather than the compose file. Those two processes never execute `startup-policy.ts` and never read an object store, and a contract check that demands configuration from a process which does not enforce the contract trains people to satisfy checks mechanically — which is how a real one gets ignored. The rule now matches on the API dockerfile, so renaming the service cannot opt it out. Three of the checks in that module came from getting it wrong first and are worth recording: the extractor returns a **map** rather than a key set, because the first version read values with a whole-file search and so could take one service's `NODE_ENV` from another service's block; an **interpolated** endpoint like `${OBJECT_STORE_ENDPOINT}` is skipped, because it has no dot and no port and the first version flagged the repository's own production file for an endpoint resolved at deploy time; and an **unparseable** environment line throws rather than returning a partial set, because a partial set is indistinguishable from a missing variable and the finding would be unactionable. It is a parser and not a regular expression for that last reason: a grep for `OBJECT_STORE_ENDPOINT` would pass on a line in a comment, in the wrong service, or with trailing whitespace, and would keep passing after the wiring was deleted. The CI `compose:config` step sets the three new variables as placeholders; without them that step would have gone red on a missing variable rather than on anything wrong with the file, which is the worst way for a config gate to fail. The second rule in the module is the one worth keeping beyond this row: an endpoint naming a service the file does not declare produces a stack that **boots** and then fails every artifact write with a connection error, which is worse than refusing to start precisely because it gets further before it fails.
findings.confirmedBy: W1.4. Confirmed by reading `startup-policy.ts` and both compose files.

evidence.asserts: The `api` service declares all five `OBJECT_STORE_*` variables alongside `NODE_ENV: production`, depends on the new `minio` service with `service_healthy`, and `minio_data` is a named volume — so the documented production stack now boots and its artifact bytes outlive the container.

The dev `api` now points at the `minio` service that was previously declared and referenced by nothing, and waits on its healthcheck — so the dead service is load-bearing and a developer exercising artifact upload runs the same path production does.

`docker-compose.unified.yml satisfies the object-store contract` fails when the five variables are removed and passes when they are present, and `the production stack really does declare the object store` asserts the wiring directly rather than only the absence of a finding, so a change that made the contract vacuously true still fails.

Still throws when `config.objectStore` is unset in production and when the endpoint is plain HTTP without `OBJECT_STORE_ALLOW_INSECURE` — the enforcement this row was about is unchanged, and the deployment now satisfies it rather than the other way round.

findings.title: The licence gate failed on apps/api without naming the offending dependency
findings.summary: `scripts/license-check.mjs` derives its workspace list from the pnpm workspace rather than a hand-maintained array, and then runs `pnpm --dir <workspace> exec license-checker-evergreen --failOn GPL-3.0;AGPL-3.0;UNLICENSED;UNKNOWN` per package. For `apps/api` the tool reported `Found license defined by the --failOn flag: "UNLICENSED"` and exited, but it named no package, while `pnpm --dir apps/api licenses list --prod --json` reported zero production dependencies — a red light pointing at nothing. Fixed in commit 92397a7, which changed the forbidden list to `GPL-3.0, AGPL-3.0, UNLICENSED, UNKNOWN` reported as a comma list and made the gate pass for all 22 workspace packages. The general defect is worth keeping: a gate that fails without naming the thing it found is a gate that gets deleted, and this one was the last reason `pnpm verify` was red.

evidence.asserts: The gate derives the package list from the workspace, fails loudly, and `node ./scripts/license-check.mjs` prints `License check passed for 22 workspace packages`.

findings.title: pnpm security:static hung forever instead of reporting
findings.summary: `scripts/static-analysis.mjs` spawned both scanners with `spawnSync` and no timeout, so the gate could not return a verdict at all. Measured on the Windows development host: `semgrep scan --config .semgrep.yml` over a *single* small package (`apps/worker/src`) produced no output and no exit in 15 minutes, and `pnpm security:static` was killed twice at 30 and 50 minutes. This is worse than a red gate, because it hid the state the gate exists to report — the 27 historical gitleaks findings `.gitleaks.toml` deliberately leaves red. The runners are now async and shell-free with a wall-clock ceiling, and the process *tree* is killed rather than the child, because adding `timeout` to a `shell: true` `spawnSync` did not help: on Windows the child is `cmd.exe`, killing it orphans the real scanner and the inherited pipe keeps `spawnSync` blocked. Measured after the fix with a 30s budget: 34 s, the scanner named, and the gitleaks half reached and reporting its 27.

evidence.asserts: `runBounded` is the ceiling, and it kills the process tree rather than the child, because a grandchild left holding the inherited pipe is the hang this replaced.

`a scanner that never returns is stopped, and reported as stopped` spawns a child that genuinely holds its event loop open and asserts `timedOut: true`, `status: 1`, a wall clock under 60s, and a message naming the wait.

findings.title: A PGlite migration hook had the default 10s budget and failed under load
findings.summary: The second confirmed instance of the class D-3 names, and it was found by the full `pnpm verify` run rather than by a test: `packages/db/src/repositories/repositories.test.ts:55` runs `beforeAll(async () => { new PGlite(); await client.exec(migrationSql()) })` with Vitest's default `hookTimeout` of 10 000 ms. Applying the real journal-ordered migration graph to an in-process Postgres is one of the two costs in this repository that scale with the *tree* rather than with the test — every migration ever added is paid again on every run. Observed failure under `pnpm verify` with turbo running thirty-odd package suites at once: `Error: Hook timed out in 10000ms`, 96 of the file's 107 tests green and 11 skipped. The failure is a statement about load, not about a repository. The hook now carries an explicit 60 000 ms budget with the reason recorded, matching the treatment `index-production-composition.test.ts` and the contract-suite capability-register already have. The remaining question for a later wave is whether applying the whole graph per test file is right at all; there is one PGlite instantiation in the package today, and that number should not grow.

evidence.asserts: `PGLITE_MIGRATION_TIMEOUT_MS` is passed as the `beforeAll` timeout, so the hook's budget is stated in the file rather than inherited as a 10s default that only fails on a loaded machine.

findings.title: semgrep does not complete on the Windows development host
findings.summary: The pip-installed `semgrep.exe` on the Windows host used to develop this repository never returns: `semgrep scan --config .semgrep.yml` over a *single* small package (`apps/worker/src`) produced no output and no exit in 15 minutes, and with the W0 ceiling in place the gate reports `semgrep did not finish within 10m and was stopped` after burning the full budget. This is an environment limitation rather than a repository defect, and it is recorded so nobody spends an hour rediscovering it. It is also not invisible: G-2b's fix is what turned a silent hang into that named line, which is how it was found. CI is unaffected — `.github/actions/install-scanners` installs semgrep 1.178.0 from PyPI on ubuntu-24.04, where it is a normal fast run. The only consequence on this host is that `pnpm security:static` and therefore `pnpm security:verify` cannot go green here, and no amount of repository-side work changes that. If a Windows-local semgrep run is wanted, the thing to investigate is the pip install's interaction with this host, not the ruleset.
findings.resolution: The defect is not the hang — semgrep still hangs on this host, and no repository change will make it not hang. The defect the row names as a *consequence* is that `pnpm security:static`, and therefore `pnpm verify`, could not complete here at all, and that is fixed. `AUTOMATE_HOST_SCANNERS=unavailable` records a scanner that cannot scan as `not_configured` and exits 0; `pnpm verify:local` runs the full thirteen-step chain with it set, and does so green on this host. Three properties keep the opt-in narrow: a scanner that *ran* and reported something still fails; a scanner killed at the ceiling is `unavailable` rather than clean, so a ten-minute stall can never become a green gate; and `AUTOMATE_SCAN_TIMEOUT_MS` is clamped to [1 min, 1 h], because a ceiling small enough to guarantee a kill was a second, unmentioned route to the same outcome. The last of those was found by review, not by the original author, and it is recorded here because the row's lesson is that a gate which cannot run is a gate nobody can trust to say yes.

evidence.asserts: The whole policy: `exitStatusFor` fails on `found` whatever the host asked for, degrades only `unavailable`, and `scanTimeoutMs` clamps the ceiling to [1 minute, 1 hour] so a timeout cannot be set small enough to guarantee a kill.

The wiring. A hung scanner is recorded `unavailable` and never as clean, and there is one outcome message on stdout — the degraded run used to fall through to a `console.log` claiming semgrep and gitleaks 'reported nothing' about a scan that never ran.

The command. It spawns the real `verify` chain — not a smaller one — with the opt-in set on the child process only, and does so with the platform-correct spawn: the first version passed `shell: false` unconditionally and died with `EINVAL` on the one platform it existed to serve.

`auditHostDegradation` walks every YAML file under `.github/`, composite actions included, and reports any that sets the opt-in. Reading only `.github/workflows/` left the hole open in `.github/actions/install-scanners`, whose step-scoped `env:` every later step in the calling job inherits.
The boundary, from both sides: a scanner that ran and found something fails even with the opt-in, a scanner killed at the ceiling is never a clean scan, and a one-millisecond ceiling cannot be set.

findings.title: gitleaks reported 27 historical values, and none of them was a credential
findings.summary: `gitleaks detect` over all commits reported 27 credential-shaped values, and the gate was red on them. Every one has now been read at its source line, in the commit gitleaks named, and not one is a provider-issued credential. The evidence, by kind: `ai-explain.test.ts:269,276` hold the literal string `sk-12345...efgh`; `SlowestTests.tsx:67` is a Recharts `<Bar dataKey="…">` prop, so the `generic-api-key` rule matched a column identifier; `saml-slo.test.ts:517` is a three-line PEM stub whose body is the single word `MIIE`; `hardening-checks.test.ts:29` is the detector’s own fixture, so deleting it would delete the evidence that the rule works; and the remaining 21 are `apiKey:`, `token:` and `key` fields inside `*.test.ts`. The working tree reports zero gitleaks findings in product source throughout. Resolved with `allowlist.commits` — the narrowest instrument gitleaks offers, and the one `.gitleaks.toml` itself named — keyed on the nine specific commits rather than on a path, because two of the affected files still exist and must keep being scanned.
