Verified that the allowance did not blunt the scanner: a freshly generated 40-character `ghp_` token in a scratch directory is still reported as a leak. GitHub push protection still refuses the pre-unification branches that contain these commits (GH013), which is correct and unchanged: suppressing a local report does not unblock a push, and it is not meant to.

evidence.asserts: `allowlist.commits` names the nine confirmed commits, and the block comment above it records the classification for each kind of finding and why a commit is narrower than a path.
The structural check still passes — `the gitleaks allowlist exempts nothing broad` — so nine commit hashes are not a broad exemption.

findings.title: A third of the dashboard schema is dormant
findings.summary:
Roughly 35 tables in `schema/dashboard.ts` have no reader and no writer, so they are neither exercised nor served. `locator_suggestions` has no `updatedAt` column at all. Each needs a reader, writer, route, UI and test, or a written justification in `docs/quality/capability-justification.md`.

**Confirmed by reading the code, 2026-09-28.**

**Partly true, and the row's headline count is arithmetically impossible.**
`schema/dashboard.ts` defines **33** `pgTable` exports in total, so "roughly 35 tables
with no reader and no writer" cannot be true as written. The `locator_suggestions`
sub-claim **is** confirmed: the table has no `updatedAt` and no `updated_at` column at
all (`:646-663`).

**Correct tally from a full read-and-search of all 33 tables.**

- **8 have a production reader and/or writer:** `runners`, `runs`, `tests`,
  `canonicalRunResults`, `quarantine`, `qualityGateConfig`, `auditEvents`
  (write-only), `schedules`.
- **25 genuinely have neither:** `workspaces`, `suites`, `results`, `attachments`,
  `trends`, `knownFailures`, `defectCategories`, `fingerprintCategories`,
  `blobShards`, `nlQueryHistory`, `failureTaxonomyRules`, `failureClassifications`,
  `testFailureCorrelations`, `locatorSuggestions`, `failureClusters`, `users`,
  `roles`, `apiKeys`, `agentSessions`, `agentSessionRuns`, `agentSessionFiles`,
  `generatedTestSuggestions`, `repairAttempts`, `agentConflicts`, `samlConfig`.
- **Of those 25, 21 have genuinely zero access outside schema-shape assertions.** Four
  have test-only access: `samlConfig`, `apiKeys`, `generatedTestSuggestions`,
  `workspaces`.

**Two corrections that matter, because this row decides "build each table or justify it".**

1. **`schedules` is NOT dormant.** It has one reader and two writers, in
   `apps/worker/src/postgres-store.ts:388, 467, 590` — written as raw SQL rather than
   through Drizzle. A sweep that searched for `.from(`/`.insert(` would have missed it,
   which is exactly the "inferred from a grep" failure this ledger has already produced
   twice.
2. **`auditEvents` is write-only, not dormant.** Four production writers, zero
   production readers. A justification saying "no reader" is correct; one saying "no
   writer" is wrong, and `modules/dashboard/audit-sink.ts:4-7` explicitly records the
   *no-writer* state as an already-fixed defect. It is not a C-6 candidate.

**`.kilo/plans/1790582734810-findings-remediation-plan.md` §4 2.6 sizes this wave at
"`~35` tables"; the real figure is 21.** The wave should be re-tallied before it is
scheduled, since the count is what makes it look like one wave at all.
findings.owner: unassigned — a wave that owns schema surface
findings.removalCondition: Each of the 21 tables named in `docs/quality/capability-justification.md` gains a production reader or is deleted in a migration. When the last row of that file is gone the file is deleted with it. The condition names what could happen: a reader being written.
findings.resolution:
**Taken as debt, with the justification written down.** The row requires each dormant table to gain a reader, a writer, a route, a UI and a test — or a written justification. `docs/quality/capability-justification.md` is that justification: it names all 21 tables, states why each exists and why it is still here, and separates them from the 8 that have production access and the 4 with test-only access.

**The count correction in the summary is the load-bearing part of this disposition.** The plan sized the wave at `~35` tables; the real figure is 21, because `schema/dashboard.ts` defines 33 in total. Two tables the row's own analysis corrects are the ones a grep gets wrong: `schedules` has a reader and two writers in `apps/worker/src/postgres-store.ts` written as **raw SQL** rather than through Drizzle, and `audit_events` is write-only with four production writers. Both are listed in the justification as read-or-written, and neither is a candidate.

**These are debt, not defects, and the distinction is the whole point.** Nothing writes the 21, so nothing can read a wrong value out of them. The cost of leaving them is migration surface and reader confusion, not a wrong number on a screen — which is why this is not a Major open finding against v1.0.0. `locator_suggestions` is called out separately because it has no `updatedAt` column at all: a table with no freshness column has no defined staleness, so any row in it is permanently current by construction. It should be dropped before it is built, and the justification says so.

**Deliberately not closed.** The row is `debt` rather than `fixed` because building twenty-one product surfaces is real work that has not been done. Closing it would record the documentation as the feature.

evidence.asserts: Every dormant table is named with its reason, separated from the 8 with production access and the 4 with test-only access.

findings.title: The superseded plan's D4 and W2.1 would have broken working execution
findings.summary: The plan that seeded this ledger carried decision D4 and task W2.1, which together said the worker's absent `JobHandler` was "the largest single gap in the repo" and directed that a handler be wired into `apps/worker/src/main.ts`. Executing it would have broken execution rather than repaired it. `ExecutionWorker`'s in-process claim path queries the same `runners` and `jobs` tables the API serves, so a handler in the worker would put a process with no execution capability in competition with `apps/runner` — which claims over `POST /api/v1/runners/:runnerId/jobs/claim` and is the thing that actually runs jobs. Every job the worker won would have ended `infra_failed` or bounced through requeue. The trap is that the underlying observation is true and the conclusion is inverted: the worker genuinely does pass no handler, and genuinely never executes a job, and neither is a defect. The reversal is recorded in the ledger's `$waves.W2` note so it is visible from this file, and D4 is struck in the plan itself. The plan is excluded from version control by `.git/info/exclude`, so the *tracked* guarantee is not the annotation: it is the comment at the composition site plus the two cases in `worker.test.ts` that pin the invariant. A later reader has to change a test to reintroduce the bug, which is the point. One correction came out of checking rather than assuming — the comment cited a test named `claims nothing in production composition, because the runner executes`, and no such test exists; the two real cases are named in the evidence below. A pointer to a test that is not there defeats the only mechanism the comment relies on.

evidence.asserts: The `ExecutionWorker` construction passes no `handler`, and the comment above it states that execution belongs to `apps/runner`, names the claim route, and cites the two `worker.test.ts` cases by their real names.

`claims nothing without a handler, even when a job is claimable` composes the worker with no handler and asserts a claimable job stays `queued` with no active job ids, so adding a handler to `main.ts` fails this test rather than passing quietly.
`still does its scheduler work without a handler` pins the other half — that going without a handler is not going inert — so the fix for the first case cannot be to reintroduce one.

findings.title: The migration rehearsal never ran, and the tenancy wave landed anyway
findings.summary: **Confirmed, and now part-built.** D1 is "rehearse before breaking": a destructive migration does not merge until a rehearsal has restored a post-migration database **and re-opened every encrypted row**. W7 is roughly ten irreversible tenancy migrations, so D1 is the gate in front of the largest irreversible work in the programme — and `pnpm smoke:rehearsal` is not it: `scripts/migration-rehearsal.mjs` calls `assertLocalRehearsal`, writes a report whose own field reads `rehearsalPerformed: false` with `performedPhases: ['local-target-guard']`, and prints "No rehearsal was performed". **What now exists: the half with teeth.** `scripts/lib/vault-rehearsal.mjs` is the verification, as a pure function with the opener injected — so it is testable with no database, no encryption key and no vault. A dump/restore proves the database came back; it does not prove the **ciphertexts are still readable**, which is the property a migration can silently destroy. Renaming a column the AAD is bound to, a narrowing type change, or a re-seal under a different key each leave a restored database that looks perfect and holds nothing anyone can read. P-8 is the same failure in the other direction: the ciphertext was readable and belonged to the *wrong row*, so nothing looked broken at all — which is why the verifier classifies rather than concatenates. Three properties make it a gate rather than a log line, and each is a test: **every row is attempted**, because stopping at the first failure reports one broken row and hides the other four, and an operator who fixes the first re-runs and meets the second, one migration at a time. **A run that verified nothing fails**, because an empty table and a query that matched the wrong shape are indistinguishable from here, and declaring a destructive migration safe on the strength of a rehearsal that opened nothing is the failure this exists to prevent. **Nothing opening is reported as a probable key problem** rather than N unreadable rows, because a rotated secret fails every row identically and treating that as N broken rows sends the operator after the data. **What is still missing: the transport half.** There is no `pg_dump`, no restore onto a clean instance, and no reconciliation — the parts that need a live second database and are therefore not something this environment can demonstrate. **And the row stays `open`**, because D1 is not satisfied by half a harness. What a completion needs: a `migrate:rehearse` command that dumps, restores, runs the verifier above over every sealed row, and fails the migration if any row will not open; plus the run recorded against a real installation before W7 begins. Until then D1 is a policy with a verifier and no way to run one, which is a real improvement and not the gate. **Progress in findings-remediation wave 1.1, 2026-09-28: the transport half exists, and the row stays `open` because a harness is not a run.** `pnpm migrate:rehearse` now exists, and the sequence is the content. `pg_dump` the source; `pg_restore` onto a **clean** instance; apply the migration graph **to the restore**; re-open every sealed row in the restore through the product's own `vault-crypto` module; fail if any will not open. **The migration goes to the copy, and that is the step people get wrong.** A rehearsal that migrates the source has proved that a migration runs — which CI already proved against an empty schema yesterday. The open question is whether it runs over *data*, and the only data is in the source, so the copy is what gets destroyed. The command refuses a restore target equal to the source, which is asserted by running the command rather than by a comment. **The opener is the product's own, loaded from `apps/api/dist`.** A rehearsal that opened rows with a second implementation of the decryption would prove the second implementation still works, which is the same mistake as testing a copy of the code rather than the code. A missing build is reported as a missing build, not as an unreadable vault. **The sequence is a function with injected transports, so it is testable with no database.** `scripts/lib/rehearsal-run.mjs` has eleven cases covering the mistakes that live in the sequence rather than in the crypto: the migration applied to the source, a failed dump reported as an empty vault, a failed restore continuing, a classified row failure, and a report that derives `rehearsalPerformed` from the phases instead of asserting it. **The eleventh case found a real bug in the implementation, one commit after it was written:** `ok` was computed from structural problems only, so a run with one unreadable row and nothing else wrong reported success. A rehearsal that is green over a vault it could not read is worse than no rehearsal, because it is a *green* one. **The seven refusals are tested by running the command.** `scripts/lib/migration-rehearse.test.mjs` spawns `scripts/migration-rehearse.mjs` and asserts each one: no `REHEARSAL_MODE=local`, a non-loopback source, no restore target, a non-loopback restore, a restore that *is* the source, no `VAULT_SECRET`, and publication or cutover. The last of these is the existing guard being called rather than reimplemented — a second copy of that decision is a second decision. **What is still missing, and it is the half that matters.** The command is `never-in-ci` in `scripts/gate-tooling.json`, with `pg_dump`, `pg_restore` and `psql` recorded as dependencies, for the reason `migrate:apply` is: a rehearsal needs a live second database and CI has none, so a rehearsal against a service container would prove that `pg_dump` is installed. **No run of this command has happened against a real installation.** Until one does, D1 is a policy with a complete harness and no evidence, and the tenancy wave must not start on the strength of the harness. The row stays open for exactly that reason, and the first half of what it needs is now off the list.
findings.confirmedBy: W6. Confirmed: `smoke:rehearsal` is a local-target guard and rehearses nothing. The verification half of the harness is now built; the transport half is not.

evidence.asserts: The sequence, with every transport injected: dump, restore, migrate the *restore*, fetch, verify. A phase that throws is recorded as `failed` and the run stops, because a rehearsal that restored from a half-written dump would be reporting on a database nobody had. `ok` requires `verification.ok` as well as no structural problems, which is the term whose absence made an unreadable vault report as a pass.

Eleven cases, and the load-bearing one is the first: the migration is asserted to be applied to the restore and never to the source, and to come after the dump. A failed dump yields `verification: null` rather than a zero-row result, because a stopped run and an empty vault are indistinguishable in a report and must not be indistinguishable in the data.

The command itself. It calls the existing `assertLocalRehearsal` rather than reimplementing the loopback refusal, requires a *distinct* restore URL, and loads `openSecret` from the built `apps/api` so the rehearsal exercises the decryption the product runs. A report is written either way and the exit code is 1 on any failure, so a CI step or a human both see the same thing.

Seven refusals, each proven by spawning the command and matching its stderr. A refusal asserted about the source rather than about the process is a comment, and the one that matters most is a restore target equal to the source — the mistake D1 exists to prevent, which the command would otherwise perform silently and report as a pass.

`migrate:rehearse` carries `pg_dump`, `pg_restore` and `psql` as dependencies and the tier `never-in-ci`, and the `smoke:rehearsal` note no longer claims the harness does not exist — it says what that script still is, and that the rehearsal command calls its guard rather than replacing it.

`migrate:rehearse` exists as a root script, which `gate-tooling.test.mjs` requires in both directions: a manifest row naming a script that does not exist is a finding, and so is a root script with no tier.

findings.owner: Nobody can discharge this from a development host. It needs an installation with real sealed rows, a second database to restore onto, and the `vault-crypto` module built — `pnpm migrate:rehearse`, run on the reference hardware, once. ADR-006 and ADR-003 are the decisions this row rested on; both are superseded by the scope decision recorded in `resolution`.
findings.removalCondition: One run of `pnpm migrate:rehearse` against a real installation — dump, restore onto a clean instance, migrate **the restore**, re-open every sealed row through the product's own `vault-crypto` — with the date, the installation, and the row count verified recorded in `resolution`. That is condition (a), and it is the only thing that closes this row. Condition (b) — W7 entering scope — **fired on 2026-10-02** and is what put the row in the `Blocker` band with `status: open`; it is a trigger, not a removal, and it is machine-checked from `docs/quality/wave-gates.json` rather than read out of this sentence.
findings.resolution:
**Not cleared. The rehearsal is runnable on a developer machine; this one stopped short of it.

A full run was attempted on 2026-10-03 and the environment was built and then torn down. What was
established, so the next attempt does not repeat it:

- **Two independent PostgreSQL instances are not the obstacle.** Docker is present on a developer
  machine, and two `postgres:16` instances on a user-defined network answer `pg_isready` within
  seconds. The guard's actual requirement — a restore target that is not the source, on loopback —
  is satisfiable.
- **`pnpm build` then `node ./scripts/migration-rehearse.mjs` is the right sequence** and the script
  reads its environment exactly as documented: `REHEARSAL_MODE=local`, `DATABASE_URL`,
  `REHEARSAL_RESTORE_URL`, `VAULT_SECRET`, `REHEARSAL_REPORT_DIR`. All five were supplied and the
  guard accepted every one.
- **The blocker is the client tools, and it is a platform one rather than a repository one.** The
  script reaches `pg_dump`, `pg_restore` and `psql` through `spawnSync`, which on Windows calls
  `CreateProcess` and therefore resolves `pg_dump.exe` only. No PostgreSQL client is installed on
  this host, `@embedded-postgres/windows-x64` ships `initdb`/`postgres`/`pg_ctl` and **not** the three
  clients, and a `.cmd` shim is invisible to `CreateProcess`. A GitHub runner has the clients and
  does not have Docker, so neither machine has both by default.

**The fix belongs in the harness, not in an operator's PATH.** A `pnpm migrate:rehearse` that cannot
be run on the machine it is meant to be developed on will keep being skipped, and this row has now
survived more than one wave for exactly that reason. Two ways to close it honestly, and the choice
is a maintainer's:

1. **Run the rehearsal in a container** — a `node:24-alpine` image with `postgresql16-client` and
   the two PostgreSQL instances in it, the repository mounted. The tools are then native, the URLs
   are genuinely loopback, and "two instances" means two postmasters on two data directories rather
   than two databases on one server.
2. **Install the clients as a dev dependency of the harness** — a package that ships the Windows
   clients rather than only the server, so `pnpm migrate:rehearse` works on a developer machine the
   same way it does on CI.

Until one of those lands the row stays **open**, because a Blocker that has a harness and no run is
precisely the state this ledger exists to keep visible. What is now recorded is the blocker itself,
which was not written down anywhere before.

findings.title: Five waves carry a gate obligation that no ledger row tracks
findings.summary: A gate with no row is a gate that can be skipped silently, because nothing in this repository checks that a wave's gate was met — `pnpm findings:check` fails on rows, and a wave whose only deliverable was a gate has no row to check. Tallying `wave` across all 104 rows: **W6, W14, W15 and W17 have no rows at all**, and W2's only row is X-1, which records the handler *decision* rather than the wave's gate ("a job runs worker→runner on PostgreSQL"). W6's missing gate is RF-5 and is tracked separately because it is a missing tool rather than a missing row. The four that remain untracked need a row each: W14's axe-green-in-both-themes gate, W15's tiering of the eight new QA gates inside the D6 budget, and W17's site-doctor's ten checks. Adding the rows is the cheap half; the point is that the wave is now visible in the same place a reader looks for every other obligation.
findings.resolution:
**Delivered, which is what this row was for.** The row asked for a ledger row per untracked gate
obligation, and its own removal condition records that all four were added. Tallying `wave` across
the ledger no longer leaves W6, W14, W15 and W17 without a row, so `pnpm findings:check` can see a
wave whose only deliverable was a gate.

Closed as delivered rather than as newly done: re-opening it to "fix" it would have meant writing
rows that already exist.

evidence.asserts: The ledger's own checker is the evidence: `pnpm findings:check` passes with RF-6a through RF-6d present, which is the property the row asked for. A row recording the existence of other rows cannot cite the file it lives in and mean anything.

findings.impact: Resolved. Every wave named in this row now has a row of its own, so a gate obligation cannot be skipped silently.

findings.title: The performance gate compares real traffic to thresholds nobody ever measured
findings.summary: `performance/thresholds.json` records `release` thresholds as k6 expressions — `p(95)<500`, `p(99)<1500`, `rate<0.01`, `rate>0.99` — and the cross-check against `performance/smoke.js` is genuinely sound: a scenario that tightens or relaxes a threshold without the record changing fails the gate, and so does a record edited alone. What the file cannot tell you is whether the numbers mean anything. `observed_on_reference_hardware` reads `recorded: false`, all three observed values are `null`, and its own `reason` field says so: "Never measured … every number in `release` is an unvalidated estimate." So the gate is well-built and protects nothing — it detects drift from a baseline that was never taken, which is the same defect as no gate wearing a threshold's clothes. The fix is to measure against recorded reference hardware and then *tighten* the thresholds to the measured value, so the gate catches a regression rather than restating an intention. Until then a real p95 of 900 ms passes a `p(95)<500` check on a machine nobody ran it on.

findings.title: The E2E suite runs on one engine, so a rendering defect in another is invisible
findings.summary: `playwright.config.ts` declares two projects — `vertical-slice` and `product` — and both set `use: { ...devices['Desktop Chrome'] }`, at `:118` and `:127` respectively. There is no WebKit project, no Firefox project and no mobile viewport, so "E2E green" means "E2E green in Chromium" and the suite is one engine narrower than the claim. That matters more than a routine coverage gap, because of what is planned: the design language in the v2 plan introduces `backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%)` as the signature effect, and WebKit is the engine with the longest rendering history for it. A single-engine suite is the instrument most likely to let a glass bug reach a release. The existing non-empty-project assertions and the CI guard that throws when `product` matches nothing must be preserved when the matrix is added — a three-project config where only one collects tests is worse than one project, because it looks like coverage. Narrow the full matrix to nightly and run a Chrome+WebKit pair on PRs, so the PR cost stays bounded and WebKit is still on every merge.
findings.refutedBy:
**Refuted by reading, 2026-10-01. The premise is about a v2 plan that is not implemented, and the risk it names is one cross-engine defect away from nothing.**

The row is explicit that the concern rests on the v2 plan introducing `backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%)` as its signature effect. That property is **in no stylesheet in this repository**: `blur(20px) saturate(180%)` occurs in `performance/rendering-budget.json` and in the header comment of `scripts/lib/rendering-budget.mjs` — the two places that argue *against* it, by name — and nowhere else. The only `backdrop-filter` in the built stylesheet is Tailwind's stock `--tw-backdrop-blur: initial` variable declaration, which is emitted for every Tailwind project regardless of what it uses. There is no glass chrome to render on WebKit, so the instrument the row asks for would be measuring a defect that cannot occur.

**What survives is real, and it is already tracked.** A single-engine suite is a genuine coverage claim this repository does not currently make. That is `PERF-1`, whose row already records the measurement as absent and whose disposition is to stay open. Keeping RF-10 open as well would double-count one gap and leave a row whose stated removal condition — "the cross-engine glass defect exists" — impossible to satisfy honestly, because the plan that would create it is not on the roadmap this repository is executing.

**Refuted rather than fixed deliberately.** Building a three-engine matrix for a rendering risk that does not exist would spend CI minutes on a property of a plan, and would be a decision made by reading a design document rather than the code — which is the failure mode `docs/quality/findings-ledger.mjs` exists to prevent.
findings.premiseExpires:
**The refutation rests on a premise with an expiry date, 2026-10-03.** It is sound today and it is not sound indefinitely, and the date is recorded here rather than left to be discovered.

The refutation holds because `backdrop-filter: blur(20px) saturate(180%)` is in no stylesheet in this repository, so the WebKit rendering defect it names cannot occur. `.kilo/plans/1791024280658-cinematic-design-language-and-docs-overhaul.md` §4 (D6-6) now schedules `backdrop-filter` into the chrome of `NavBar`, the app shell, the `Command Center` and the `Toaster` — blur 8–16px, saturation 1.05–1.15 — and that plan **is** on the roadmap this repository is executing.

Phase 1 of that plan ships none: `DESIGN-1` and the ESLint ban in `eslint.config.js` make `backdrop-filter` an error in every `.ts` and `.tsx` file, so the refutation is correct for as long as that ban holds. The moment Phase 2 opens the allowlist, the property this row refuted exists, and the refutation needs re-reading rather than re-running.

**The disposition when that happens is already recorded.** The refutation's own text says the surviving gap — a single-engine suite — "is `PERF-1`, whose row already records the measurement as absent and whose disposition is to stay open." So the right move on the day Phase 2 lands is not to reopen `RF-10` (`false-positive` is terminal, and `isForward` in `scripts/lib/findings-ledger.mjs` does not allow it) and not to add a ninth row: it is to widen `PERF-1`'s summary to name the cross-engine glass case explicitly, so one row carries the measurement gap rather than two rows carrying halves of it.

findings.title: No OpenAPI document exists, and a deferred back-item's entry criterion is that it does
findings.summary: A repo-wide search for `openapi` or `swagger` returns one prose mention and no artifact: `packages/shared-contracts/README.md` notes that the `*.schema.json` files are preserved for tooling that *would* generate a spec. There was a second mention, in a superseded draft PRD for the product's former name, which has since been deleted — so the row now cites one document rather than two, and the count is stated so it can be re-derived. There is no `docs/openapi.json`, no generator dependency, and no drift gate. That is a gap in itself, but the specific defect is the coupling: BK-5's recorded entry criterion is "W9.6 OpenAPI document exists", and W9.6 is not a task in the plan that seeded this ledger. A back-item gated on a task that was never written can never legitimately be unblocked, and the failure mode is someone generating a document by hand to satisfy the sentence. Generating the document from the Zod contracts that are already authoritative — plus a gate that fails when the document and the schemas disagree — makes the criterion checkable and removes the hand-written path. `shared-contracts` is the right source because it is `real` and is what both the API and the client already validate against, so a spec generated from it cannot disagree with the code without the drift gate firing.
findings.resolution:
**The row identifies a real coupling defect and names a remedy it did not check.** Its complaint is not that no OpenAPI document exists — it is that BK-5's entry criterion is "W9.6 OpenAPI document exists" and **W9.6 was never written as a task**, so a back-item can never legitimately be unblocked and the pressure lands on someone hand-writing a document to satisfy the sentence. That is the defect, and it is confirmed.

**The row also says generating the document needs a generator dependency the repository does not have. It does.** `@asteasolutions/zod-to-openapi` is already a dependency of `packages/shared-contracts` — `packages/shared-contracts/package.json` lists it, and `packages/shared-contracts/src/openapi.ts` generates from the same Zod schemas the API validates against. So both halves of the proposed remedy exist: the generator is present and `shared-contracts` is already the single source.

**What is actually missing is the drift gate**, and that is a smaller thing than either. The row's own diagnosis — a spec generated from the contracts 'cannot disagree with the code without the drift gate firing' — means the generator is the cheap part and the gate is the load-bearing one. Generating the document today without it would produce an artifact that drifts silently, which is worse than no artifact: it reads as a specification and is not enforced.

**Keeping the row open, and why that is the honest disposition.** The OpenAPI document genuinely does not exist, so the gap is real and closing this row would claim otherwise. What is closed here is the row's framing as "no generator dependency" — corrected against the tree. The remaining work is one command and one gate: emit the document in `docs:capability-register` (or a sibling), and fail `docs:check` when the emitted document differs from the committed one. BK-5's criterion should be reworded to name that gate rather than a wave that was never written.

findings.title: A plan claim that `vitest-axe` is unused is false, and acting on it would delete working accessibility infrastructure
findings.summary: Question 4 of the superseded plan's §8 records `vitest-axe` as "declared and unused", and reasons from there toward replacing it. It is used, in both packages, through small shared helpers: `apps/web/src/test-axe.ts:14` imports `axe` from `vitest-axe` and `packages/ui/src/test/axe.ts` does the same for the component library. Both wrap it in `expectNoBlockingAxeViolations`, which fails on `serious` and `critical` violations. The band is Minor rather than higher because nothing is broken — the risk is entirely in the *next* reader, who is being handed a documented reason to delete a package that two suites depend on. Mitigation so far is procedural: the supersession banner on the plan and decision D20 in the plan that replaced it. The durable fix is the gate this row is really about — a `docs:check` that fails on a capability claim with no executable command behind it (RF-2 in the same plan), which is the general form of the failure C-1 and C-2 are both instances of. Recorded as a row rather than a note so it cannot be quietly closed by the next sweep.
findings.resolution:
The claim is refuted where it is made, and the general form is now a gate. The superseded plan recorded `vitest-axe` as "declared and unused" and reasoned from there toward removing it; it is used in two packages through `expectNoBlockingAxeViolations`, so the note was handing the next reader a documented reason to delete working accessibility infrastructure. `docs:check` now fails on a document that calls a named identifier unused, dead, unreferenced or obsolete while the workspace still uses it — and the plans under `.kilo/` are in scope, because a plan is read by the next person exactly as a README is and the only thing that made the difference feel safe was that a plan looks like a record rather than a description.

**The gate immediately found a second false claim nobody had recorded.** The QA roadmap said `Toast` — the one component already setting an `aria-live` region — "is unused", and reasoned toward adding new live regions instead. `Toast` is rendered in 15 places. Both claims are now struck through in place with the correction beside them, so the refutation is findable next to what it refutes.

Two false positives the gate produced on the way are worth recording, because a gate that reports the truth as false gets switched off. `ThemeToggle` and `RunExplorer` are exported, rendered by their own tests, and mounted by nothing — those claims are **true**, and the first version counted a component's own test as a use. And decision D20, which refutes the original claim, was read as making it — three different window-and-quote implementations all got that wrong, and the fix is to strip quoted and struck-through text before scanning rather than to reason about distance. A document must be able to write down what a superseded plan wrongly said, or it cannot correct anything without tripping the gate.

evidence.asserts: A document calling an identifier unused, dead, unreferenced or obsolete is a finding when that identifier is still used — across README, AGENTS, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG and every non-historical plan. Quoted and struck-through runs are removed before scanning, so a recorded refutation is not read as the claim it refutes; a component's own test is not a use; and the test asserts the gate can see the claim that started the row, that the plans are actually in scope, and that an unimported name is not reported. The plans this was written against (2 files under `.kilo/plans/`) are local session artefact excluded by `.git/info/exclude`, so they have never been committed and cannot be cited. The ledger rule that a closed finding must name an existing path is right and refused them; the gate is the durable proof and the plans were the example.

findings.title: The OCI release gate could never pass, and the repair it got had no row
findings.summary:
`pnpm oci:verify` was a gate nobody should have trusted rather than one that happened to be strict, for three independent reasons, **any one of which was sufficient on its own**. It required `"buildStatus": "built"` and a `sha256:` digest in every runner manifest, and **nothing in this repository ever wrote either** — `oci:build` ran `docker build` and discarded the result, so the committed JSON carried a claim no build had made and the only way to satisfy the gate was to type the claim in by hand, which is the exact falsification the old verifier's own header described having removed. It required that digest to match `RepoDigests`, which only exists for an image pushed to a registry; ADR-006's distribution model builds these on the host that runs them, so they are never pushed and there was nothing to compare. And it read the declared isolation out of the same JSON that declared it, which proves nothing about the image that would run. **This gate was the reason 2.2.0 was untagged**, so the cost of never noticing was a release held back by a check that was unsatisfiable rather than unmet.

**The repair changed what is measured rather than what is demanded, and it had no row of its own** — which is RF-6's own words: *a gate with no row is a gate that can be skipped silently.* Commit `726dfa9` moved the rules into a pure function and made every one of them answerable from two independent sources: the record `oci:build` wrote in the run that built, against the image the runtime actually holds.
findings.confirmedBy: Read against the tree after the repair landed, and checked against the scripts' own headers and test names rather than against the commit message.
findings.resolution:
**A gate that cannot pass is worse than a gate that is too strict**, because it teaches reviewers to read red as noise — which is the failure mode the rest of this repository's gate design exists to prevent. So the rules now assert what is checkable, and the things that are genuinely unavailable are *reported* as unavailable with what would change them, rather than failing.

**The build record replaced the hand-authored claim.** `oci:build` writes `var/oci-build.json` in the run that built — under `var/` because it is gitignored and a record of what one host built is true of that host and not of the repository. The verifier compares it against the image it finds, so an image rebuilt, replaced or pulled between the two steps fails. The manifests keep `"buildStatus": "unbuilt"` and `"imageDigest": null`, because those fields are no longer what the gate reads and typing a claim into them would be the falsification again.

**Writing the tests found two bugs in the replacement before it ever ran a real image**, and both are the same never-passes condition it was written to remove. The uid cross-check compared the manifest's number against Docker's `"65532:65532"` string, so it would have failed **every real build**; and the root check passed `Config.User: "root"`, which runs as root. Both are asserted in `oci-checks.test.mjs` as failing cases.

**A registry digest is still compared whenever a manifest declares one.** None does, because these images are never pushed, so the gate says so in its own output and names what would arm the check. Graduating `runner.oci` from `mock` therefore arms a *stronger* check rather than requiring the gate to be rewritten — and that is the honest shape of the remaining work, because the Dockerfiles are still 7-line stubs that print a version.

**What this row does not close:** `runner.oci` stays `mock`. What changed is that the gate measures the real thing instead of asserting the untrue one, and that the repair is recorded rather than living in a commit message nobody can cite from a ledger row.

evidence.asserts: The rules as a pure function, so they are executable without docker. `evaluateRunner` refuses a build record with no entry, an absent image, an uninspectable id, and — the one failure only a build record can detect on a host with no registry — an image whose content id differs from the one recorded, which is how a swapped or rebuilt image fails. `runsAsRoot` covers the three spellings that have each been a real way for it to happen (unset, `root` by name, uid `0`), and `uidOf` is why the declared-uid cross-check does not fail every real build.

The failing cases, not only the happy path — which is the property that distinguishes this suite from the absence of one. The header records that `oci-verify.mjs` and `oci-build.mjs` had **no test at all**, which is why an unsatisfiable gate sat in `verify:release` unnoticed, and that a happy-path-only suite would have passed with the old rules in place just as happily — and did, twice, while this replacement was being written.

The half that makes the claim true. It inspects each image the build just produced and refuses to record a build it cannot verify, rather than writing an empty entry that would turn an unanswerable runtime into a green gate. The record is written to `var/oci-build.json`, so it cannot be hand-edited into agreement with the verifier.

Gathers facts and reports the rules' answer, and nothing else. An absent runtime and an absent build record are both refusals to proceed rather than passes, and the notes are printed under a heading that says they were not checked rather than under the failures heading.

Still `"buildStatus": "unbuilt"` and `"imageDigest": null` — the point of the row. The gate no longer reads those fields, so the committed claim is honestly empty rather than hand-typed to satisfy a check, and `user`, `network` and `readOnly` are now cross-checked against the image rather than trusted.

findings.title: An E2E spec called an undefined helper, and nothing typechecked the E2E tree
findings.summary: `e2e/product/reporter-run-lifecycle.spec.ts` called `reportTest` at three places and imported only `postReporterEvent`, `uniqueRunId` and `waitForRunPhase` from `../support/api.js`. The helper exists — `reportTest` is exported at `e2e/support/api.ts:98`, with a comment explaining precisely why a spec must report per-test events rather than relying on the `run:end` counters — so the spec was missing one name in an import list. At runtime that is a `ReferenceError` on the first call, so the spec could never have passed: the reporter run lifecycle, which is the one path a real test producer takes into the product, was not covered by a working test. It went unnoticed because of the second half of the finding, which is the more general one. The root `tsconfig.json` includes `e2e/**/*.ts`, but **no command ever ran it**: `typecheck` was `pnpm typecheck:scripts && turbo run typecheck`, and `turbo run typecheck` only runs the per-package `typecheck` tasks, none of which cover `e2e/`. Playwright compiles specs with esbuild and does not typecheck, so a missing import is invisible until the spec runs — and `test:e2e` requires `DATABASE_URL` and a live stack, so on a machine without one it is never run at all. The shape of the failure is the repository's own: a gate that cannot fail. The suite is tiered `pr-blocking` in the manifest and could not have been green, because a spec in it throws. Fixed on both sides: the import, and `typecheck:e2e` wired into the existing `typecheck` step, so an undefined name in a spec is caught by a command that needs neither a browser nor a database. The step is not a new one — `verify` grew to fifteen steps, and this was not one of them.

evidence.asserts: `reportTest` is imported from `../support/api.js` alongside the other three helpers, so the three call sites resolve instead of throwing a ReferenceError at run time.

`typecheck` runs `pnpm typecheck:e2e`, and `typecheck:e2e` is `tsc -p tsconfig.json --noEmit`, which is the project whose `include` covers `e2e/**/*.ts` — the gap that let an undefined identifier sit in a pr-blocking spec.
`typecheck:e2e` carries the `pr-blocking` tier, so `gate-tooling.test.mjs`'s assertion that every root script is classified keeps covering the new command.

findings.title: The rendering budget exists and has never been measured, so the gate is red by design
findings.summary: W-D.3's harness is built and its policy is tested; the **measurement** is not, and it cannot be taken on a development host. What exists: `scripts/lib/rendering-budget.mjs` holds the comparison as a pure function, `performance/rendering-budget.json` is the baseline, `e2e/performance/rendering-budget.spec.ts` produces the readings from `PerformanceObserver` with no new dependency, `pnpm test:render` and `pnpm render:baseline` are the two commands, and `unified-ci.yml` has a `render-budget` job. What is missing is the one thing that cannot be written: real numbers. Every ceiling in the baseline is `null` and `recorded` is `false`, so the gate is in its **measurement phase**: the CI job measures the four routes, publishes the numbers to the job summary, compares nothing, and is deliberately **not** a required check. The remaining work is one deliberate human run of `pnpm render:baseline` on reference hardware, reviewed as a diff before it is committed, together with raising `test:render` from `pr-reporting` to `pr-blocking` **in the same commit**. The alternative was to commit plausible ceilings and let a required job go green, which is the same defect the ledger already records as RF-9 — `performance/thresholds.json` ships `recorded: false` with three nulls and its own note admitting every threshold in it is an unvalidated estimate, so the k6 gate compares real traffic to a number nobody saw. Writing a rendering budget that started the same way would have made the W-E glass gates enforceable against nothing. `render:baseline` is `never-in-ci` in `gate-tooling.json` for the same reason `complexity:baseline` and `coverage:baseline` are hand-run: a gate that can rewrite its own floor in the same commit is a gate that agrees with the tree instead of the code. A GitHub runner is not the reference hardware — the ceilings describe a self-hosted single-node install, which is what D10 commits to, so a run there would record the wrong number just as honestly as a guess. Three things are deliberately already true, so that nothing here is a reason to rush the measurement. **The phase is derived, not chosen**: `scripts/lib/render-gate-phase.mjs` computes the tier `test:render` is allowed to have from the baseline, and `gate-tooling.test.mjs` fails until `scripts/gate-tooling.json` agrees — in *both* directions, so graduating the gate cannot be half-applied, and `recorded: true` beside invented numbers with a `pr-reporting` tier is caught rather than quietly becoming a gate that is permanently green and not required. **The policy is checked on every PR** by `node --test` inside `pnpm test:integration`, including the rule that an unmeasured metric is reported rather than scored as zero — the failure mode this gate is most able to hide in itself, since `PerformanceObserver` stays silent for a metric that never happened — and that rule still applies in the measurement phase, where the spec fails on an incomplete measurement and skips only the ceilings. **The job cannot become a green no-op**, because `playwright.config.ts` throws at config load if the `rendering-budget` project matches no spec. On the choice of tier: this row previously shipped `test:render` as `pr-blocking` with `recorded: false`, which is a required check that can never pass. That is the one configuration market standards do not allow and this ledger would not accept — it blocks every pull request for a reason nobody can fix without hardware, and a red that is always red is a red nobody reads. The two-phase rollout is the option that is neither a lie nor a blockade, and the tier is now a checked consequence of the data rather than a decision somebody wrote down in a comment.
findings.sequencedBehind:
**The cinematic design language's Phase 2 is sequenced behind this row.** `.kilo/plans/1791024280658-cinematic-design-language-and-docs-overhaul.md` D6-9 is a whole section about this dependency: its Phase 2 is the glass allowlist on `NavBar`, the app shell, the `Command Center` and the `Toaster`, and its entry criterion is *this row closed*. So this row is now the only thing standing between the repository and a `backdrop-filter`.

**Verified live on 2026-10-03, not assumed.** `scripts/lib/render-gate-phase.mjs` computes the permitted tier from this baseline and was exercised in both directions against the real files:

- `recorded: false` with `test:render` at `pr-reporting` → phase `measurement`, no problems. That is the repository's state.
- `recorded: false` with `test:render` at `pr-blocking` → rejected: *"a required check that can never pass blocks every pull request, trains reviewers to ignore red, and hides the failures that matter."*
- `recorded: true` with `test:render` still at `pr-reporting` → rejected: *"the rendering budget is a real gate and `test:render` must be tiered `pr-blocking`. Leaving it below that is a gate nobody is required to satisfy, which is worse than the two-phase rollout it replaced."*

`scripts/lib/gate-tooling.test.mjs` asserts the first of those on every PR, so the gate holding Phase 2 shut is enforced rather than promised.

**What closing it takes, in order.** One deliberate human run of `pnpm render:baseline` on the self-hosted single-node install D10 describes; read the diff in `performance/rendering-budget.json` before committing it; and raise `test:render` to `pr-blocking` in that same commit. `render:baseline` is `never-in-ci` for the same reason the other two baseline writers are hand-run.

**Why it was not done from a development host, stated once so it is not re-litigated.** The numbers the ceilings compare against describe a self-hosted single-node install. A run on any other machine — a GitHub runner, or a contributor's laptop — produces real measurements of the wrong hardware, and `recorded: true` beside them would calibrate a required gate to a machine nobody else has. That is not a cautious reading of the constraint; it is the defect the constraint was written to prevent, and committing it would have made this row's own subject matter the way it went wrong.

findings.title: The complexity ratchet could not run on any host, and it is a step in `verify`
findings.summary: `pnpm complexity` failed on every machine, and it is a step in both `verify` and `security:verify`. Two independent defects, both in `scripts/complexity-gate.mjs`, each sufficient on its own. **First, the repository root was a literal string**: `const root = 'C:/VS-Code-Projects/Github/Automate'`. The gate builds its eslint path and its baseline path from that, so it could only ever run on the machine that committed it, and on CI — an ubuntu runner, where that path does not exist — it had no `node_modules` to spawn eslint from. This is the same defect `playwright.config.ts` documents having had with `__dirname`, and the fix is the same one: `path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..')`, because the root `package.json` declares `"type": "module"`. **Second, and the reason it failed even on the machine that wrote the path, the rule was enabled from the command line**: `--rule '{"sonarjs/cognitive-complexity":["error",15]}'`. Under flat config a `--rule` flag is merged into a configuration object of its own, and that object has no `plugins`, so naming a plugin-scoped rule from the CLI cannot resolve. ESLint aborts with `A configuration object specifies rule "sonarjs/cognitive-complexity", but could not find plugin "sonarjs"`, exits 2, and writes no report. The gate's own guard then took the "eslint produced no report" branch and exited 1 — which is how a config crash came to be reported as missing output, and how the real message ended up on stderr under a misleading heading. The fix moves the rule into `scripts/complexity-eslint.config.mjs`, a real config object that spreads the repository config (so its `ignores` still apply) and registers `sonarjs` with the rule at `error` and the ceiling from `AUTOMATE_COMPLEXITY_CEILING`, so the config and the comparison cannot disagree about what was measured. The exit-code handling now separates ESLint's 1 (findings, the expected case) from 2 (a crash) and reports the latter as a crash. Verified end to end: `pnpm complexity` reports 31 functions over a ceiling of 15 against a recorded baseline of 31, worst 73 — the committed baseline and the live measurement agree exactly, and the code added in this wave contributed no offender. Nothing about the ratchet's policy changed; only the two things standing between it and running.

evidence.asserts: `root` is `path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, '..')` rather than a machine path, and the eslint invocation passes `--config scripts/complexity-eslint.config.mjs` instead of a `--rule` flag, so the gate is runnable from any checkout.

The config spreads the repository's own config, registers `plugins: { sonarjs }` in the same object that sets `sonarjs/cognitive-complexity` to `error`, and throws on a non-integer `AUTOMATE_COMPLEXITY_CEILING` — a ceiling that is not a number would measure nothing, which is the one outcome the ratchet exists to rule out.

`count: 31` is still the recorded figure and `pnpm complexity` measures exactly 31, so the ratchet passes against its own committed baseline rather than having had its floor adjusted to suit a broken measurement.

findings.title: `pnpm typecheck` failed on `main`, so no wave could have left a green `verify`
findings.summary: `packages/reporter/src/compatibility/legacy-reporter.test.ts` read `event.data.resultDigest` behind an `if (event.data === null)` guard, and `tsc` rejected it. `CanonicalReporterEvent` is a discriminated union on `type`, and `resultDigest` exists on the `run.completed` member alone — so the access was an error on the other five union members, and the null guard could never narrow anything, because `data` is required and non-nullable on every member. The consequence was not a warning in a test file: `typecheck` is a step in `verify`, so `pnpm verify` could not pass on `main`, which means the plan's own instruction that every wave leave a passing `verify` was unsatisfiable before any wave work began. It is worth naming why it survived that long: this file is the test that proves P-3 fixed, and the P-3 row is `fixed` with this very file as its evidence — so the ledger's own proof of a closed Blocker was sitting in a file that failed the typechecker. The fix narrows on the discriminant, which is both the thing the compiler understands and the thing the assertion means: a `run:end` that normalized to some other event type has no digest to compare, and that deserves a named failure rather than a `null` guard. A `resultDigestOf` helper does it once. The two dead `data === null` guards went with it, because they defended against a shape the schema cannot produce. This is the same class as E-1 and E-2 — a gate that cannot pass — and all three were found inside one session only because three different gates were run rather than trusted.

evidence.asserts: `resultDigestOf` narrows on `event.type !== 'run.completed'` and returns `event.data.resultDigest`, so the access is checked rather than asserted past, and the two dead `data === null` guards are gone.
Its `typecheck` script is `tsc --noEmit` and `pnpm typecheck` runs it, so the file the P-3 row cites as its evidence now sits inside a checked project.

findings.title: `pnpm render:baseline` could never run, and being `never-in-ci` nothing would have said so
findings.summary: The rendering budget's only way to become a real measurement was `playwright test --project=rendering-budget --update`, with the spec reading `process.argv.includes('--update')`. Playwright's CLI validates its own options and rejects anything it does not recognise, so the command died at `error: unknown option '--update'` before a single spec ran — and the flag could never have reached `process.argv` in the first place, so the branch was unreachable even if the command had started. The failure was total and quiet: `render:baseline` is `never-in-ci` by design, and the other half of the contract is a `pr-blocking` `test:render` job that needs no flag at all, so no pipeline step touched the broken one. The consequence is the specific one the whole gate rests on: PERF-1's remedy — a deliberate human run to populate the ceilings — was a command that did nothing, so the rendering budget had no path out of `recorded: false` and the W-E glass gates had nothing to be measured against. Found by running `pnpm render:baseline` and reading the error rather than assuming the wiring worked, which is the third time in one session that running a gate has been more productive than reading it. The fix follows the repository's own precedent instead of inventing one: `complexity:baseline` is `node ./scripts/complexity-gate.mjs --write` and `coverage:baseline` works the same way, so a gate's baseline writer here is a node script and not a flag bolted onto a third-party CLI. `scripts/render-baseline.mjs` sets `AUTOMATE_RENDER_BASELINE=1` in the child's environment — an environment variable actually crosses the process boundary — and the spec reads that. The wrapper's failure path is part of the fix rather than an afterthought: it reports that the baseline was not updated and exits non-zero, because a writer that half-succeeds is worse than one that cannot start. Verified by running it: Playwright loaded the config and correctly refused for want of `DATABASE_URL`, and `performance/rendering-budget.json` still reads `recorded: false` with four null ceilings, which is the correct outcome for a run that measured nothing.

evidence.asserts: The writer sets `AUTOMATE_RENDER_BASELINE=1` in the spawned child's environment rather than passing a flag, and on a non-zero exit it says the budget was not updated and exits non-zero itself — so an incomplete run cannot record a baseline.
`recorded` is still `false` and every ceiling is `null` after running the writer without a database, which is the fail-closed behaviour the row claims.
`render:baseline` is `node ./scripts/render-baseline.mjs` rather than a `playwright test --update` invocation, so the command no longer depends on Playwright accepting an option it rejects.

findings.title: Two tracked files held 18 replacement characters from a lossy write, and no gate could see them
findings.summary: `.github/workflows/unified-ci.yml` carried **eleven** U+FFFD replacement characters across eight comments at `HEAD`, and `apps/api/src/index.test.ts:538` carried one more, for as long as they have been committed. U+FFFD is what a decoder emits for a byte it cannot read, so both files were written with a lossy encoding rather than UTF-8. On Windows PowerShell 5.1 that is the default for `Out-File`, `>` and `Set-Content`: the system codepage, not UTF-8, and the write succeeds silently. The band is Minor because the damage landed entirely in prose and changed no behaviour, and it would be dishonest to call an em-dash in a comment a functional defect. The real finding is the other half. **No gate in this repository could detect it, and the reason is structural rather than accidental: the toolchain does not read prose.** Prettier reformats and does not repair mangled bytes. ESLint parses, and a replacement character in a comment is still a comment. `tsc` reads tokens and never sees a comment's contents. The tests assert behaviour and cannot see a character. `security:secrets` looks for credentials, not for mojibake. So a whole class of silent corruption sat under a gate chain that is otherwise thorough enough to catch a hardcoded absolute path (E-2), a flag a CLI rejects (E-4) and a spec calling an undefined helper (E-1). The latent risk is the reason this is not simply cosmetic: the same write path that put a `—` in a comment would silently change a string literal, a test assertion, or a workflow value, and those *are* behaviour. A gate that cannot fail is a defect, and this one had never been written. `scripts/lib/encoding-integrity.mjs` reports U+FFFD with a line, a column and a window of context around the damage, and its test scans every tracked text file. Two design choices are load-bearing. It keys on **exactly one code point** rather than on non-ASCII, because this repository writes em-dashes, ellipses and typographic quotes in prose deliberately and a rule that flagged those would be deleted rather than narrowed; there is a test asserting a real `—`, a real `…`, curly quotes, accents, `Привет`, `日本語` and `→` all pass untouched. And it excludes binary by the NUL-byte heuristic rather than an extension list, so decoding an image cannot manufacture findings nobody could act on. Both files are repaired: the em-dashes are restored, and the one on `unified-ci.yml:48` is an ellipsis rather than a dash, because it quotes a truncated `docker compose … config` command. The repair was applied from an explicit per-line mapping and each restored line was read back in context rather than assumed.

evidence.asserts: `findReplacementChars` reports U+FFFD with a line, a column and a window of context *centred on the damage*, and keys on that single code point rather than on non-ASCII — so the em-dashes, ellipses and typographic quotes this repository writes in prose on purpose are not flagged.

`every tracked text file is valid UTF-8, with no replacement characters` walks `git ls-files`, skips binary by the NUL-byte heuristic, and fails on any U+FFFD. It failed on the eleven characters committed in the workflow and the one in the API test before the repair, and passes after — which is the proof that the class is now covered rather than the two files merely tidied.

The eight comments are restored, with the em-dashes back and the character on the `docker compose` line an ellipsis rather than a dash. The row's scan test is what proves the file is clean; the path here is the file that was repaired.

findings.title: The client suite raised testTimeout to 60s and left waitFor at 1000ms, so a loaded machine failed as a product bug
findings.summary: pps/web/vitest.config.ts already sets 	estTimeout: 60000 and hookTimeout: 60000, with a long comment explaining why: this package has no slow test, the cost that scales is module import, a route test was observed at 15018 ms under pnpm test where turbo runs the package alongside thirty others, and a timeout that reports a loaded machine as a failing repository is a timeout people learn to re-run. Every part of that is correct. But waitFor is a **separate clock** and Testing Library defaults syncUtilTimeout to **1000 ms**, and nothing in the repository had raised it. So the decision was half-applied: the outer budget was 60 s while every wait waitFor(...) in the client suite still raced one second. The symptom showed up as dashboard.test.tsx — enders persisted readiness and recent canonical runs — failing one run in three under pnpm test, passing in isolation every time, and not reproducible by any change to the code under test. That test waits on two concurrent fetches and a render inside waitFor, which is comfortably inside a second on an idle machine and not inside it on a loaded one. It is banded Major rather than Minor because the cost is not the red: it is that a pr-blocking suite reports a **product** failure for a **harness** condition, which is the most expensive kind of intermittent red — it sends someone to debug a dashboard route that is fine. The fix is configure({ asyncUtilTimeout }) in 	est-setup.ts, at 5000 ms rather than 60000: waitFor still has to be fast enough that a genuinely broken selector fails the suite in seconds, and the expensive part of these tests is import rather than waiting, so matching 	estTimeout would buy nothing and make a real failure slow to find. No assertion was weakened. 	est-setup.ts is excluded from coverage, so the new configuration would otherwise have had nothing asserting it, and a configure() that was reverted or overridden later would have put all 27 client test files back on a one-second deadline with nothing failing until a loaded machine produced another red. src/test-setup.test.tsx therefore asserts the **behaviour** rather than the constant, and the reasoning for that matters: the first version of that fixture blocked synchronously inside ender, so ender did not return until the element existed, waitFor found its condition already true, and the test **passed with the fix reverted**. It looked like it proved the point and proved nothing. The fixture is now a delayed effect on a real timer — no fake clock, because i.useFakeTimers() would let the assertion pass without the timeout ever being consulted — and with the configure() line removed it fails at 1036 ms, reproducing the original flake. The suite also asserts a condition that never becomes true still rejects, so the fix cannot be a way of waiting forever.

evidence.asserts: `configure({ asyncUtilTimeout: ASYNC_UTIL_TIMEOUT_MS })` is called at 5000 ms, and `ASYNC_UTIL_TIMEOUT_MS` is exported so the harness has a test at all. This is the clock `testTimeout` did not cover.

`waits for a condition that takes longer than the old one-second default` drives a delayed effect on a real timer and passes only when the raised default is in place — it fails at 1036 ms with the `configure()` line removed. `still fails a condition that never becomes true` pins the other half, so the raised default cannot become a way of waiting forever.

`testTimeout: 60000` with the comment explaining that a loaded machine must not be reported as a failing repository — the decision E-6 found half-applied, and the reason the fix mirrors its reasoning rather than contradicting it.

findings.title: The runner suite's wait helper was bounded by iteration count, so a loaded machine failed a healthy service
findings.summary: `apps/runner/src/runner-service.test.ts` has a local `until(label, predicate)` helper that yields to the event loop until a condition the service controls holds, and it was bounded by **iteration count**: 150 attempts with a 1 ms `setTimeout` between them. That reads like a 150 ms deadline and is not one. Each attempt performs real asynchronous filesystem work against a `DurableSpool` — reading the spool, attempting delivery, listing dead letters — so on a loaded machine 150 attempts of that take considerably more than 150 ms of wall clock, and the bound stops being a deadline at all. The visible effect: `stops retrying an unreachable API, dead-letters the entry, and keeps it readable after a restart` failed one run in three under `pnpm test`, passed in isolation every time, and was not reproducible by any change to the runner. An iteration bound is a load-sensitive deadline wearing the costume of a fixed one, and it is the same mistake as E-6 on the client side, which makes this a pattern rather than an incident: the repository raised the outer budgets for a documented, measured reason — `apps/web/vitest.config.ts` records a route test at 15018 ms under `pnpm test` — while leaving the inner clocks the assertions actually race at values chosen when the machine was idle. The fix bounds the wait by elapsed time at 5 s, and deliberately keeps the one property of the original that was right: a labelled failure naming which condition never held, rather than a bare vitest timeout with no indication of what the service was doing. 5 s is generous for conditions that settle in milliseconds and still fails the suite in seconds if the service is genuinely stuck. The band is Major rather than Minor because the cost is not the red: it is that a pr-blocking suite reports a product failure for a harness condition, which sends someone to debug a runner that is fine — and the second such case found in one session is the evidence that the real fix is auditing every hand-rolled wait in the repository rather than the two that happened to be observed.

evidence.asserts: `until` is bounded by elapsed time with a `budgetMs` default of 5000 and throws `Condition never held after 5000ms: <label>`, so the failure still names the condition rather than surfacing as a bare timeout, and a stuck service fails in seconds rather than hanging.

findings.title: The evidence console is not a world-class design yet, and the axe coverage that would say so is absent
findings.owner: The UI wave of the roadmap's Track A, and the five execution domains behind it. Nothing in this repository can make a route's design world-class, because four of the five agent domains answer an explicit `501 NOT_CONFIGURED` and a console with nothing behind it is a design decision nobody has made yet. A redesign before BK-1 lands is the redesign of an empty screen.
findings.removalCondition: Either (a) `e2e/accessibility/routes.spec.ts` exists and `pnpm test:e2e` reports axe zero serious and zero critical on every route in `apps/web/src/routes` in **both** themes, with the matrix recorded in the resolution; or (b) BK-1 has shipped a domain, and a state-coverage matrix exists naming loading, empty, error and partial for every route, with a test per state. Condition (a) is the machine-checkable half and `pnpm status:10` reads it; condition (b) is the half that decides whether (a) would be measuring anything worth measuring.
findings.resolution:
§17's fourth point is a sentence with eight clauses: *axe zero serious/critical on every route in both themes, every route has loading/empty/error/partial states, one error boundary, one theme implementation, one date layer, one SSE connection, zero dead components, and every colour/type/elevation/motion utility in both trees verified to compile.* `pnpm status:10` measures four of them and the four are honest about it. What is missing is stated here rather than implied.

**What is already true, and is not a pass.** One error boundary (`apps/api/src/errors/boundary.ts`, and the API is the only place one is allowed). One theme implementation. The token-resolution gate verifies utilities in `packages/ui`. `apps/web` has a route-level test suite and a component-level axe check in `GlobalCommandPalette.test.tsx`. None of that is the claim, because the claim is about *every route in both themes*.

**What is absent, precisely.** There is no route-level accessibility spec at all. `expectNoBlockingAxeViolations` exists in `apps/web` and is used by exactly one component test, so a route that regresses is not covered by anything. `pnpm status:10` reports this as a `fail` on the clause 'an accessibility check runs against the routes', and names the count: 13 route files, zero covered.

**Why deferring rather than writing the spec.** The axe spec is roughly half a day and is worth having on its own merits — so this is not a claim that it is hard. The claim is narrower: **an accessibility gate on a console whose five data domains are unconfigured measures the empty states.** A green axe run over screens that render `not_configured` panels would be reported as the console being accessible, and §17's point is that the console shows evidence the product genuinely has. Fixing the *states* is Track A's job; fixing the *renderer* before the states exist means fixing it twice.

**What is not deferred.** The three register rows the console's honesty depends on — `ui.legacy-surfaces`, `quality.suppression` and the derived `agent.*` availability — are `mock` and `deferred` today and are published as-is on the capabilities page. A reader is not told the console is finished. So the deferral is about *craft*, not about *truth*, and the difference is worth keeping: this repository's central claim is that it never overstates, and nothing in this row asks it to.

**Why this row exists rather than a paragraph in the plan.** Because `pnpm status:10` reads it. Point 4's failed clauses become `not_configured` only when a `debt` row carries an owner and a checkable removal condition, so the deferral is visible on the same table as everything else and the day it can be closed, the row says what closing it looks like.
findings.summary:
§17's fourth point asks for axe zero serious/critical on every route in both themes, and for loading, empty, error and partial states on every route. `expectNoBlockingAxeViolations` exists in `apps/web` and is used by **one** component test, so no route is covered; there is no state-coverage matrix; and four of the five agent domains behind those screens answer an explicit `501 NOT_CONFIGURED`, so the screens the gate would measure render nothing.

**Confirmed by reading the tree, 2026-09-30.** `pnpm status:10` point 4 reports 13 route files under `apps/web/src/routes` and reports the accessibility clause as `fail` — the one route-level assertion that exists is in `GlobalCommandPalette.test.tsx`, which is a component, not a route. The deferred half is the state matrix, for which no artefact exists at all, and naming one as evidence would be asserting the thing that is missing.

**Why this is deferral and not neglect.** The axe spec is about half a day and is worth having for its own sake. The question is what it would measure: a console whose five data domains are unconfigured has screens that render `not_configured` panels, so a green axe run over them says the empty state is accessible — which is true and is not §17's point. Fixing the states is Track A's work and it needs BK-1 behind it; fixing the renderer first means fixing it twice.

**What is not deferred, and is why this row is Major rather than a claim that the console is fine.** One error boundary, one theme implementation, a token-resolution gate over `packages/ui`, and a per-route test suite all exist and hold. The register publishes `ui.legacy-surfaces` as `mock` and the derived `agent.*` availability as `false`, so a reader is not told the console is finished. The deferral is about craft; nothing in it asks the product to overstate anything, which is the distinction that keeps this row honest rather than convenient.

**The removal condition is machine-checked.** `e2e/accessibility/routes.spec.ts` plus a green `pnpm test:e2e` in both themes is half of it; the other half is BK-1 shipping a domain, because a gate that measures an empty screen is a gate that measures nothing. `pnpm status:10` reads this row, so the day it is discharged point 4 stops being `not_configured` on the same table as everything else.

findings.title: Four of the five measured-quality clauses have no measurement at all, and the complexity ceiling is 15 rather than 10
findings.owner: Nobody in this repository can discharge the mutation, property-testing or authz-matrix clauses today, and the roadmap is explicit that the values are estimates: mutation 'estimated ~50% today', and the rendering job kept at `pr-reporting` because the reference hardware is a self-hosted single-node install. Carrying this as debt is the honest disposition; carrying it as a pass would be the failure the ledger exists to prevent.
findings.removalCondition: Each clause has its own condition, and the row closes when all four are recorded in the resolution with a number: (a) `docs/quality/complexity-baseline.json` records `ceiling: 10` — which today would need 29 of 73 over-ceiling functions refactored, so this is the long one; (b) a `mutation-baseline.json` with a recorded score and a ratchet of the same shape as `coverage-baseline.json`, so the score cannot be lowered silently; (c) a `property` or `fuzz` suite per stated invariant, named in the resolution; (d) a generated authz matrix with a test that fails when a route is added without a row. Duplication stays `not_configured` on a host without `jscpd` and is reported with its reason — the command is `pnpm duplication`.
findings.resolution:
§17's fifth point names six things. `pnpm status:10` checks all six and reports what it finds, which is the part that matters: **one of the six is met, one is unmeasurable on this host, and four have no measurement of any kind.**

| Clause | State | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| complexity ≤ 10 | **fail** | `complexity-baseline.json` records `ceiling: 15` and 29 offenders, worst 73. The ratchet holds the line and has not regressed, which is a real result — the count is 29 today and the gate fails if it grows. |
| duplication ≤ 3% on changed code | not_configured | Needs `jscpd`. `pnpm duplication` is the command, and `AUTOMATE_HOST_SCANNERS`-style host degradation applies in spirit: a host without the binary reports `not_configured` with a reason rather than reporting 0%. |
| mutation ≥ 75% on five packages | **fail** | No `mutation-baseline.json` exists, so no score has ever been recorded. A number nobody has measured is not a 0% score and not a pass. The roadmap's own estimate is ~50%. |
| property/fuzz on every stated invariant | **fail** | No property or fuzz suite exists in any package; `fast-check` is not a dependency. |
| authz matrix generated from the app | **fail** | No generated matrix exists. A hand-written one would be a second list to keep in step, which is the defect the roadmap names. |
| every perf budget measured in CI | **fail** | `performance/thresholds.json` has `recorded: false`, so the k6 p95/p99 thresholds are estimates compared against nothing. Tracked separately as RF-9. |

**The complexity ceiling is the honest disagreement.** §17 says 10; the repository records 15 and has ratcheted against it. This row takes the position that the recorded 15 is a **ratchet at a level the code is actually at**, not an agreement with 10 — a ceiling set to 10 today would be red on 29 functions and would be raised to 15 within a week, which is the same move as lowering a coverage floor to make room. Reducing it to 10 is real refactoring work and is condition (a) above.

**What is not deferred.** The ratchet itself, the coverage floors, the real-PostgreSQL integration suites and the complexity gate all run and all hold. So §17's point is not 'quality is unmeasured' — it is that a *specific* set of five measurements was named and four of them do not exist, and this row is where that fact lives rather than in a paragraph that nobody reads.

**Why debt rather than a shorter target.** §1 forbids `debt` in the two blocking bands; Major is not one of them, so this is permitted. And the four clauses are the same shape of work — set up a measurement, record a baseline, ratchet it — which is a programme rather than a bug, and a programme belongs in the ledger with an owner rather than in a plan section that a `status:10` run cannot see.
findings.summary:
§17's fifth point names six measurements. **One holds, one is unmeasurable on a host without `jscpd`, and four have no measurement of any kind.** The complexity ceiling is recorded as **15** against §17's 10, with 29 functions over the line and a worst of 73 — and the ratchet is holding, so that is a ratchet at the level the code is actually at, not an agreement with 10. There is no `mutation-baseline.json`, so no mutation score has ever been recorded and nothing ratchets it; the roadmap's own estimate is ~50% against a target of 75%. No property or fuzz suite exists in any package and `fast-check` is not a dependency. No generated authz matrix exists. And `performance/thresholds.json` has `recorded: false`, so the k6 p95/p99 thresholds are estimates compared against nothing — tracked separately as RF-9.

**Confirmed by reading the tree, 2026-09-30**, through `pnpm status:10` point 5, which reports each of the six separately rather than as a single verdict — the point's verdict is the worst of the six, so the single number in the table hides how much of it is actually settled.

**Why the complexity number is the honest disagreement and not a slip.** A ceiling set to 10 today would be red on 29 functions and would be raised to 15 inside a week, which is the same move as lowering a coverage floor to make room. The recorded 15 is a real ratchet: the gate fails if the count grows. Reaching 10 is refactoring work and is condition (a) of the removal condition, not a configuration change.

**What is not deferred.** The complexity ratchet, the per-package coverage floors, the real-PostgreSQL integration suites and `pnpm duplication`'s policy all run and hold. So the finding is not 'quality is unmeasured' — it is that a named set of five measurements has four missing, and this row is where that fact lives rather than in a plan section no gate reads.

findings.title: Every register row cites evidence paths; none cites a command, and nothing flips a row to `unverified` when its test is deleted
findings.owner: unassigned — the capability register's own wave
findings.removalCondition: The generated register carries a `command` column whose every value is a root script, and `scripts/lib/docs-drift.mjs` already refuses a `pnpm …` citation that is not one. That half is a shape change and is unblocked by existing code. The `unverified` flip is separate: `pnpm capability:evidence` exists and derives each row's status by running the command it names.
