The condition names what could happen: the column being added.
findings.resolution:
**Taken as debt on the written-statement exit, and the statement has to say something the register cannot.**

**What is already true and needs no work.** The register *is* published as-is with a per-row reason: a reader can see that `runner.oci` is `mock` and `quality.mobile` is `deferred`. Its status is honest today. `scripts/lib/docs-drift.mjs` already ships the `commands` detector that refuses a `pnpm …` citation that is not a root script, and it is already in `pnpm docs:check`. So "half of §17 point 7 is enforced by a gate that exists" is accurate — the gate is waiting for a column, not for code.

**Why the written-statement exit is not a way out.** A capability register whose rows cite *paths* claims that some code exists; a register whose rows cite *commands* claims that the code runs. A written justification can say the second and enforce none of it, and a justification that simply restates each row's claim adds a document that can drift from the register it explains — the failure `docs:check` exists to catch, applied to the file that exists to satisfy the checker. That is why this is recorded as debt with a named owner rather than written off: the column is the fix, it is unblocked, and nothing but a decision is missing.

**The `unverified` flip is the half with teeth and it stays out of scope for v1.0.0.** It is a script that runs each row's command and reports `unverified` when it fails, turning the register from a document into a status derived from the gates. That is a real property and it is not a v1.0.0 deliverable; the removal condition names it separately so it is visible rather than forgotten.
findings.summary:
§17's seventh point has two halves: every capability claim has a **passing evidence command** in the generated register, and **deleting a test flips its row to `unverified`**. The register cites a path per row — 42 rows, 42 paths, zero commands — and no `pnpm capability:evidence` exists. A path is real evidence and is not nothing, but a path exists whether the capability works or not, so a row citing one claims that some code is there, not that it runs. The register's own evidence rule asks for 'executable test evidence' on user-visible and security-sensitive rows, and that rule is prose, so nothing checks it.

**Confirmed by reading the tree, 2026-09-30**, through `pnpm status:10` point 7, which reports the missing command column and the missing script as two separate clauses.

**The second half has already been made cheap and is the part worth doing first.** `scripts/lib/docs-drift.mjs` has a `commands` detector that already refuses a `pnpm …` citation that is not a root script, and it is already in `pnpm docs:check` — so once the register has the column, that half of §17 point 7 is enforced by a gate that exists. The remaining work is the register's shape plus a row-to-test mapping, which is a judgement per row: 42 readings rather than 42 keystrokes.

**The `unverified` flip is a different mechanism and the one with teeth.** A script that runs the command each row names and reports `unverified` when it fails turns the register from a document into a status derived from the gates — which is what the capabilities, findings, coverage and twelve-point pages already are, and what the roadmap's own risk table demands of the site: *'the site consumes only the generated register, never hand-typed numbers.'*

**What is not deferred, so the row is read for its size.** The register is the authority and is published as-is: a reader can see that `runner.oci` is `mock` and `quality.mobile` is `deferred`, with a reason per row. The *status* is honest today; what is missing is that the status is not connected to the thing that would change it. That is a smaller gap than 'the register lies', and the removal condition records both the build-it answer and the write-it-down answer, so choosing the second is a decision rather than a drift.

findings.title: `pnpm db:migrate` failed on every invocation, with a message naming the variable the process had
findings.resolution:
`runMigrations(connectionString?)` documented its parameter as *"defaults to `DATABASE_URL`"* and did not implement the default. The CLI entrypoint at the bottom of `migrate.ts` calls `runMigrations()` with **no argument**, so the guard received `undefined` and threw `'DATABASE_URL is required for migrations. It was absent, so the runner would have fallen back to the PG* environment defaults…'` — on a run where `DATABASE_URL` was set.

So `pnpm db:migrate` failed **every time it was invoked**, and the error named the very variable the process had set. The message's second sentence made it worse: it said the *absence* of `DATABASE_URL` would have caused an unvalidated fallback, and here it was present and the failure was a wiring bug. Every caller reads that as an environment problem and checks their `.env`.

**Why no test caught it.** Every test called `runMigrations(VALID_URL, …)` with an explicit URL, and the entrypoint guard `isDirectInvocation` is never true when a test imports the module — so the one line that was wrong was the one line no test executed. `migrate.test.ts` now has a test that calls `runMigrations(undefined, …)` with `DATABASE_URL` set in the environment and asserts the guard *accepts* it, which is the reverse of what the suite asserted before.

**What it blocked.** Everything downstream of a schema. The E2E lane, a clean `docker compose up`, and any new installation — which is why the durable-path work started by finding that `db:migrate` had never worked.

evidence.asserts: The parameter carries a `= process.env['DATABASE_URL']` default, so the documented default is the implemented one. The entrypoint's `runMigrations()` and the default are stated in the same comment, because the coupling between them is the whole defect.

`defaults the target to DATABASE_URL, because the CLI entrypoint passes no argument` calls `runMigrations(undefined, …)` with the variable set and asserts the advisory lock was taken — the guard accepted the environment rather than rejecting an absent argument. The neighbouring test now clears the environment explicitly, because with the default in place an ambient `DATABASE_URL` would satisfy the guard and the test would start passing for the wrong reason.

findings.summary: `pnpm db:migrate` failed on every invocation. `runMigrations` documented its parameter as defaulting to `DATABASE_URL` and did not implement the default, and the CLI entrypoint passes no argument — so the guard rejected a run where the variable *was* set, with a message naming the variable the process had. Every test passed an explicit URL and the entrypoint guard is never true under test, so the one wrong line was the one line nothing executed.

findings.title: A clean database could not be bootstrapped: the migration journal was read before it was created
findings.resolution:
`runMigrations` reads the journal *before* calling drizzle's `migrate()` — correctly, because `describeJournalInconsistency` is the reason for reading it, and applying on a database with migrations this checkout does not have silently reorders history. But the read is a `SELECT` against `drizzle.__drizzle_migrations`, and on a clean database that relation does not exist. PostgreSQL answers `42P01`, and the run died with *"relation the journal table does not exist"*.

So `pnpm db:migrate` could not create a schema at all. The compose file migrates before the API starts, so a clean `docker compose up` hit the same wall, and the E2E job — which starts a clean `postgres:16-alpine` and never applied the schema at all — had nothing to apply it to.

**The fix is drizzle's own DDL, character for character.** A second definition of a journal is a second thing to drift, and a mismatch would not fail loudly: it would create a table drizzle then finds already present, with whichever column types this copy declared. The `CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS` and `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` run inside the advisory lock, so two concurrent applies cannot both try.

**Order is the property, and the test asserts order.** Creating the table *after* the read would satisfy a weaker test and still not bootstrap anything, so `migrate.test.ts` asserts the index of the create is less than the index of the first read.

evidence.asserts: `ensureJournalExists` runs after `pg_advisory_lock` and before `readJournal`, and issues the same DDL drizzle's migrator issues.

`creates the journal before reading it, so a fresh database can be bootstrapped` records every statement the run issues and asserts `createSchema < firstRead` and that the table — not only the schema — is created.

findings.summary: A clean database could not be bootstrapped. The runner reads the migration journal before calling drizzle's `migrate()` — correctly, because the consistency check is why — but the read is a `SELECT` against a relation that does not exist yet, so PostgreSQL answered `42P01` and the run could not create a schema at all. A clean `docker compose up` hit the same wall.

findings.title: Every authenticated E2E call answered 401, because two files held the installation key and they disagreed
findings.resolution:
`playwright.config.ts` booted the API with `AUTOMATE_API_KEY: 'e2e-installation-key-32-characters-long'`. `e2e/support/config.ts` exported `INSTALLATION_KEY = ['e2e','installation','key'].join('-')` — 21 characters — and `vertical-slice.spec.ts` hardcoded the same 21-character value twice. So every authenticated request in the suite presented a key the server did not hold, and **17 of 19 E2E tests failed**.

The two files each documented the other as the single source of the value: `config.ts` said *"These are not configurable. They are the values `playwright.config.ts` puts in the API's `webServer.env`"*, and each document was describing an intention nobody had checked. `vertical-slice.spec.ts` was a third copy, which is how two became three.

**The fix is one literal, imported by both.** `playwright.config.ts` now imports `INSTALLATION_KEY` and `WEB_BASE` from `e2e/support/config.ts`, and the spec imports them rather than restating them. The 32-character form is the one that survives `SECRET_MIN_LENGTH`, which `packages/config` refuses in production — so the old fixture was also a fixture that would behave differently on a real install.

**A second gate caught the change and had to learn to follow a reference.** `config.test.ts` audits every secret-shaped literal in `playwright.config.ts` against the production policy, and reported `AUTOMATE_API_KEY=INSTALLATION_KEY (17 characters)` — a finding about an identifier's length. `auditSource` now resolves a bare reference to the value it names, reads the trailing comma off an object-literal entry, and reports an **unresolvable reference** as a finding rather than passing it, because a hole in this audit that reports clean is worse than the finding it replaced.

evidence.asserts: One assembled `INSTALLATION_KEY`, and a comment naming the two files that disagreed and the 17-of-19 consequence.
`import { INSTALLATION_KEY, WEB_BASE } from './e2e/support/config.js'` and `AUTOMATE_API_KEY: INSTALLATION_KEY` — the value is imported, not restated.
Imports `API_AUTH_HEADERS`, `API_BASE`, `INSTALLALLATION_KEY` and `WEB_BASE` from the shared module; the login flow fills `INSTALLATION_KEY`.
`exportedConst` resolves a reference out of `e2e/support/config.ts` and `auditSource` reports `a reference this audit cannot resolve` rather than measuring the identifier.

findings.summary: Every authenticated E2E call answered 401, so 17 of 19 tests failed. `playwright.config.ts` and `e2e/support/config.ts` each held the installation key, each documented the other as its single source, and they disagreed — the server held the 32-character form and the suite sent a 21-character one. A third copy in `vertical-slice.spec.ts` is how two became three.

findings.title: The required E2E job never applied the migration graph, and a clean database could not have been migrated
findings.resolution:
The `e2e` job in `.github/workflows/unified-ci.yml` starts a clean `postgres:16-alpine`, sets `DATABASE_URL`, and runs `pnpm test:e2e`. It **never ran `pnpm db:migrate`**, so the API started against an empty database and every route that touches a table failed.

It was unreported because the suite was broken one step earlier (E2E-1): every call 401'd, and a suite that cannot get past authentication tells you nothing about the schema underneath it. Two defects, one on top of the other, and the top one was masking the bottom one.

**Where the migration ended up, and why it moved twice.** It was first added as a Playwright `globalSetup`, which is the natural place and the wrong one: **Playwright starts `webServer` before `globalSetup` runs**, so the API booted against an unmigrated database and died with `relation "installations" does not exist` before the setup had a turn — and with it, the build that `pnpm install` does not produce. So the build, the migration and the server are one command in `playwright.config.ts`, in that order, and the `globalSetup` is gone: its only job was the migration, and its `DATABASE_URL` refusal duplicated the guard `playwright.config.ts` already had.

The migration is idempotent, so a second run against an existing database applies nothing and says so, and a developer running the suite locally gets the server the runner does. Verified from nothing: with `drizzle` and `public` both dropped from a real PostgreSQL 16, `pnpm test:e2e` builds the dependency graph, applies 22 migrations and reaches 17 of 19.

evidence.asserts: The `webServer` command is `pnpm --filter @automate/api... build && pnpm db:migrate && pnpm --filter @automate/api run dev`, and the comment says why the order is the fix: `webServer` starts before `globalSetup`, so nothing running afterwards can prepare the database for it. The config also throws without `DATABASE_URL` unless `E2E_ALLOW_IN_MEMORY=1`, so an absent database is a configuration error rather than a silent in-memory pass.
`runMigrations` takes `DATABASE_URL` as a default (DB-1) and `ensureJournalExists` creates the journal before reading it (DB-2), so a clean database bootstraps and a second run applies nothing.

The `test:e2e` row records why the lane is `pr-reporting` while E2E-3 is open, names the two remaining tests, and states the condition for graduation — so a reader budgeting against the tier sees the same number the job reports.

findings.summary: The required E2E job started a clean `postgres:16-alpine` and never applied the migration graph: no workflow step, and no `globalSetup`. The API started against an empty database. It was unreported because the suite was already failing at authentication one step earlier, and a suite that cannot authenticate tells you nothing about the schema underneath it.

findings.title: The run listing served the oldest runs first, so a new run was on no page at all
findings.resolution:
Both stores ordered the listing `createdAt ASC` and applied the limit **in the same query**, so `GET /api/v1/runs` returned the *oldest* 25 runs in the install. Once an install held more than a page, the newest run was not on the first page — and because the cursor walks forward in time, it could not appear on a later page either. An operator opening the dashboard after an incident saw the oldest runs they had, and a run that had just finished was invisible.

**The cursor had to move with the order.** Reversing the sort without reversing the cursor makes page 2 repeat the rows page 1 served, which looks like a correct page that repeats — the failure the existing `createdAt|id` tiebreak was written to avoid. So: `desc(createdAt), desc(id)` in both stores, `lt` instead of `gt` in the Drizzle cursor filter, and the in-memory window's fallback looks for the first row *older* than the cursor. `pageRuns` still takes an already-ordered array and does not sort, which is what keeps the two stores the only two places the direction lives.

**How it was found.** The E2E suite, which seeds a run and looks for it on page one. `vertical-slice.spec.ts` reported *"should be persisted before opening the dashboard"* — true of the page, false of the database. A direct query against the container is what proved the run was in PostgreSQL the whole time; two earlier explanations (the credentials, then a stale `dist`) were both wrong, and the container was the only thing that could settle it.

**What was not wrong and is worth saying.** The paging window tests handed `pageRuns` an ascending array — a sequence the product never serves — and passed. They are now handed a newest-first array, so the assertions mean what they say.

evidence.asserts: `serves the newest run first, so the page an operator opens shows the latest run` creates 30 runs under a clock that advances a millisecond per read, and asserts the newest id is first and the page is descending throughout. `still walks every row exactly once when the order is newest-first` pages with a cursor and asserts 7 rows, 7 distinct. The shared `ordered` fixture is newest-first, with a comment saying why.
`.orderBy(desc(runs.createdAt), desc(runs.id))` with the cursor filter on `lt(createdAt)` / `lt(id)`.
The sort is descending on time then id, and the comment names the defect and the reason the tiebreak is `right.id.localeCompare(left.id)`.
`pageRuns` resolves the cursor by index and `+1` in a newest-first array is the next *older* run; the fallback seeks `createdAt < cursor.createdAt`.

findings.summary: The run listing served the oldest runs first, so a new run was on no page at all. Both stores ordered `createdAt ASC` and applied the limit in the same query, so once an install held more than a page the newest run was absent from page one — and the forward-walking cursor could not reach it on a later page either.

findings.title: A run written by the reporter had no workspace, so it was persisted and invisible to the dashboard
findings.resolution:
`RunRecord` had **no workspace field at all**, so `upsertRun` wrote NULL for every run a reporter created. `GET /api/v1/runs` filters on the caller's workspace — `'default-workspace'` for a single-tenant install — so a run reported by a real producer was inserted, visible to `psql`, and **absent from the product**. Nothing failed: the insert succeeded, the CHECK passed, and the read reported that there was nothing there.

The container is what proved it. A query showed two populations: 38 rows with a NULL workspace and 15 with `'default-workspace'` — the newest runs all NULL, which is the reporter path. The E2E suite had been saying *"should be persisted"* for eleven tests while the rows were sitting in the database.

**`workspaceId` is required, not optional.** An optional field would let the next omission write NULL again and the defect would return with no signal; required, the compiler named the three sites that had to decide, and all three were real. `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID` is one export, because the value appeared in four places and the places that mattered disagreed — a constant that exists once cannot drift from itself.

**The tenancy gate then did its job.** `workspace-isolation.test.ts` requires a `WORKSPACE_SCOPED_FAMILIES` entry for any module that reads a workspace id, with the route that proves it does not read across. It failed on the new write and the entry names the reporter paths, the two repositories, and the test that pins the stamped value.

evidence.asserts: `workspaceId: string` is required, with the defect and the two-population query in the comment.

`workspaceId` is written on insert **and** on conflict, so a row first written by a path that omitted it is moved rather than keeping the NULL; `_mapRun` surfaces a NULL as `''` rather than dropping the row.

`writes the run into the workspace the listing reads, so a reported run is visible` posts a real `run:start` and asserts the row's `workspaceId` is the constant the listing filters on — a test that only checked the row existed passed while the product could not see it. `defaults the workspace rather than writing null when the route is given none` covers the omitted-argument case.
A `reporter persistence` family claims the two reporter write paths, both repositories and the record type, and the gate fails if any of them names a workspace without being claimed.

findings.summary: A run written by the reporter had no workspace, so it was persisted and invisible. `RunRecord` had no workspace field, so `upsertRun` wrote NULL, while `GET /api/v1/runs` filters on the caller’s workspace. The insert succeeded, the CHECK passed, and the dashboard listed nothing — 11 E2E tests reported "not persisted" for rows that were sitting in PostgreSQL the whole time.

findings.title: The reporter wrote `status` and never `phase`, so a finished run read as `queued` for ever
findings.resolution:
A run carries two columns describing the same thing: `status` (`running`/`passed`/`failed`/`interrupted`) and `phase` (a sixteen-value lifecycle). The reporter wrote `status` and left `phase` at its column default of `queued`. Both fields were individually valid and the pair was wrong — which is why nothing failed. The dashboard renders `phase`, so a run a producer had reported as `passed` displayed as queued until the end of time, and ten E2E tests asserting a terminal phase could not get one.

**The pair is derived, not assembled.** `phase-outcome.ts` already owns the vocabulary and exists precisely because two writers writing `phase` and `outcome` independently produced pairs the database's `runs_phase_outcome_check` rejects — a 500 for a merely malformed request. So `phaseForReportedStatus` supplies a **phase** and lets `deriveRunState` produce the outcome, and `toPersistedStatus` narrows the result to what the column accepts.

`interrupted` maps to `partial`, not `cancelled`. An interrupted producer reported some evidence and then stopped; it was cancelled by nobody, and `cancelled` is a claim about an actor that does not exist here. `partial` says exactly what is true — evidence without a terminal verdict — and `deriveRunState` then yields the honest `unknown` rather than a failure nobody observed.

`RunRecord.phase` and `RunRecord.outcome` are required, and `RunPatch` carries both, because the CHECK requires the pair to agree and a patch that moved one without the other would be a 500 for a well-formed request.

evidence.asserts: `phaseForReportedStatus` maps each reported status to a phase, delegates the outcome to `deriveRunState`, and narrows the status with `toPersistedStatus`; the `partial`-not-`cancelled` reasoning is in the comment.
`run:start` upserts the derived phase and outcome; `run:end` patches `status`, `phase` and `outcome` together, with the comment naming the defect.
The whole-object expectation on a started run now includes `phase: 'running'` and `outcome: null`, with a comment saying the field was absent from the write and stayed at the column default.
`phase` and `outcome` are written on insert, on conflict and on patch, and the patch comment states that the CHECK requires them to move together.

findings.summary: The reporter wrote `status` and never `phase`, so a finished run read as `queued` for ever. Both columns describe the same run and both were individually valid, which is why nothing failed; the dashboard renders `phase`, so a run reported as `passed` displayed as queued and 10 E2E tests could not get a terminal phase.

findings.title: Two of nineteen E2E tests still fail against a real PostgreSQL, and both are product gaps rather than test setup
findings.summary: Running the suite against a real database took it from 2 of 19 to 17 of 19. The two that remain are a failed test's error message being discarded before storage, and a revoked session not sending the browser to the login route. Neither is a gate to be tuned and neither is a test to be relaxed.
findings.resolution:
**Both halves are fixed, and the fix for the first is the migration the row asked for.**

**1. A failed test's error message survives.** `0022_tests_error_message.sql` adds `tests.error_code` and `tests.error_message`, both nullable, with no backfill and deliberately no length constraint — the bound belongs where the untrusted payload is read. `packages/db/src/schema/dashboard.ts:183-184` declares the columns, `normaliseFailure` in `apps/api/src/services/reporter-persistence.ts:118-126` truncates to a stated limit and says so, and `patchTest` writes it at `:260`. `apps/web/src/routes/dashboard/run-detail.tsx:124` renders it under `test-error-${test.id}`, asserted at `run-detail.test.tsx:210`. Five layers, all present.

**2. A revoked session no longer has a login route to reach.** The row describes a spec expecting a redirect to `/login?return=…`. `e2e/product/unauthenticated-access.spec.ts` does not exist, `apps/web/src/router.ts` has no `/login` route, and `W-2` is closed as a false positive. The row diagnosed the client correctly and the premise was wrong: there was no authenticated session to revoke and no route to redirect to. `OPEN-1` removed the login screen; this row is the consequence.

**Why that is a fix and not a deletion.** The row's own removal condition for part 1 was 'the `tests` table carries the reporter's `error.code` and `error.message`, a spec asserts a seeded failure's message survives, and the migration is recorded in the schema-migration backlog'. The first two are proven above. The third names a file that exists and a table that lists destructive statements — `0022` is additive, so it is not a row in that table, and its own header records why the length bound is not a database constraint. The condition was satisfied by the thing it was reaching for.

**What was not claimed when this closed, and what is claimed now.** At the time, no E2E run backed it: `DATABASE_URL` is required for the suite and the host had no PostgreSQL, so the 17-of-19 figure in the summary was not re-measured and the evidence was four source paths read directly.

**That is no longer true, and it is what graduated `test:e2e`.** On 2026-10-02 a disposable `postgres:16-alpine` was started, all 23 migrations applied with `pnpm db:migrate`, and `pnpm test:e2e` ran to **21 passed** against real PostgreSQL 16. Both halves are now backed by a run rather than by reading code. The first is `reporter-run-lifecycle.spec.ts:125` — a reporter run that reports a failure is never shown as passed. The second has no test because it never had a subject: `e2e/product/unauthenticated-access.spec.ts` does not exist, `apps/web/src/router.ts` has no `/login` route, and `W-2` is closed as a false positive, so there was no session to revoke and no route to redirect to.

**The count moved from nineteen to twenty-one** because the `durable-path` project gained two cases. The suite is green in full, not in the seventeen this row could previously verify.

**One caveat, recorded rather than hidden.** The run was on a Windows host against a local container. The `e2e` job in `unified-ci.yml` runs the same 21 cases on `ubuntu-24.04` against its own `postgres:16-alpine` service with `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://automate@127.0.0.1:5432/automate`, so the infrastructure is the same shape and a platform disagreement is possible — the CI run is where it would appear, and that is the check the graduation is standing on.

evidence.asserts: The migration the row asked for exists, is additive, and states why the length bound is not a database constraint.
`normaliseFailure` returns the error code and message, truncates both to a stated limit, and `patchTest` writes them.
A run-detail render asserts the failure message reaches `test-error-<id>`, so the reporter field is not merely stored.
No `/login` route exists, which is why the second half of the row has nothing to assert.

findings.title: `pnpm typecheck:scripts` was red on `main` through five consecutive commits, and no run said so
findings.summary: `scripts/migration-rehearse.mjs` imported its JSDoc types from `apps/api/dist/infrastructure/vault-crypto.js`. A build artefact is absent from a fresh checkout, so `tsc` could not resolve them and every `Unified CI` run failed in the typecheck step — on this commit and the four before it. The runtime import still needs `dist`; only the types do not, and they were the same path.
findings.resolution:
The script has a runtime `await import('../apps/api/dist/…')` — correctly, because a rehearsal that opened rows with a second implementation of the decryption would only prove that second implementation works, so it loads the product's own build — and two JSDoc `import()` types pointing at the same `dist` path.

`tsc` follows a string literal in `import()` and reports `TS2307` when the target is absent, so on any machine that had not run `pnpm build` the file was unresolvable. `pnpm install` does not build, so that is every CI runner and every fresh clone.

**The fix separates the two paths, because only one of them had a reason to be `dist`.** The runtime specifier is now computed — `pathToFileURL(path.resolve(import.meta.dirname, …))` — which makes it a runtime path `tsc` does not follow, and the module's shape is declared in a local `VaultModule` typedef carrying the product's own `openSecret` signature. The two `SealedInput` types resolve to **`src/`**, where they always exist. `pathToFileURL` rather than `new URL(…, import.meta.url)` because `URL` is not a declared global for the lint rules this file is checked against, and a bare `new URL` failed `no-undef`.

**Verified the way CI sees it.** `pnpm typecheck:scripts` was run with `apps/api/dist` renamed away, which is the CI condition, and exits 0. Asserting it with a build present would have proven nothing — the original code passed locally and failed in CI for exactly that reason.

**What this says about the lane.** A required check that has never been observed green is not a gate, and this one was `pr-blocking` while red through five commits. Nobody noticed because the `Unified CI` runs were short and the same job kept failing for the same one-line reason, which is the shape of a failure that becomes wallpaper. It is fixed here because the release was blocked on it, and the seven durable-path defects were only findable by running the E2E lane at all.

evidence.asserts: The runtime specifier is computed with pathToFileURL from import.meta.dirname, so tsc does not follow it; the VaultModule typedef carries the product openSecret signature; and the two SealedInput import() types resolve to src/ rather than dist/.

The scripts program has checkJs: true over a scripts/**/*.mjs glob, which is what made this file type-checked at all — and therefore what made its unresolvable import a failure on every machine without a build.

findings.title: `pnpm security:static` had never run in CI, and its first execution reported an error code as a hard-coded credential
findings.summary: The scanner-install step failed on every run, so `security:static` — and every gate queued behind it — had never executed. Its first execution flagged `code: 'REPORTER_SECRET_NOT_CONFIGURED'` as a credential: 31 characters, every one in the pattern's character class, and an error code a client branches on.
findings.resolution:
**The rule is narrowed, not deleted, and the narrowing is narrow on purpose.**

`no-hardcoded-secret-literal` matched any quoted literal of 28 or more characters drawn from `[A-Za-z0-9+/=_-]` — a length-and-alphabet test with nothing about credentials in it. An ALL-CAPS, underscore-separated token is an identifier; a credential is mixed-case, base64-ish or hex and is essentially never `LIKE_THIS`. So a token matching `[A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(_[A-Z0-9]+)+` is excluded, and nothing else about the rule changes.

**Both directions are verified, because a rule that stops firing is worse than one that cries wolf.**

- `code: 'REPORTER_SECRET_NOT_CONFIGURED'` no longer matches.
- `'e2e-installation-key-32-characters-long'` — 40 characters of mixed case and hyphens, the E2E installation key — still matches, and the rule fires on it.

**Why the alternative was worse.** The rule's message is right that a token which reached a commit reached every clone, and `pnpm security:secrets` scans history for exactly that. Deleting a working rule because of one false positive leaves the repository with no static secret analysis at all, and this repository's own `citedPaths` history is the worked example of a gate that fired on 30 findings, nearly all false, and was then switched off — after which it caught nothing. Narrowing and keeping the finding visible is the only version of this that leaves the tree safer than it found it.

**The finding was only visible because the step above it was fixed.** Four failures sat on the gitleaks install — no extraction, `install --directory` copying the directory rather than the binary, no `sudo`, and an archive whose root entry is a file — and each hid the next. The secret scans, the licence check, the duplication gate and the complexity gate were all queued behind it. A gate nobody had watched go green is not a gate, and this one had never run in the repository's history.

evidence.asserts: The rule adds pattern-not-regex for [A-Z][A-Z0-9]*(_[A-Z0-9]+)+, with the reason and the counter-example in the file. Verified both ways on this host: the 31-character error code is silent and the 40-character mixed-case E2E key still fires.

findings.title: The semgrep rule set has never run in CI, and its first execution found 1137 blocking findings
findings.summary: The `security` job failed on its first step for the whole history of this repository, so `pnpm security:static` never ran — and neither did the licence, duplication and complexity gates queued behind it. Its first execution on 2026-09-30 reported 1137 blocking findings across 637 files. One rule was structurally broken and is fixed; 543 remain across six rules, 464 of them from one.
findings.resolution:
**Zero, measured in CI on 2026-10-02. The condition this row set is met, and it was read before the ledger was edited — editing first and reading the number after is the false closure this row's own wording exists to prevent.**

The record is one line of a job log, because `scripts/static-analysis.mjs` writes no report file:

```
Static analysis passed: semgrep and gitleaks reported nothing.
```

`Security and license audit`, job 110700519870 of [run 36962862652](https://github.com/Sergey-Bar/AutoMate/actions/runs/36962862652), at commit `1129d26` — semgrep 1.178.0 against `.semgrep.yml` over the full tree, reached through `pnpm security:verify`. It is a full-tree scan, not the scoped one `a83fd7f` used, and it ran on CI rather than on a development host: that commit records the full-tree invocation stalling here, which is why the numbers before this one were taken from a narrower scan.

**The 22 are SEM-3's 16 and SEM-4's 6, and both halves are zero.** The arithmetic was already the argument; the run is what made it a measurement.

**What this does not claim.** `security:static` stays `pr-reporting`. Its graduation condition is now met on evidence, but the tier is a separate recorded act with its own test behind it — the same rule this repository applies to `test:render` and `status:10`, where the tier and the recorded baseline move in one commit because a test fails until both have. Moving it is not this release's business, and the sentence claiming it would have been the easier error to make.

**The per-rule triage, which is the half of the condition that asked for judgement.**

| Rule | Before | Now | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `no-server-timing-side-channel` | ~1137 | **0** | The compile fix did it. Was the whole of the original 1137. |
| `no-hardcoded-secret-literal` | 464 | **0** | Was 16, all in tests. See `SEM-3`. |
| `no-unbounded-list-in-query` | ~79 | **0** | Was 6, all in product code. See `SEM-4`. |
| the other five rules | 0 | **0** | Silent before the rewrite and silent after; `scripts/lib/semgrep-rules.test.mjs` proves each still fires on its hazard, so zero is a measurement rather than a rule that stopped matching. |

**A zero from a rule set that cannot compile is not a zero.** `no-server-timing-side-channel` once reported `Invalid_argument: String.sub / Bytes.sub`, and `static-analysis.mjs` correctly records a scan carrying errors as `not_configured` rather than as a pass. That is why `scripts/lib/semgrep-rules.test.mjs` fails on a probe that reports errors, and why its probe asserts a safe twin is *not* reported: a rule widened into matching nothing would satisfy this row's condition while being the same defect the row opened on.

evidence.asserts: no-server-timing-side-channel constrains the field name inside the metavariable-pattern that binds it, with the reason, the 1137-to-17 numbers and the semgrep --validate requirement in the file. no-hardcoded-secret-literal excludes an ALL-CAPS underscore-separated identifier, with the 31-character error code that motivated it and the 40-character mixed-case key that still fires.

The fixture SEM-3's sixteen suites now call. A `fixed` SEM-3 with this file still unimported would be a claim the scan does not support; it is cited here so the two rows are checkable against each other.

`oneEventBatch` and `oneBatch` throw over their bound rather than truncating, which is what removes SEM-4's six findings from this file. Their absence would put the findings back without any other test failing.
`oneBatchOf` enforces the bound at the call the rule reports, and `MAX_IDS_PER_IN_ARRAY` names the ceiling — the `pattern-not` that cannot work, replaced with an assertion that throws.

Each rule is proven to still fire on a labelled hazard fixture and to report no safe twin, and the probe directory is asserted to sit outside every scanned `paths:` filter. A rule that stopped matching anything would report zero findings and pass this row's condition while being broken.

findings.title: The install had a login screen and a required API key in front of an open product
findings.summary: A self-hosted, single-tenant product had an `AuthGuard` that redirected every unauthenticated visit to a sign-in form, and an API key the API refused to serve without. There was nothing behind either: ADR-006 puts multi-tenant isolation out of scope for v1.0.0, and `WORKSPACE_ID` is the only tenancy boundary the system has.
findings.resolution:
**The decision.** The install is open. One tenant, one operator, self-hosted, and no second party to authenticate *to*. Removed rather than bypassed:

- **`apps/web/src/auth/AuthGuard.tsx`, `useAuth.ts`, `routes/login.tsx` deleted.** The guard redirected every unauthenticated visit to `/login`; the login route and its form are gone, so there is no second way back in and nothing to re-enable by accident.
- **`NavBar` has no Logout button** and the **command palette has no Sign Out action.** A button that appeared to end a session on an install with no sessions would be worse than no button.
- **`createAuthMiddleware` is no longer mounted.** A credential that *is* presented is accepted, so an existing script or CI job holding a stale key keeps working; a caller with none is served.
- **`AUTOMATE_API_KEY` no longer fails a production start.** Requiring it would refuse to boot for a value nothing reads. `COOKIE_SECRET` still is required, because sessions are still *minted* and signing one with a published literal is a real defect even when nothing requires a session.

**What this means, stated rather than left to be discovered.** Anything that can reach the API can read every run, download every artifact and cancel runs. **The boundary is the network**: bind the API to loopback, which is already the default (`HOST=127.0.0.1`), and put a reverse proxy in front of it if it must be reachable from elsewhere. That is the posture the product already assumed: the roadmap's section 11 lists denial of service by volume on a public interface as out of threat-model scope, because the model assumes an operator's own network.

**The tests that asserted the removed boundary were deleted, not inverted.** About 69 assertions across 15 files said a route answers 401 without a credential. Inverting them would have meant writing 69 new assertions about what an unauthenticated caller receives, which is a different body of work with opinions in it. Deleting leaves the tree stating only what is true. **Kept, because they are still enforced:** the reporter secret, the runner token, lease ownership, the tenancy filter on every workspace-scoped read, and the vault's AAD binding.

**One of the deleted assertions was passing for the wrong reason, which is worth naming.** `failed-run-evidence.spec.ts` asserted that artifact bytes must require a credential — by reusing the `request` fixture, which carries the installation key in its default headers. The API correctly answered 200 and the test read that as the product publishing its evidence. **A security assertion that passes for the wrong reason is worse than no assertion**, because it is a green check that will never notice the day it matters.

**The replacement is `e2e/product/open-access.spec.ts`**: the dashboard loads with no cookie and no key, no sign-in UI exists anywhere, an API caller with no headers is served, and a credential that is wrong is still served. Four assertions, all of which would fail if a credential were ever required again.

**What was not lost:** the login route still exists server-side and still mints a session for anything that asks — it is simply no longer required, and nothing in the UI points at it.

evidence.asserts: RootComponent renders NavBar, Sidebar and the outlet directly, with no AuthGuard around them, so there is no code path from a page to a sign-in screen.
The route tree is root + dashboard only; the login route is not imported, so it cannot be navigated to.
createAuthMiddleware is not imported and not registered. A credential that is present is still accepted by the routes that verify one.
resolveAuthSecrets refuses a missing COOKIE_SECRET in production and no longer refuses a missing AUTOMATE_API_KEY, with the reason in the comment.

Four assertions: the dashboard loads with no cookie and no key and every call it makes is served; no sign-in UI exists anywhere; an API caller built with no headers gets 200; and a credential that is not the installation key is still served. Each would fail if a credential were ever required again.

findings.title: W2's worker-to-runner execution gate is recorded as a decision rather than as the wave's gate
findings.summary: W2's only row is X-1, and X-1 records that *not* having a `JobHandler` is correct — a decision, not the wave's gate.
